bad: The public explorer is deliberately aggregates-only: the Space README states it uses only the processed tables under data/clean/ and contains no raw clinical data, private preprocessing code, credentials or identifying metadata — so its results cannot be reproduced or audited end-to-end from the public Space, and the underlying benchmark code and data are not part of what is published there. It is a static Space (sdk: static) serving an explorer, not a runnable harness.
took: The aggregates-only publication pattern — benchmark explorers publish processed result tables, never raw data — as a precedent for what any public wiki statistics page may contain.
didnt: Corroboration — its aggregates-only publication pattern (processed result tables in public, raw data and preprocessing kept out) confirms the boundary for any public wiki statistics surface; the clinical benchmark itself is out of scope for a personal knowledge wiki and carries no licence for reuse. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PyVis Knowledge Graph From Markdown + KnowledgeGraphEditor (awacke1)
licence: MIT (PyVis Knowledge Graph From Markdown, as recorded in the deep dive)
good: Two HuggingFace Spaces confirming that markdown→graph works as a build step over files (PyVis renders a graph straight from markdown), plus an AI + Mermaid graph-editing variant.
bad: Demo-grade and dormant: both Space pages report the Space is sleeping due to inactivity, and both READMEs are metadata-only — title, SDK, app file and licence, with no usage documentation, evaluation, tests or maintenance information on either page. They are single-author demonstration Spaces (the PyVis one rendering a graph from markdown, the other an AI + Mermaid editor), not maintained tools with a documented interface.
took: Confirmation of the Lens architecture (graph as a build step over files, not a platform), and in-page Mermaid graphs as a zero-dependency graph surface for individual wiki pages.
didnt: Corroboration — the pair confirm from the wild that markdown-to-graph works as a build step over files rather than a platform (the Lens architecture), and that in-page Mermaid graphs serve as a zero-dependency graph surface for individual pages; neither Space is adopted as a component, as both are sleeping single-author demos with metadata-only documentation. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PaperClip
good: A tool "designed to support AI researchers in their daily work of reviewing papers… Serving as their 'second brain,' PaperClip allows researchers to effectively keep track of important details and findings" across ML/CV/NLP papers (tool page fully opened).
bad: The file records "The harvest is the card discipline (details + findings per paper, nothing else), not the hosted product."
took: Per-source "details and findings" cards as the atomic unit of a literature wiki — recorded as independent validation of the wiki's source-page pattern.
didnt: The hosted product itself.

name: JabRef
licence: MIT ("Free Open Source (MIT)" per AlternativeTo badges, as recorded in the deep dive)
good: "Bibliography reference manager. The native file format used by JabRef is BibTeX." The file records it is "the only catalogue item that fits the fit test as a tool rather than a platform — its database *is* a plain-text .bib file that can live in git next to the wiki".
bad: Scope is bibliography management only: the README's whole feature set is collecting, organising, citing and sharing BibTeX/BibLaTeX libraries, with no citation verification, claim checking or knowledge retrieval, and team work is offered through sync via a SQL database rather than the plain-text file alone. It is also a large separate Java/JavaFX desktop application (25,127 commits in the opened repo) that would have to be installed and maintained outside the wiki rather than living in it.
took: The .bib file in git as a citation-workflow store feeding the wiki's scholarly sources. Verdict recorded: "FOR US".
didnt: Adopt/build — the pattern only: a plain-text .bib file held in git beside the wiki as the citation-workflow store for scholarly sources; JabRef the desktop application is not taken as a system component, since our need is the file format and its git custody, not a second installed tool. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Magnemo
good: Governed agent memory in plain local markdown files where nothing becomes memory until the user approves it: agents get only four MCP tools (`retrieve`, `stage`, `bootpack`, `handoff`) and promotion is explicitly not one of them — the human promotes or rejects (rejection reason required) from the CLI. Every note carries provenance frontmatter (author, written, source, status, reviewed_by, supersedes, strength), search returns canonical promoted notes only, superseded notes archive with a forward link rather than deleting, partition walls are enforced per agent, and every promote/reject lands in an append-only `trust_ledger.jsonl`; it is Python 3.11+, zero dependencies, and `magnemo doctor` scans the package for any network module on every run. Additionally: "agents can only stage; promotion is never an agent tool; rejections recorded in an append-only Trust Ledger".
bad: The page labels it open beta and tells users to read KNOWN_LIMITS.md before trusting it with anything they cannot lose. Only the Claude Code client is marked tested; Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Cline, Continue, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI and Zed are all listed as untested, and the page shows 3 stars and 17 commits. Additionally: The file records it is young (17 commits, 3★, created 2026-09-16).
took: (a) Rejection-with-required-reason written to the ledger, (b) the bootpack pattern (canonical state + clearly-marked staged items + last handoff), (c) the provenance frontmatter field set incl. `strength`. Verdict recorded: "FOR US — patterns copyable under Apache-2.0.". Additionally: Cited under wave-2 governance: "these are its next refinements, one mechanism at a time" (for the gateway).
didnt: Adopt/build — rejection-with-required-reason written to an append-only trust ledger, the bootpack pattern (canonical state plus clearly-marked staged items plus last handoff) and the provenance frontmatter field set including strength, as refinements to our approval-gated memory and gateway design; patterns copyable under Apache-2.0. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Inspeximus
good: A self-correcting memory layer with key-based supersession: restating a stale value does **not** resurrect it (measured: inspeximus 100% correction retention / 0% resurrection; mem0 53.3% / 46.7%); `forget_subject()` leaves a signed content-free tombstone and `erasure_certificate()` lets a third party verify the erasure offline; a signed, hash-chained action ledger has its chain head outside the store so a tail cut is detected.
bad: Its guarantees are narrower than the headline: the README states the erasure proof covers this store only — not a vector index, prompt logs or backups — and that it is an integrity primitive, not a compliance certification. Supersession is keyed, so a statement written with no key is a new fact outside the guard, and re-ingesting a stale document without keys lets that text compete on its own merits. The README also says it is not the right tool for a hosted service with a dashboard, a knowledge graph over documents, or the highest conversational-recall scores.
took: Supersession-must-stick semantics for claim updates; tombstone + erasure certificates for the forget flow; anchoring the Black Box chain head outside the ledger file. Verdict recorded: "FOR US — the strongest correction/erasure semantics found in either wave; MIT."
didnt: Adopt/build — the semantics as patterns in our own store: supersession-must-stick on keyed claim updates, a signed content-free tombstone plus an offline-checkable erasure certificate for the forget flow, and anchoring the Black Box chain head outside the ledger file; the inspeximus package itself is not embedded as a dependency. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AsDecided (formerly Lore / rac-core)
good: A typed Markdown corpus with a deterministic engine and a read-only MCP server (299★, "the most mature project in this wave"); `decided validate` / `decided gate` run in CI and reject malformed artifacts, broken/ambiguous links, and references to superseded decisions; artifact IDs (RAC-…) survived the product rename, and the MCP door cannot write. Called "the closest published analogue to our wiki + Lens read path".
bad: Maintenance and scope limits are stated in its own README: the Governance section says AsDecided core is solo-maintained and supported on a best-effort basis, and the Architecture section says the retired Python engine is preserved only for historical review and is not maintained. Retrieval is deliberately deterministic with no embeddings, model call or hosted index, so there is no semantic/similarity recall — it serves typed decision artifacts, not general knowledge retrieval.
took: (a) A validator rule that fails on links *to superseded pages*, (b) durable artifact IDs independent of file names, (c) federation-with-pinned-parents. Verdict recorded: "FOR US — patterns copyable".
didnt: Adopt/build — the patterns only: a validator rule that fails on links to superseded pages, durable artifact IDs independent of file names, and federation with pinned parents; the AsDecided engine itself is not adopted, because our wiki plus its read-only Lens door already provide the typed-Markdown corpus and read path it would duplicate. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GENOME
good: An auditable memory layer with a bi-temporal fact log keyed to domain time, a deterministic re-derivable store, and a "memory firewall" tagging every write with an origin (`user` / `agent` / `tool` / `web`): web-origin content can never UPDATE or DELETE what the user said, even if a prompt-injected resolver asks; `explain_search()` reports why non-returned candidates were excluded. Additionally: Its "bi-temporal facts and 'memory firewall' origin classes" are recorded as bearing on the pending Phase-2 decision.
bad: The README itself states answer accuracy only ties Mem0 (no significant win in either direction), synthesis/consolidation was accuracy-neutral and hybrid/graph retrieval did not help, and the bi-temporal win is on synthetic TempBelief text with explicit dates — 'the edge shrinks on natural speech'. The core install is also heavy (numpy, sentence-transformers, scikit-learn, with PyTorch pulled in), and the project is small and new (10 stars, created 2026-07-14).
took: Per-record origin class + origin-bound write authority as a gateway rule, and explainable-recall output for Lens search results. Verdict recorded: "FOR US — patterns copyable under Apache-2.0.". Additionally: "Recorded as references only, under decisions already pending" — "reference, not recommendation".
didnt: Not recommended — pending Phase-2 (bi-temporal fields) decision.

name: Lians
good: Lians Guard, an evidence gate for agent work: evidence is typed (`measured_local`, `measured_ci`, `human_confirmed` can satisfy a completion criterion; `agent_attested` and `inferred_activity` cannot), an agent cannot promote its own checkpoint into a trusted class, checkpoints bind to current git state, and the terminal state is `READY FOR HUMAN REVIEW` — explicitly never a claim that work is correct or approved.
bad: The README's own status table puts the core value in preview: typed evidence and the evidence-backed task gate, Git-workspace fingerprinting, attested GitHub Actions intake and local Guard reporting are all 'Developer preview', automatic stale-evidence invalidation is 'In development', the shared team queue is only 'Planned', and cross-platform clean-install CI is still pending its first hosted run. Desktop builds remain release candidates pending signing/notarization.
took: The evidence-class taxonomy for the claim lifecycle and merge review — agent-attested filings stay context, measured/human-confirmed evidence opens gates. Verdict recorded: "FOR US — pattern copyable under Apache-2.0."
didnt: Adopt/build — the typed evidence-class taxonomy (measured_local / measured_ci / human_confirmed can open a gate; agent_attested / inferred_activity cannot) as a pattern for the claim lifecycle and merge review; the Guard product itself is not adopted, as it is still developer preview. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Zaxy
good: Event-sourced agent-team memory: "Eventloom" append-only JSONL with SHA-256 hash chains projected into a temporal knowledge graph; parent and worker sessions stay isolated until findings are reviewed and merged via approval packets. The file records its README publicly withdrew its LongMemEval claims (2026-07-03) with a detailed explanation — "a notable integrity signal".
bad: The file records "Capture is partly automatic (a watcher), which we would not take."
took: Approval packets for merge-back of worker findings and per-session log sharding. Verdict recorded: "FOR US — patterns copyable under MIT; take the log + merge discipline, not the auto-capture."
didnt: The auto-capture (a watcher).

name: WhiteMagic
good: Local-first governed memory over MCP with a hash-chained audit ledger plus signed continuity receipts: a handoff between sessions produces a receipt bundle a stateless verify endpoint (or offline check) can validate; conversation capture is explicit tool calls only, never automatic.
bad: The file records it is "very new, single-author, open alpha" (805 commits, 0★).
took: Signed handoff receipts for the Mehmed ↔ Grok/Hark filings flow. Verdict recorded: "FOR US — pattern copyable under MIT; the project itself is alpha — borrow the receipt design, not the dependency."
didnt: The dependency itself (alpha) — receipt design only.

name: Personal Understanding
good: Verbatim-first personal memory: the full message is stored byte-for-byte with SHA-256 + timestamp + session id, immutable, and everything derived is recomputable; a five-layer fact taxonomy (verbatim fact / user's evaluation / user's interpretation / model hypothesis / unconfirmable) is kept permanently separate, model guesses stay `candidate` forever and never promote to fact, and its semantic audit scans for a summary posing as a verbatim quote, a hypothesis quietly promoted, and misattribution. Called "the closest doctrinal match to our raw/wiki split found in either wave".
bad: A very young, small project (3 stars, created 2026-08-30) whose README is primarily in Chinese and whose design notes document a history of live incidents it was patched against — a classifier locking personal content out of the archive, undated records silently buried by time decay, and a duplicate-archiving accident. The README presents no benchmark evaluation of its own recall quality.
took: (a) The five-layer taxonomy as a refinement of claim status/confidence axes, (b) "summary posing as verbatim" and "hypothesis quietly promoted" as named lint-lane checks, (c) 180-day decay of unconfirmed imports to weight 0 (kept, searchable, never deleted). Verdict recorded: "FOR US".
didnt: Adopt/build — the five-layer fact taxonomy as a refinement of the claim status/confidence axes, the 'summary posing as verbatim' and 'hypothesis quietly promoted' semantic-audit checks as named lint lanes, and 180-day decay of unconfirmed imports to weight 0, as patterns for our raw/wiki split. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GEML
good: A block-addressed document layer that works on existing Markdown without conversion: `geml list/get/set` address one section/block/table cell instead of whole files, writes land as byte splices with whole-document re-validation (a bad write is refused before it lands), and every save appends a revision to a `.gemlhistory` sidecar, revertible per block or per file.
bad: The README calls GEML 'a small, young spec' and states there are two implementations but 'one author behind both — so there is still one set of opinions behind the spec'. Its primer has only been exercised on Claude, the Obsidian integration renders but is not in the community store, the browser viewer works only on Chrome, and several integrations (LangChain/LlamaIndex, Logseq marketplace listing) are reference implementations or not yet merged.
took: Section-addressed, validate-then-splice writes for gateway page edits, plus per-section history sidecars. Verdict recorded: "FOR US — pattern copyable under MIT; no format migration required, which is the point."
didnt: Adopt/build — section-addressed, validate-then-splice writes for gateway page edits plus per-section .gemlhistory-style history sidecars, as a pattern over existing Markdown with no format migration. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GoodMemory
good: Local-first auditable memory whose mechanism is a fail-closed benchmark-claim gate: a number may enter the public claims table only after a strict gate validates a committed declaration (complete coverage, zero execution failures, a no-memory baseline, deterministic scoring or an independent judge, a verified dataset licence, a reproducible run); self-attestation cannot open the boundary, and the project withdrew its LongMemEval claims publicly.
bad: By its own fail-closed gate, the current release has no claim to show: the README states GoodMemory 0.8.3 'has no current or versioned historical benchmark claim', no end-to-end benchmark runner is currently allowlisted so promotion is unavailable, LongMemEval is withdrawn pending a clean rerun, and it 'does not claim that GoodMemory has already proven an improvement in Codex coding outcomes'.
took: The claim-gate as a pattern for the wiki's own numbers (golden-set scores, survey counts): a figure enters only via a validated declaration, never via an agent's say-so. Verdict recorded: "FOR US — evidence-discipline pattern, MIT."
didnt: Adopt/build — the fail-closed benchmark-claim gate as a pattern for the wiki's own numbers (golden-set scores, survey counts): a figure enters only via a validated committed declaration, never via an agent's say-so; the memory product itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BaseMouse
good: Its transferable design is the context pack: a versioned export format (`basemouse.context_pack.v1`) carrying citations, provenance, document versions, checksums, relevance, truncation state and agent instructions, with per-signal retrieval annotation; writes are append-only revisions, DELETE is a tombstone, and PUT supports `expectedVersion`/If-Match optimistic locking.
bad: The file records "the repo is 6 commits / 0★ (created 2026-07-24) and is the open-core front of a paid hosted product" and "the product itself is NOT FOR US (hosted open-core, embryonic repo)".
took: The pack format only: a checksummed, versioned context-pack format for Lens Ask answers and gateway handoffs. Verdict recorded: "FOR US (the pack format only)".
didnt: The product itself — hosted open-core, embryonic repo.

name: Stellarjay
good: An append-only business fact store where every change is kept and attributed to the agent that made it (per-agent role tokens), history is tamper-evident, and rollback can undo everything one agent did in a time window, with a preview first; a write carrying a stale `expected_root` is refused.
bad: The licence restricts it to ideas only.
took: Per-agent rollback-with-preview as a gateway operation, and the root-hash write precondition — ideas only, re-implement. Verdict recorded: "FOR US (ideas) — AGPL, so re-implement only".
didnt: Code/copying rejected on licence grounds (AGPL-3.0).

name: obsidian-tc
good: A governed Obsidian vault server where every tool call runs one pipeline: auth → folder ACLs → read-only kill switch → HITL confirmation on destructive ops → audit log, with capabilities declared in separately gated scope classes (read / write / delete / bulk / execute / admin) and a 3-tool discovery facade over a 164-tool surface. Called "the closest scope pipeline to our gateway in the wild".
bad: The licence restricts it to ideas only; the file also records "the README notes headline figures were withdrawn in 2026-08 as unreproducible".
took: Ideas: distinct scope classes for delete, bulk and execute; a read-only kill switch as a first-class gateway control; the discovery-facade pattern. Verdict recorded: "FOR US (ideas) — AGPL".
didnt: Code/copying rejected on licence grounds (AGPL-3.0-only).

name: Brainy
good: A self-hosted shared brain over plain Markdown in Git: writes go through optimistic concurrency (`expected_git_commit`) plus a server-side write lock (concurrency-tested: 20 racing writers yield exactly 1 commit and 19 conflicts), per-space ACLs, agents propose changes and a human approves/rejects, and the append-only audit log is enforced by a database trigger; it adds atomic task claims with leases and resource claims over file areas.
bad: The file records it is "very young" (11 commits, 0★, created 2026-09-30) — "maturity is the caveat, not the design" — and AGPL + CLA means re-implement only.
took: Ideas: resource claims/leases for parallel agent work areas, and trigger-enforced audit appends the application layer cannot bypass. Verdict recorded: "FOR US (ideas)".
didnt: Code/copying rejected on licence grounds (AGPL + CLA).

name: Kage
good: Verified memory for coding agents: memory is plain Markdown (OKF-conformant), every memory cites the code it describes, and citations are verified at write time (a memory citing a nonexistent file is rejected on the spot), at recall time, and at diff time; memory whose cited files changed or vanished is withheld from recall until re-verified; `<private>…</private>` spans are never stored.
bad: The licence restricts it to ideas only, and the file records it is "aimed at code".
took: Citation-liveness as a recall gate — when a raw source changes, claims citing it are flagged/withheld until re-verified. Verdict recorded: "FOR US (ideas) — GPL, re-implement only".
didnt: Code/copying rejected on licence grounds (GPL-3.0).

name: Contextium
good: Its listing promised "versioned, permissioned knowledge", and the repo shows whole "workspaces" (agents + skills + libraries + workflows) loaded as a single context unit, plus restorable trash deletes.
bad: The file records "the open repo is an 8-commit, 0★ thin MCP client; the versioning/permissions live in the vendor's hosted backend (contextium.io) and are not inspectable here".
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: The whole product — verdict recorded: "NOT FOR US — hosted platform; recorded so the listing's promise isn't mistaken for a verified mechanism." ## From wave2-obsidian-plugins.md — Deep dives (the 20 PROMISING, repos opened and licences verified) Note recorded in the file: "this ecosystem is young — most of these projects were created in 2026 and have handfuls of stars. The value is in the patterns…; only #1, #5 and #17 have real adoption."

name: MCP Connector
good: Exposes a vault to MCP clients (Claude Desktop/Code, Cline) with semantic search, templates, file management and *gated* command execution; described as "the most-adopted MCP face over a markdown vault in the registry" (109★, pushed 2026-10-18).
bad: The README leads with a known issue: on Obsidian 1.14.4 the window can go blank while the plugin loads (roughly one load in ten, in the author's tests) with 'no workaround from the plugin side yet'. The 3.0.0 broker change is breaking — existing Codex entries return 401 until reinstalled — and the shared broker is hosted by an open vault, so closing that vault causes a short outage before another vault takes over.
took: Its command-gating model as the reference design for any MCP door over the wiki. Verdict recorded: "study first among the MCP entries; licence-clean and actively maintained."
didnt: Corroboration — its gated command execution, per-client tokens and tool profiles confirm the gating design for any MCP door over the wiki; it is a reference design only, being an Obsidian-plugin implementation rather than our gateway. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Atomic

bad: The file records it has been "quiet since May 2026" (3★, pushed 2026-05-13).

(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PackUp4AI

bad: The file records it is "dormant a year" (pushed 2025-10-24).

(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Nexus AI Chat Importer

bad: The licence restricts it to ideas only (GPL).

name: Auto LLM Wiki

Its optional auto-ingest (off by default) applies validated changes without opening the review modal, and the project is small (13 stars, 47 commits).

(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Cited

name: LightRAG
good: Dual-level retrieval — each query is split into low-level (entities/details) and high-level (themes) keywords, retrieving from both an entity/relation graph and text chunks, then fused — plus incremental graph updates, document deletion with automatic KG regeneration, native citation functionality and a pluggable reranker (40,226★, EMNLP 2025 paper).

didnt: The server product.

name: Microsoft GraphRAG

Additionally: The file records "the README now states the project is largely in maintenance mode (bug fixes and CVE work only)".
took: The community-summary methodology, re-implemented over the markdown graph (cluster the link graph → summarize each cluster → refresh on ingest) to automate standing summaries. Verdict recorded: "FOR US". name: Sleep-time Compute
good: Spending idle time precomputing answers to predictable likely questions cut test-time compute roughly 5× at equal accuracy, with gains growing when queries are predictable. It gives a research basis for making the nightly sweep anticipatory rather than only tidying what exists.
bad: The abstract's evidence is narrow and conditional: gains are shown on modified versions of two reasoning tasks (Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME), a Multi-Query variant of GSM-Symbolic, and one case study of an agentic SWE task. The paper itself finds the predictability of the user query is well correlated with efficacy, so precomputation spent on unpredictable queries is wasted compute rather than a saving.
took: Anticipatory sweep (sleep-time compute; sweep precomputes answers while idle) — built 2026-10-20 — source/inspiration: arXiv:2504.13171
didnt: Adopt/build — the anticipatory sweep: the nightly sweep precomputes answers to predictable likely questions while idle, because the paper gives a research basis (roughly 5x less test-time compute at equal accuracy on its tasks) for making the sweep anticipatory rather than only tidying what exists (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Generative Agents
licence: arXiv perpetual, non-exclusive licence 1.0 (rights retained by the authors; no Creative Commons licence shown at source)

took: The file records that our observations pass (built 2026-10-19, currently parked) is this paper's observation→reflection idea, and that our search already blends recency/relevance signals.
didnt: Corroboration — retrieval scored on recency, relevance and an importance score written at ingest, plus threshold-triggered reflection, confirms our recency/relevance search blend and the parked observation-to-reflection pass design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Reflexion
good: After failure the agent writes a short verbal reflection on why it failed, stores it in an episodic buffer, and conditions its next attempt on it — no weight updates. It lifted HumanEval pass@1 to 91% vs 80% without reflection.

The paper also notes it relies on the LLM's self-evaluation capabilities and has no formal guarantee of success.
took: Built (marathon records): Failure post-mortems as memory

name: MemoryBank
licence: arXiv perpetual, non-exclusive licence 1.0 (rights retained by the authors; no Creative Commons licence shown at source)

bad: The paper states no limitations section; its quantitative evaluation is observably narrow — 10 days of conversations with 15 virtual users simulated by ChatGPT and 194 probing questions, in a single AI-companion scenario — and Table 2 shows the open-source variants scoring far lower on correctness (0.418-0.479) and coherence than on retrieval accuracy (0.81-0.86).

good: Recall probability is modelled as halving every h days, with h learned by regression from features of the item and its history, beating fixed-schedule baselines. A new claim gets a sensible first re-check date from its own features before it has a verification history.
bad: The file flags this as the weakest verification in the file — the ACL Anthology page carries no abstract, so mechanism detail rests on the published record and spaced-repetition literature rather than a full-text read.

good: A careful modern replication confirms the classic curve and shows power-type functions fit better than a single exponential, with a visible bump around 24 hours consistent with a sleep/consolidation effect. It is the empirical grounding for FSRS's power-law choice and the nightly-consolidation rhythm.
bad: The file classifies it as evidence, not machinery — cited inside the FSRS entry rather than proposed as its own feature.

(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Lost in the Middle
licence: arXiv perpetual, non-exclusive licence 1.0 (rights retained by the authors; no Creative Commons licence shown at source)
good: Accuracy is U-shaped in a fact's position in long context — high at the start and end, degraded in the middle — so ordering retrieved evidence by this curve is a near-free quality gain. The file calls it "the single cheapest quality improvement in this lane".
bad: The paper is diagnostic rather than a remedy: it documents that model performance also degrades substantially as input contexts grow longer and that extended-context models are not necessarily better at using their context, and it offers evaluation protocols — ordering evidence by the U-shaped curve mitigates but does not restore middle-context accuracy.
took: The Lost in the Middle packing rule — Tier A; boarded in Round 3, Waiting — most relevant pages first or last in assembled context, never buried mid-pack (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Adopt/build — the context-packing rule for assembled evidence: most relevant pages first or last, never buried mid-pack, boarded Tier A in Round 3 (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Prioritized Experience Replay
good: Replaying experiences with probability proportional to TD error (surprise) beat uniform replay on 41 of 49 Atari games. As an ordering principle it allocates consolidation/re-verification budget by surprise density rather than uniformly or by age.
bad: The paper itself lists greedy prioritisation's failure modes: TD errors are only refreshed for transitions actually replayed, it is sensitive to noise spikes and bootstrapping error, and it focuses on a small subset of experience, losing diversity and becoming prone to over-fitting — hence its need for stochastic prioritisation and importance-sampling bias correction. Its evidence is also confined to DQN on the Atari 2600 suite.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — surprise-proportional ordering as a principle for allocating consolidation and re-verification budget in the wiki, as an idea only; the RL replay machinery itself has no place in a knowledge store. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Cognitive Offloading + the Google Effect (Risko & Gilbert; Sparrow, Liu & Wegner)
good: People who expect information to remain accessible remember where to find it instead of the information itself — the wiki functions as transactive memory, so index, standing questions and search quality are the product. A fact stored but not findable is functionally forgotten.
bad: Offloading decisions are metacognitive and error-prone, arguing for the wiki making its coverage visible rather than presenting a confident blank. Both source papers are paywalled at the journal and were read via PubMed abstracts.

It evaluates models and agents, not the citation fidelity, supersession or abstention of a personal corpus.

name: τ-bench / τ²-bench (pass^k)
good: Frozen benchmark task sets with pinned data, and the pass^k metric — a task counts only if all k independent trials succeed — measuring consistency rather than best-case luck. GPT-4o fell from under 50% pass^1 to under 25% pass^8 in retail.

took: Judge calibration + pass^k gates (calibration machinery built and run; certification refused — 0 of 100+ owner-labelled) — built 2026-10-20 — source/inspiration: τ-bench pass^k, as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md.
didnt: Adopt/build — pass^k consistency gating for judge and agent calibration, as already built in our programme; the retail/airline task sets themselves are out of scope for a personal LLM-wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Who Validates the Validators? (Shankar et al.)
licence: CC BY 4.0 (arXiv:2404.12272 — the arXiv page carries the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence icon)
good: A judge-calibration recipe: ≥100 human-labelled binary examples from real traces, deploy the judge only when true-positive and true-negative rates are both ≥ 0.8, and pin the judge prompt and model snapshot in git with weekly alignment checks. It names criteria drift as the central finding.
bad: The arXiv PDF timed out in the session and was not retried; content was verified via a secondary summary, and the file says the figures should be re-checked against the paper before being written into any schema.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — judge certification against owner-labelled examples with TPR/TNR gates: the dispositions record judge certification as parked for the owner, with calibration machinery built but certification refused because 0 of 100+ owner-labelled examples exist, so the recipe stays on the board pending the owner's labelling step (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AgentOps
licence: MIT (repo README 'Open Source' section and GitHub licence metadata — this resolves the earlier contradiction in favour of the repo itself over the hosted product's FAQ)
good: Session replay with step-by-step execution graphs, cost tracking, a large eval-benchmark catalogue, and prompt-injection/exfiltration detection. The session-replay pattern is worth borrowing for black-box ledger visualisation.
bad: The platform itself is hosted/commercial and its licence is unclear.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected — a hosted agent-observability platform duplicates our own session/ledger records and its normal use routes trace data to an external commercial service, against local-first custody; the session-replay pattern is already captured in the existing record, and no code or service was adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Hamel Husain's evaluation practice
good: Error analysis first: open-ended notes on ≥30 real traces recording the first failure in each, axial-coded into a counted failure taxonomy; judges calibrated against domain-expert labels with TPR/TNR reported. Zero cost, no licence issues.
bad: The method is deliberately manual and expert-bound: the page requires a domain-expert ('benevolent dictator') annotator, at least 30 traces annotated by hand before agent assistance and roughly 100 diverse traces to reach saturation, with the process revisited frequently. It supplies no automated metric, tool or licence terms, so it does not scale without sustained human labelling time.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — error-analysis-first practice (first-failure open coding axial-coded into a counted failure taxonomy, judges checked against expert labels) confirms our approach of building evaluations from real traces rather than generic platform metrics; there is no separate artefact to adopt (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026)
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International — OWASP GenAI project documents and OWASP project pages carry this licence)
good: A threat taxonomy specific to agents (ASI01–ASI10, including ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning) with attack scenarios and red-team test plugins, framed by a "Least-Agency" principle. A ready-made checklist for threat-modelling the gateway, Ask door and filings pipeline.
bad: It is guidance, not enforcement: the official page presents a peer-reviewed risk list with mitigations but no code, scanner, tests or conformance check, so every control still has to be implemented and verified locally. Coverage is also bounded by the ten consensus risks (ASI01–ASI10).
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning and the Least-Agency framing confirm the threat model already used for the gateway, Ask door and filings pipeline; it serves as checklist vocabulary, not as a build (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CaMeLS
licence: Apache-2.0 (companion code repository google-research/camel-prompt-injection, per its GitHub API licence metadata; the paper itself is arXiv:2503.18813)
good: The only prompt-injection defence in the lane with a design-level guarantee: a quarantined LLM extracts structured values from untrusted content but can never call tools, and every value carries provenance/capability tags enforced by an interpreter. It solved 77% of AgentDojo tasks with security guarantees vs 84% undefended.
bad: Its stated non-goal is text-to-text attacks that never touch control or data flow.
took: Built (marathon records): CaMeLS quarantine
didnt: Board — the full CaMeLS quarantined extractor: the dispositions record the datamarking layer as built and the extractor as 'documented as the next step, not built' and still quarantined under the hard gates, so the full build stays on the board pending its gate (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Spotlighting (Microsoft Research)
licence: CC BY 4.0 (arXiv:2403.14720 — the arXiv page carries the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence icon)
good: Marking untrusted text by datamarking or encoding cuts attack success to under 2% with minimal task-quality loss, versus over 50% for plain delimiting — a near-free context-assembly addition.
bad: Microsoft's LLMail-Inject challenge showed determined attackers can still defeat these transforms — friction, not a guarantee; it must layer under design-level defences, never instead of them.
took: The datamarking layer of the Ask-door injection defence by design — built 2026-10-20, with Spotlighting recorded in the lane8 dispositions as a source/inspiration for that build alongside DeepMind CaMeLS.
didnt: Corroboration — provenance-marking transforms (delimiting, datamarking, encoding) confirm the cheap first layer of our injection defence, explicitly as friction layered under design-level defences rather than as a guarantee (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MCP tool-poisoning defence — manifest pinning + policy broker (mcp-scan pattern)
licence: Apache-2.0 (snyk/agent-scan, the successor repository to invariantlabs-ai/mcp-scan — GitHub repo metadata lists Apache License 2.0)
good: Pinning tool-manifest SHA-256 hashes and diffing on change defeats rug-pulls, and a deterministic policy broker between model and tools adds allowlists, argument constraints and rate limits. Manifest pinning is a small script against our own gateway tool registry.
bad: Attack success for poisoned tool descriptions measures above 60% (peak 72.8% in MCPTox), and approval gating alone trains reviewers to approve on reflex (63 prompts/hour in one soak test).
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: The file directs borrowing the pattern but not adopting the hosted scanner, because mcp-scan sends tool names/descriptions to invariantlabs.ai's API — "it exfiltrates exactly the metadata we're protecting".

name: NeMo Guardrails (NVIDIA)
licence: Apache-2.0 (README License section and LICENSE-Apache-2.0.txt in the repo root; GitHub metadata reports Other/NOASSERTION)
good: Five rail types — input, dialog, retrieval, execution, output — declared in Colang policy files, including retrieval rails that can reject/alter RAG chunks. The taxonomy is a useful design vocabulary.
bad: The runtime itself is heavyweight for our stdio gateway.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected — the Colang guardrails runtime is heavyweight for our stdio gateway and adds a second policy engine we do not need; its five-rail taxonomy is useful as design vocabulary only, and no runtime or code was adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: The lethal trifecta + dual-LLM doctrine (Simon Willison)
good: A one-line design gate — an agent with private data, untrusted content and an external communication channel together can be made to exfiltrate — with documented exploits across major products, and role-splitting (dual-LLM) as the defence.
bad: A guardrail that stops 95% of attacks is "a failing grade"; the file records that vendors will not save you and the defence is to avoid the combination.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the lethal-trifecta gate (never combine private data, untrusted content and external communication in one agent) and the dual-LLM privileged/quarantined split confirm our approval-gated, least-agency design; it is a doctrine to check designs against, not code to adopt (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MCP authorization specification (OAuth 2.1 resource-server model)
licence: MIT (specification repository README License section; GitHub metadata reports Other/NOASSERTION)
good: The MCP server as an OAuth 2.1 resource server with audience-restricted tokens, Protected Resource Metadata discovery, and token passthrough explicitly prohibited — the reference if a hosted gateway door is ever taken.
bad: Authorization applies to HTTP transports only; our gateway is stdio today, so this is not current work.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — the OAuth 2.1 resource-server model with Protected Resource Metadata discovery, audience-restricted tokens and prohibited token passthrough, to be revisited only if the hosted gateway door (a gated owner decision) is ever taken; it applies to HTTP transports only and our gateway is stdio today (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Biscuit tokens
good: Capability tokens validated decentrally with public info only; holders can only attenuate rights offline, and third-party caveats can require discharge by an approval service — owner-approval expressed cryptographically. The closest published match to our gateway scope model.
bad: Revocation needs external state — a known non-goal recorded in the file.
took: Biscuit tokens for owner approvals — Tier C; Waiting — wave 3, as recorded; re-expresses the owner's approval cryptographically; a gateway/security-surface change (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Board — Biscuit capability tokens for owner approvals, boarded as Tier C and Waiting for the owner's ruling, since they re-express approval cryptographically as attenuable tokens validated decentrally with public information only; Apache-2.0, but revocation needs external state. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SPIFFE / SPIRE workload identity
good: Workloads receive identity from attested environment properties via a local socket — no secret file or env var exists to steal — with short-lived auto-rotated X.509 SVIDs, so a compromised agent's blast radius is a 403.
bad: Running SPIRE for a handful of agents on one VM is over-engineering today; the demo had no cross-trust-domain federation and MCP has no shipped identity answer yet.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — attested workload identity with short-lived auto-rotated X.509 SVIDs and no stealable secret file boarded as a design reserve for agent identity; running SPIRE for a handful of agents on one VM is over-engineering today and MCP has no shipped identity answer yet. Apache-2.0. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: in-toto attestation framework
good: An owner-signed layout defines pipeline steps and authorised keys; each step emits signed link metadata, and verification fails closed if any step was skipped or substituted. It underpins GitHub Artifact Attestations and Kubernetes SLSA L3.
bad: The framework itself targets software supply chains; the file proposes a lightweight home-grown pattern version rather than the framework.
took: Signed pipeline receipts (HMAC pipeline receipts) — built in Round 3, lane TB3 — source/inspiration: in-toto, as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md.
didnt: Adopt/build — the signed-pipeline-receipt pattern, re-implemented lightweight as HMAC receipts in our own pipeline rather than adopting the supply-chain framework itself (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: A2A (Agent2Agent) protocol
good: Signed Agent Cards as a capability directory and a formal Task lifecycle (including input-required / auth-required states) across HTTP+JSON-RPC, gRPC, REST and SSE transports.
bad: Agents are deliberately opaque black boxes with no shared memory across the boundary — the opposite of our wiki-mediated coordination — so "full adoption makes no sense". Adoption figures (150+ orgs, 22k stars) are project self-reports, flagged as such.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected — full A2A adoption, because its agents are deliberately opaque black boxes with no shared memory across the boundary, the opposite of our wiki-mediated coordination, so full adoption makes no sense for our system; Apache-2.0, and only its Agent Card and Task lifecycle shapes remain of interest as ideas. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MCP Tasks (SEP-1686)
good: A call-now/fetch-later task primitive with a requestor-generated task ID and server-defined TTL — exactly the Ask door's shape for questions that take minutes.
bad: The SEP itself records it as the historical record of an experimental feature; the draft spec moves tasks out of core into an extension (SEP-2663), which the file says to track rather than the frozen SEP.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — the call-now/fetch-later task primitive (requestor-generated task ID, server-defined TTL/result-retention) as a shape for long-running Ask-door questions; track the SEP-2663 extension rather than the frozen SEP-1686 (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MCP Agent Mail
good: Advisory file reservations (glob-pattern leases with TTL, auto-expiring so crashed agents cannot deadlock the repo) plus a pre-commit guard, with all messages, reservations and profiles stored as files in per-project git repos. Reservations-with-TTL are the missing piece in our multi-agent branch discipline.
bad: Vendor claims (40–50 concurrent agents, a 10-scenario stress gauntlet) are unverified self-reports.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — advisory file reservations (glob-pattern leases with TTL, auto-expiring) plus the optional pre-commit guard, as the missing piece in multi-agent branch discipline; the code itself is ideas-only under house discipline because its licence is a custom MIT variant with an added rider (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ink & Switch local-first essay
good: Seven local-first ideals (network optional, data outlives applications, ultimate user ownership, etc.) as an explicit checklist for judging any proposed sync/interface feature. Our wiki already scores unusually well against it.
bad: The essay's own account limits it: the three prototypes were tested exploratorily with about ten external users and no formal evaluation methodology, the authors state their CRDT libraries do not fully realise the local-first ideals, industrial CRDT use was still relatively little, and access permissions beyond secret URLs are named an open research question.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the seven local-first ideals (local copy as primary, longevity, ultimate user ownership, network optional) confirm the wiki's existing local-first custody design, and serve as its judging checklist (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Jujutsu (jj)
good: A VCS layer on top of existing git repos with stable Change IDs, first-class conflicts, an operation log making any operation undoable, automatic snapshotting and multiple workspaces. The file calls it "arguably the best-fitting tool in this whole lane" — Azure stays canonical and custody does not change.
bad: The README itself calls Jujutsu an experimental version control system: Git compatibility is stable, but there may still be work-in-progress features, suboptimal UX and workflow gaps that make it unusable for a particular use; safe concurrent replication is flagged experimental with possible backwards-incompatible storage changes, and only the Git backend is production-ready.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — jj as an optional VCS layer over the existing git repos (stable Change IDs, operation log/undo, automatic snapshotting) while Azure stays canonical and custody does not change; its experimental, pre-1.0 status in its own README bars making it load-bearing yet (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Radicle
good: A sovereign peer-to-peer git forge: replicas over a gossip protocol, cryptographic identities, and social artifacts inside git, fully local-first and usable offline. The file calls it technically elegant and permissively licensed.
bad: Its entire point is replacing the single canonical host with P2P replication, which would dissolve our one-canonical-remote (Azure) custody rule.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "Adopting Radicle would dissolve that [custody rule]".

name: TRMNL e-ink display + BYOS
licence: Firmware GPL-3.0; framework and BYOS server implementations MIT (per the project's developer page and repos); hosted core is commercial
good: A pull-only ambient display: no listener, no push channel, no app runtime on the device; it only ever renders a PNG our own self-hosted server produced. The file calls this "the only ambient-surface design compatible with our rules".
bad: The developer page shows the limits: BYOD access to the full web app and plugin API costs a $50 one-time fee, two listed BYOS reference implementations (Phoenix and Django) are marked Inactive, and the firmware licence is presented inconsistently on the same page (headed GPL-3, then described as available under MIT). The hosted core remains commercial rather than open.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — the pull-only ambient display served by a self-hosted BYOS server rendering our own PNG, as an ambient surface compatible with the no-push/no-listener rules; GPL-3.0 firmware code is ideas-only under house discipline (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Apple Shortcuts dictate-to-file
good: A four-action owner-initiated recipe (Record Audio → Transcribe → Create File → Save File) needing no third-party service; each dictation lands as a plain file in an inbox folder and nothing enters the wiki until normal ingest runs. Zero cost.
bad: Platform-locked by construction: the Apple guide frames shortcuts as actions chained inside Apple's own app on Apple devices, with no cross-platform route documented. The guide documents no transcription accuracy or quality guarantee for a dictate/transcribe action, and the recipe ends at a saved file — nothing enters any other system until a separate ingest step runs.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — the owner-initiated four-action dictate-to-file recipe as a zero-cost capture front end: each dictation lands as a plain file in an inbox folder and enters the wiki only through normal ingest (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Cleft Notes
good: Transcription runs entirely on-device with Whisper — audio is never sent to a server — with markdown export and an Obsidian integration, proving the on-device pattern ships in a consumer product.
bad: Summarisation sends note text to OpenAI or Groq, and synced notes live on the vendor's EU-hosted servers — the vendor-cloud sync half violates our no-third-party-platform rule.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected — a proprietary, sign-in product whose summarisation and vendor-cloud sync half conflicts with local-first custody (see existing bad); its on-device Whisper transcription is corroboration of the pattern only, not an adoption (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Limitless Pendant
good: A wearable Pendant (with desktop and web apps) that recorded conversations and meetings into transcripts its users could later access — the vendor's own site documents continued access to previously recorded meetings through 2026, support for existing Pendant customers through 2026 with the Unlimited Plan made free, and a built-in feature to export all of a user's data or delete it.
bad: It records all the time into searchable lifelogs synced to the vendor's cloud; Consent Mode is off by default. Meta acquired Limitless on Dec 5, 2025, the pendant is no longer sold, and support is time-bounded through 2026.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "always-on ambient capture of the owner's life is precisely the auto-discovery pattern the owner has already rejected — and this instance also uploads to a third-party cloud and is a sunsetting product". ## Wave 3 — Community / Practitioner Knowledge

name: Explicit capture triggers and a do-not-record list (Vellum Labs)
good: Recording only on explicit triggers (a choice was made, a decision reversed, a rule stated, something measured) with an explicit noise list ended the "should I record this?" problem. The author's verdict: "Noise, not missing entries, was the failure mode."
bad: The evidence is the author's own four wikis over three months, with no controlled evaluation, and the post discloses it was written by an LLM agent that operates the account. The scheme is also tied to Claude Code-specific mechanics — a /wiki-capture slash command and a Stop hook in its template — and its 'when in doubt, lean toward not recording' rule risks missing anything that does not match the four triggers verbatim.
took: Capture triggers + a do-not-record list — built 2026-10-20 — source/inspiration: Vellum Labs, as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md.
didnt: Adopt/build — explicit capture triggers plus a do-not-record list for wiki capture discipline, built 2026-10-20 in the wave-3 shortlist (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Pin the verbatim record on reversals and rejected alternatives (Vellum Labs)
good: Copying decisive words verbatim into the raw layer when a capture names a rejected alternative, a reversal, or "pin this" made a rotation-policy decision answerable only from the wiki — "RAG retrieves what was written. A wiki also records what was decided."
bad: The pin rule was adopted by its author only after the agent summarised a capture it should have pinned — summarising silently loses the part that matters later.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — a pin-verbatim trigger in capture rules: any capture naming a rejected alternative, recording a reversal, or marked 'pin this' copies the decisive words verbatim into the raw layer instead of summarising, for our capture pipeline (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Enforce raw immutability mechanically (Vellum Labs)
good: A PreToolUse hook blocking Edit/Write on existing raw files and shell overwrites (while allowing new files and appends) held where an instruction did not. The author's line: "'raw is immutable' in a CLAUDE.md is a wish, not a rule."
bad: Within days of instruction-only protection the agent had "fixed a typo" in a source CSV.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — mechanical raw-layer enforcement via a PreToolUse-style hook that blocks edits and shell overwrites of existing raw files while allowing new files and appends, replacing instruction-only immutability (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: A session cannot end with the wiki dirty (Vellum Labs)
good: A Stop hook checking `git status --porcelain` and unpushed commits, refusing to end the turn until the wiki is committed and pushed — "It solved this completely," including cross-repo setups.
bad: Before the fix, agents updated pages, reported success and stopped, leaving the repo uncommitted until a human noticed.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — a Stop hook that refuses to end a session while the wiki repo is dirty or has unpushed commits, so a reported success can never leave the wiki uncommitted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Domain pages beat event pages (Vellum Labs)
good: Long-lived domain pages with dated entries inside them survived, where one file per event became "a pile"; starting with two categories and adding a third only when three existing pages want it is a cheap brake on sprawl.
bad: A month of event-page sprawl left the wiki unusable as organised knowledge.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — long-lived domain pages with dated entries inside them, and adding a category only when three existing pages want it, confirms our preference for durable domain/entity pages over one file per event (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: The drift rule — reference sections must match (MPT / The Cloud Codex)
good: Naming production's #1 failure — dated log entries get written while present-tense reference prose stays stale — and enforcing that the present-tense prose must match before a change counts as recorded.
bad: The same piece records a sibling failure: two entity cards for one institution under name variants silently double-counted downstream, neither page knowing about the other.
took: Drift checks for the sweep (log-vs-prose drift; retired-term hunting) — built 2026-10-20 — source/inspiration: not named in lane8-dispositions.md
didnt: Adopt/build — drift checks for the sweep enforcing that present-tense reference prose matches dated log entries before a change counts as recorded, as recorded in the built drift checks (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Dead-term drift check (MPT / The Cloud Codex)
good: A small script cross-referencing retired/decommissioned terms against all files caught nine files still describing a replaced Ghost publish path as current, including the top-level README. It runs pre-commit and on a schedule.
bad: The companion advice records that past ~40 pages "run lint occasionally" is "not a frequency — it's a hope".
took: Drift checks for the sweep (log-vs-prose drift; retired-term hunting) — built 2026-10-20 — source/inspiration: not named in lane8-dispositions.md
didnt: Adopt/build — retired-term hunting in the sweep's drift checks, cross-referencing decommissioned terms against all files so dead systems are not described as current (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Preserve caveats, conditions and scope at ingest (The Effortless Academic)
good: Forcing compiled pages to carry the source's conditions, limits and scope is called the cheapest correctness insurance in the file for a wiki whose value is correctness.
bad: The demonstrated failure: the author's own niche method was compiled into a clean concept page defining it as established, pitfalls nowhere, and a past-climate model later answered a future-climate question — "you are chatting with those biases, dressed up confidently as fact".
took: Caveat preservation at ingest — built 2026-10-20 — source/inspiration: the Effortless Academic's measured caveat-stripping failure
didnt: Adopt/build — caveat preservation at ingest, forcing compiled pages to carry the source's conditions, limits and scope, as built in 2026-10-20 from this source's measured caveat-stripping failure (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Growth-stage and epistemic-status page labels (digital garden tradition; Appleton / Gwern / Zuegel)
good: Seedling/budding/evergreen stage plus planted and last-tended dates (Gwern adds certainty and importance tags) tells a reader at a glance how much to trust a page. It answers our problem that a freshly compiled page and a thrice-verified page look identical.
bad: Publishing imperfect work "requires that we make the status of our notes clear to readers" — the label is the cost of the practice.
took: Page growth-stage labels (seedling / budding / evergreen, planted and tended dates) — built 2026-10-20 — source/inspiration: digital-garden tradition

name: Book of Beliefs — a living beliefs page (Buster Benson)
good: One specific, deliberately error-corrected document of what the owner currently believes, maintained since 2012 and updated at least yearly — "a way for me to remember who I am, catch inconsistencies in how I respond to different events in the world".
bad: By design it is subjective and error-tolerant: Benson calls the beliefs his 'best guess and articulation', warns 'Caveat lector', and says he aims to be as specific as possible and quickly correct errors rather than avoid them; the individual beliefs are stated without citations or evidence, and the document is updated only at least once a year, so it can be stale between revisions.
took: A living beliefs page — built 2026-10-20 — source/inspiration: Buster Benson's Book of Beliefs
didnt: Adopt/build — a living beliefs page holding what the owner currently believes, deliberately specific and error-corrected, as built in 2026-10-20 from Benson's Book of Beliefs (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Reorientation questions for the Briefing (Naresh)
good: Six questions a returning owner actually asks — What changed? Why does this exist? What is connected to what now? What is stable? What is still evolving? What breaks if this changes? — as a concrete yardstick for whether the Lens Briefing works. Proposed as a checklist, not a feature.
bad: The diagnosis recorded: "The problem was not missing information. The problem was cognitive overload".
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — the six reorientation questions (what changed, why does this exist, what is connected, what is stable, what is still evolving, what breaks if this changes) as a checklist yardstick for whether the Lens Briefing reorients a returning owner, proposed as a checklist rather than a feature (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: The Collector's Fallacy, both directions (Tietze / Sascha)
good: Two working rules: report stored-but-unprocessed items as an ageing backlog number (a queue works only if small, time-boxed, with an exit), and treat a link whose nature cannot be stated as unprocessed material, not a connection. Gives the owner's "preserved, NOT known" rule a metric.
bad: "'To know about something' isn't the same as 'knowing something'" — collecting gives awareness, not learning; collecting connections to uncover their nature later is the same fallacy.
