didnt: Corroboration — the fallacy in both directions (collecting content, and collecting connections whose nature is left for later) confirms our preserved-is-not-known rule and the standing raw-vs-compiled backlog number built from it (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Counter-Evidence callout — preserve contradictions in place (Jim L.)
good: Holding both disagreeing claims on the concept page — finding in the main section, counter-evidence in a marked callout beneath, each cited — so querying returns both: "Honest knowledge > confident answers." The author calls it "the single most important insight" from 12 months of running the pattern.
bad: The file places it as a variant choice: the owner may prefer the callout or the Contradiction Cases file — "Not both by default".
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — the in-place Counter-Evidence callout (finding in the main section, cited counter-evidence in a marked callout beneath it, both returned at query time) as a variant for presenting contested claims, to be weighed against the contradiction Cases file rather than run alongside it by default (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Read Sources Only mode (nashsu/llm_wiki, via Hysen Labs review)
good: A mode restricting answers to the original imported material — "the setting to reach for when you do not trust a synthesized page" — and a stability argument for wikis: a written synthesized page does not reconstruct a different answer each session.
bad: The same review warns a bad ingest "produces a bad page that stays in the wiki until something rewrites it", and an unreviewed persistent wiki "degrades into an accumulation of unreviewed pages, which is worse than stateless retrieval because the errors look authoritative".
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected — the app itself is GPL-3.0 code and is not proposed for our stack, and a Read Sources Only mode for our own Ask door remains the owner's ruling to give, not an adoption; the underlying idea is already covered by our raw-layer custody and citation locking (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Community standing objections and sampled lint (Hacker News thread on Karpathy's gist)
good: The objection list in one place (error permanence/model collapse, "the grunt work IS the learning", quality degradation at ~200–300k tokens) plus a practical answer to N×N contradiction linting: lint samples and rotating subsets so most contradictions surface over time without an all-pairs pass.
bad: The thread was read through its top comment branches only (~200 of 616 extracted lines); later branches were not exhausted.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the thread's standing objections (error permanence/model collapse, quality degradation around 200–300k tokens) and its sampled, rotating-subset answer to N×N contradiction linting confirm our nightly four-lane lint and index-first retrieval design rather than an all-pairs pass (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Atomicity as a page-splitting test (Andy Matuschak)
good: Notes "only about one thing — but which, as much as possible, capture the entirety of that thing", with titles that work like APIs; the usable residue is a splitting heuristic — when one page holds two claims other pages link to independently, split it.
bad: Matuschak is honest that "there's no clear litmus test — just a bunch of tradeoffs", and our pages are deliberately entity/topic-shaped, not one-claim-shaped.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — atomicity as a page-splitting heuristic for lint: when one page holds two claims that other pages link to independently, split it, while keeping our entity/topic-shaped pages as the default shape (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Spaced re-confirmation of settled decisions (Michael Nielsen)
good: Memory can be made "a choice" at tiny cost (4–7 minutes per fact over 20 years at expanding intervals), with two filing rules including filing a striking fact regardless of obvious use. Translated: resurfaced settled decisions on a widening cadence for re-confirm or retire, because decisions rot silently.
bad: Nielsen's own limit: if review time rises much past 15–20 minutes/day he is adding too much — the practice caps its own intake.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — spaced re-confirmation of settled decisions: resurface a settled decision on a widening cadence for the owner to re-confirm or retire, with the intake capped the way Nielsen caps daily review, so decisions that rot silently get revisited (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Periodic patterns review over your own records (Stephen Wolfram)
good: The payoff of decades of personal records is review, not storage — e.g. tracing a resting-heart-rate drop to walking outdoors and changing daily infrastructure because of it. The bounded version proposed is a monthly digest over the wiki's own log only.
bad: The file states a hard boundary: the owner has rejected auto-discovery of his life, and nothing here proposes collecting new data about him.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — a bounded periodic patterns review: a monthly digest over the wiki's own log only, looking for patterns in records already kept, with no new data collected about the owner — his rejection of auto-discovery stands as the boundary (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Project checklists and noticing habits (Tiago Forte, Building a Second Brain)
good: Standardised start and completion checklists plus opportunistic "noticing habits"; the completion checklist is distinctive — a project isn't done until its reusable knowledge is extracted and the rest archived.
bad: The book's own framing limits the method: there is no time magically available to stop and reorganise — maintenance must happen inside regular work, and 'we tend to notice our systems need maintenance only when they break down', blaming our own discipline. The habits are also generic personal-productivity practice with no citation, verification or custody machinery, so the checklists carry nothing about whether what a project produced is true or sourced.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — standardised project kickoff and completion checklists for wiki work, with Forte's distinctive completion rule kept: a project is not done until its reusable knowledge (intermediate packets) is extracted and filed, and only the rest archived (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Plus / Minus / Next weekly review (Anne-Laure Le Cunff)
good: A three-column weekly review (what went well / what didn't / what next), bullet points only, designed to be too small to skip — the structure removes the blank page and the habit survives bad weeks. The Minus column also catches early burnout signals.
bad: The format survives where free-form journaling didn't — the file's lesson is that format matters more than thoroughness.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — the Plus / Minus / Next three-column format, bullet points only, as the shape for a weekly wiki review, small enough not to be skipped and with the Minus column doubling as an early-warning surface (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Two-pass ingest — Locke's commonplace method
licence: Public domain (1706 publication, imprint shown on the archive.org full text)
good: Mark on the first pass without stopping the flow of reading, then on the second pass "copy only the things that are new" — "your first job is not to accumulate but to filter", filed under a one-word Head with the index updated at filing. A triage shape for oversized sources.
bad: The method's history carries a warning: Forster inherited a Locke-indexed book, hated "this awful arrangement by topics", and bent it into a thinking notebook — the practice survived because it bent.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — two-pass ingest as the triage shape for oversized sources: mark on the first pass without stopping the reading, then on the second pass copy only what is new, filed under a single Head with the index updated at filing time (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BrainDB — naive contradiction linting warning (fex_beck)
licence: no licence stated at source (the article calls BrainDB Light+ open source but names no licence)
good: A 5,420-memory, 6-agent system whose experience names contradiction detection as "the killer feature nobody talks about" and "knowledge compounds, but only if maintenance cost is zero". A direct design note for our Contradiction Cases: resolve same-fact-at-different-times as history before flagging conflict.
bad: Its lint's first pass flagged 20,647 contradictions and 99.7% were false positives, mostly the same thing at different points in time.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — contradiction detection only pays when same-fact-at-different-times is resolved as history before flagging conflict, which confirms the temporal-first design of our Contradiction Cases and lint. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Replace markdown with a database/API at scale (BrainDB author; "LLM-Wiki Disaster" critics)
good: The critics' underlying charges are recorded as real: markdown has "no foreign keys, no schema, no permissions", so errors become permanent and duplicate pages breed.
bad: The prescriptions (Trilium, SiYuan, DokuWiki, a PostgreSQL repository, or BrainDB's API) replace the owner's chosen design; the gist source is also a polemic ending in name-calling.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "plain markdown in git *is* the design the owner chose: inspectable, portable, diff-able, and approvable page by page", with owner-approval, citations, lint and the drift/caveat finds as the answers instead of a platform migration.

name: pgvector index alongside the wiki (MPT / The Cloud Codex)
good: A vector index over ~126k chunks (vault plus session history plus legacy archives) as "a way to find the right wiki page when your brain forgot which slug you wrote it under".
bad: The author himself hedges: "Add a vector index only when the wiki genuinely stops fitting. Not before."
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US for now and by the author's own rule — our navigation is deliberately index-first, and indexing session history and legacy archives runs against the no-automatic-ingest boundary; only his trigger is kept.

name: Wiki as a retrieval cache — measured (Vellum Labs)
licence: No licence stated for the article itself; the article states the associated free template and plugin (llm-wiki-kit) are MIT
good: A reproducible head-to-head measurement: source-reading answered 4/4 at 31s/$0.48 per question; through the wiki the first pass ran 48s/$0.65, and even after write-back a repeat cost about the same as reading cold. It also records build non-determinism (identical prompt and commit: 17 pages one day, 21 the next).
bad: "There is no break-even point for this library size… Do not use a wiki as a cache for retrieval."
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US as an expectation for the Ask door — its value is decisions, synthesis and audit trail, not shaving seconds off source lookups. ## Wave 3 — Products

name: Notion — verified pages
licence: Proprietary commercial product (paid Business/Enterprise plans for parts of the feature); no open-source licence stated at source
good: A page owner can mark a page verified until a date or indefinitely; verified pages show a check in search, expiry notifies the owner, and a registry lists every verified page. It is the missing positive freshness signal beside the stale lane.
bad: Verification is a paid-tier feature at the source: verifying individual pages and database pages is stated to be available on Business and Enterprise Plans only, only pages (not databases) can be turned into wikis, and wiki conversion requires a standalone page the user has Full access to. It is a proprietary hosted workspace feature, so the signal lives inside Notion rather than in portable files.
took: Owner-attested verification (`verified_until` on pages) — built 2026-10-20 — source/inspiration: Notion pattern
didnt: Adopt/build — owner-attested page verification with a `verified_until` date, giving pages a positive freshness signal beside the stale lane, implemented in our own markdown/frontmatter rather than in Notion. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DEVONthink — Classify & See Also
licence: Proprietary commercial product (paid licensed editions); no open-source licence stated at source
good: Content analysis lists suggested filing groups with heat-mapped relevance scores, best first, with one action to file; See Also lists related documents likewise scored. At ingest this attacks the misfiling/orphan pattern lint keeps finding.
bad: The mechanic is locked inside DEVONthink's own proprietary, paid, macOS-only application and its databases: suggestions are content- or tag-comparison based within those databases, and the vendor's documentation notes the Classify command is disabled when the engine is not sure enough about a destination. Nothing at the source offers a portable, file-based version of the classifier.
took: Suggested filing at ingest (the boarded classifier's Tier A half, recorded as the same build) — built in Round 3, lane TA4 — source/inspiration: DEVONthink Classify
didnt: Adopt/build — suggested filing at ingest, with scored group suggestions presented for approval rather than auto-filing, reimplemented over our own markdown vault instead of DEVONthink's databases. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Readwise — highlights and notes layer
licence: Proprietary subscription product; no open-source licence stated at source
good: Highlights and notes are their own layer over immutable source documents — collected, reviewed and exported to markdown without ever editing the source, with derived objects independent of the highlight. The pattern for the owner's own marks on a source.
bad: The layer lives in a proprietary subscription service: the official pricing page shows a 30-day free trial followed by a monthly fee, and highlights reach local notes only through Readwise's own sync and export pipeline, so custody of the highlight layer depends on the vendor's service staying available and connected.
took: Annotation layer over raw (owner's highlights/notes in a locator-pinned file beside each raw source) — built 2026-10-20 — source/inspiration: Readwise pattern
didnt: Adopt/build — a separate annotation layer over immutable raw sources, with the owner's highlights and notes held in a locator-pinned file beside each source rather than in a vendor service. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Heptabase — highlights / quote cards
licence: Proprietary subscription product (paid Pro/Premium/Premium+ plans); no open-source licence stated at source
good: Every highlight on a PDF card is listed and can be dragged onto a whiteboard as its own linked card, with a position control jumping back to the exact place in the source. Quotes enter an ingest already pinned to their source location.
bad: Heptabase is a proprietary subscription product with no free plan at the source: its pricing page lists paid tiers with capped monthly AI credits that do not carry over, and PDF parsing limits of 350MB and 3,000 pages per file. The highlight mechanic is also narrow in its own docs — the Highlight app appears only on PDF card tabs and whiteboard tabs.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — highlights as first-class linked quote cards that can be pulled into a working view while staying pinned to their exact source location, as an idea for our annotation layer's presentation. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OpenAI Canvas — suggested edits
licence: Proprietary ChatGPT feature (rolled out to paid Plus/Team tiers at launch); no open-source licence stated at source
good: Model changes arrive as inline suggestions applied or ignored one at a time, highlighting scopes the next edit, and version history restores earlier versions. The display half would let the Lens render a staged proposal as readable per-hunk diffs.
bad: Current availability was not verified — a secondary source claims Canvas was later folded away; the teardown is of the documented mechanic, and the ruling itself stays in chat with no apply buttons.
took: Proposal diff view in the Lens — built 2026-10-20 — source/inspiration: OpenAI Canvas pattern
didnt: Adopt/build — the display half only: render staged proposals in the Lens as readable per-hunk suggested edits, while rulings stay in chat and there are no apply buttons in the portal. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Readwise Daily Review / Mastery + Logseq flashcards
licence: Readwise: proprietary subscription product, no open-source licence stated at source; Logseq: AGPL-3.0
good: Daily resurfacing of your own highlights, with Mastery cards (Q&A or cloze) returning on a spaced-repetition schedule; Logseq proves the same queue needs no new infrastructure — cards are just marked blocks in plain markdown.
bad: Mastery cards must be authored one highlight at a time in Readwise's editor, review feedback is coarse (soon / later / someday), and mobile Mastery sessions are capped at up to five cards; the Readwise half is a paid subscription service after a 30-day trial, and the combined pattern spans two separate products (Readwise and Logseq) with no integrated implementation at either source.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — a daily resurfacing and active-recall review queue over the owner's own highlights and load-bearing pages, using marked blocks in plain markdown in the Logseq manner rather than a vendor service; Logseq's AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only under licence discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Heptabase — whiteboard as synthesis surface
licence: Proprietary — service operated by Hepta Platforms, Inc. under its Terms of Service; no open-source licence stated at source
good: Cards and highlights arranged spatially on whiteboards (including sub-whiteboards), where clusters, order and proximity are part of the thinking and every card keeps its identity and links wherever it appears.
bad: The file notes the increment over a synthesis page is modest: treating arrangement as a first-class, reusable object.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — spatial whiteboard arrangement as a first-class, reusable synthesis object, where clusters, order and proximity are preserved alongside card identity and links, as an idea for our synthesis pages (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Heptabase — Insight (chunk-linked view)
licence: Proprietary — service operated by Hepta Platforms, Inc. under its Terms of Service; no open-source licence stated at source
good: A long card is split into ~300-character chunks with one generated key insight per chunk, each insight linking back to its exact source chunk — citation discipline applied to summarisation.
bad: Under Heptabase's own Terms, the Insight Generator may transmit your Content to third-party LLM providers (OpenAI, Google and Anthropic), which may retain data for a limited period (e.g. 30 days) for abuse monitoring, and AI output may be inaccurate or hallucinated — the Terms warn not to rely on AI Services as a sole source of truth or professional advice.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — chunk-linked generated insights, each insight tied back to its exact source chunk, as a citation-disciplined summarisation pattern for long cards and sources (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Google Vertex AI Memory Bank
licence: Proprietary hosted Google Cloud service; its documentation is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License and code samples are licensed under the Apache 2.0 License
good: A write-time consolidation gate (create/update/delete, refusing duplicates and contradictions), a per-memory revision holding both the final fact and the intermediate extracted memories that produced it, and TTL-based automatic expiry. The revision object is "the cleanest published design" for the claim-lifecycle audit trail.
bad: The hosted service is not adoptable, and memory-side conflict classification at write time is already covered by wave 1's FadeMem.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — memory revisions holding how a memory transforms as new information is ingested, write-time consolidation, and TTL-based automatic expiration confirm our claim-lifecycle audit-trail design; the hosted service itself is not adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Anthropic — context editing & compaction
good: Server-side clearing of old tool results and thinking blocks past a threshold, compaction into a fixed-structure summary, and a warning to save important information to memory files before clearing happens.
bad: The Cookbook itself states compaction is lossy by design: overly aggressive compaction can lose subtle but critical context whose importance only becomes apparent later, and it flattens the whole transcript — user messages, assistant messages, tool calls and prior compaction blocks — into the summary. Tool-result clearing likewise drops the bulky payload, leaving only a placeholder and the record that the call happened, so re-fetch is required if the data is needed again.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — server-side clearing of old tool results, threshold-triggered compaction into a structured summary, and saving important information to memory files before clearing confirm our context-management and sweep design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tana — supertags
licence: Proprietary — no open-source licence stated at source
good: Applying a supertag attaches a field template on the spot, with field inheritance between supertags — structure applied at tagging time wherever the note was captured, instead of by where the note lives.
bad: Tana's own help centre did not surface in this lane; supertags were verified through a detailed firsthand review plus API/CLI mirrors — mechanism confidence high, vendor-page citation indirect. The file also notes overlap with wave 2's Dendron schemas find.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — a supertag attaching a field template at tagging time, with items surfacing wherever they were captured rather than by where they live, confirms our schema-at-tagging approach (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Notion Custom Agents — preview-run
licence: Proprietary — no open-source licence stated at source
good: An agent defined by an instructions page, its own permissions and triggers is run manually and reviewed before activation, with every run in an Activity tab and changes reversible. The adoptable norm: a new agent or cron's first run is a preview for owner review.
bad: Notion's own guide warns Custom Agents could take several test runs to get right — adjust instructions based on what the output actually does, not what was intended — and that agents run with their own access, so permissions must be reviewed before sharing more broadly. Runs also consume Notion credits, shown in the credits dashboard after each run.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — the preview-run norm: a new agent or cron's first run is a manual Run reviewed in its Activity tab before any trigger or schedule is activated, with rollback through version history (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ChatGPT "Dreaming"
licence: Proprietary — no open-source licence stated at source
good: Its output shape — one living summary, kept current — is recorded as what our sweep plus current-state page already produce under owner rules, with every change visible in git.
bad: A background process scans past conversations and silently rewrites the stored summary on its own (e.g. a future trip silently becoming a past trip).
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "automatic ingest of the owner's conversations plus silent revision of what's stored — the two things the owner has explicitly rejected".

name: Gemini Personal Intelligence
licence: Proprietary — no open-source licence stated at source
good: Opt-in Personal Intelligence securely connects Gmail, Photos, YouTube and Search, with the user controlling exactly which apps to link. Google states its two core strengths are reasoning across complex sources and retrieving specific details from, say, an email or photo, often combining them across text, photos and video — for example pulling booking confirmations from Gmail into a clear timeline and retrieving a map screenshot from Photos to answer a travel-plans question.
bad: Opt-in linking of Gmail, Photos, YouTube, Search and more lets the hosted model reason across them, and new data added to those apps later is accessible to it too.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "A standing pipe from the owner's mail, photos and history into a hosted model is automatic ingest of his life by design — rejected pattern, regardless of the opt-in".

name: Microsoft Recall
licence: Proprietary — no open-source licence stated at source
good: Recall captures periodic screenshots of the active window and visualises them in an explorable, chronological timeline, with semantic AI-powered search — describe what you remember, such as a slide from a meeting, and it surfaces matching images or text — and jumping back in to the page, slide, chat, app, document or webpage. Microsoft states all snapshots, indexing and AI processing occur on-device, stored only on the device, encrypted locally, with access requiring Windows Hello.
bad: It snapshots the screen every few seconds into a local OCR + semantic index with a visual timeline — a picture archive, not knowledge — and captures other people's content shown on screen. It was described from secondary coverage; Microsoft's own support pages did not open in this lane.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "Continuous automatic capture of activity is the auto-capture pattern the owner rejected".

name: Mem
licence: Proprietary — no open-source licence stated at source
good: Its one good surface — proactive resurfacing of related notes — is recorded as the owned form of what our Briefing already does.
bad: Frictionless capture with an agent that "reviews new context in the background" and organises it for you; connectors pull Gmail, Slack and Todoist; notes live in Mem's cloud with no self-hosted option and monthly note caps.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "Background auto-organisation without per-change approval, on a hosted-only platform — fails the fit test on both counts". ## Wave 4 — Domains: Media

name: Duke Reporters' Lab — Tech & Check (Squash)
good: Squash matches claims in live transcripts against the ClaimReview database of already settled fact-checks before any new checking starts, with a human editor choosing which proposed match is real — expensive human work is reserved for genuinely new claims.
bad: By the Lab's own account Squash 'makes lots of mistakes': it converts speech to the wrong text, its matching algorithm produces bizarre matches, and it frequently sits idle because there are not enough published fact-checks to match against — 'It isn't quite ready for prime time.' The Tech & Check page also states initial development of Squash has wrapped up, so it is a concluded experiment, not a maintained product.
took: Claim matching + verdict inheritance (human picks the match, never an auto-merge) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 1 — source/inspiration: Duke / Meedan Check pattern (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Corroboration — Squash's human-editor-chosen ClaimReview matching confirms our claim-matching + verdict-inheritance design, with the human always picking the match and never an auto-merge; the live-TV automated platform itself is outside our scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ClaimBuster (IDIR Lab, UT Arlington)
good: Scores every sentence by check-worthiness via a free API, so verification effort lands on statements that are both checkable and consequential. The transferable idea is an explicit ingest triage question.
bad: The model is research code trained on political speech, not our material, so the file keeps the triage idea rather than the scorer itself.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — the explicit check-worthiness triage question at ingest (score each incoming sentence for whether it is checkable and consequential before spending verification effort), as an idea only; the scorer itself is research code trained on political speech and its licence is unstated at source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Full Fact AI
licence: Paid licence — the tools are proprietary Full Fact software made available to other organisations via a paid licence (stated on the Full Fact AI page); no open licence is offered at source.
good: A classifier labels every sentence by claim type at production scale (~330k sentences on a typical weekday) and filters out unverifiable types such as predictions, so type determines how a claim can ever be settled.
bad: The classifier and paid platform are "newsroom-scale machinery we neither need nor could run privately".
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected — fit and licence: a paid, proprietary, newsroom-scale monitoring platform (about 330k sentences on a typical weekday, built for 40+ fact-checking organisations) that a private one-owner wiki neither needs nor could run privately; only its claim-type idea is already covered elsewhere in our design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Meedan Check + Claims and Memes Database
good: Near-duplicate items are clustered and the cluster inherits the original item's tagging, annotation and verdict instead of being verified again — countering "zombie misinformation". As a dedupe rule at ingest it is a writing/linking discipline in markdown+git.
bad: The public repo is explicitly a development environment only — its README warns 'DO NOT USE IN PRODUCTION!' — with a first build of about an hour, a large multi-service Docker/Elasticsearch/PostgreSQL stack across many submodules, and some configuration credentials not provided to non-Meedan members, so self-hosting the full platform is heavy and partly gated.
took: Claim matching + verdict inheritance (human picks the match, never an auto-merge) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 1 — source/inspiration: Duke / Meedan Check pattern (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Corroboration — Check's clustering of near-duplicates with the cluster inheriting the original item's tagging, annotation and verdict confirms our claim-matching + verdict-inheritance rule as a markdown+git discipline; the platform itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ClaimsKG
licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (dataset, per the ClaimsKG paper; the creation tools are separately described as open source on GitHub)
good: Harvests fact-checks from 13 sites (74,066 claims in the Jan 2023 release) with two normalisations — every outlet's rating scale mapped onto one normalised vocabulary, and coreference merging records that are the same claim in different wording.
bad: The RDF/SPARQL stack is not our world; the file keeps it as a worked example for if our verdict vocabularies ever meet another agent's.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — the two normalisations (every outlet's rating scale mapped onto one normalised vocabulary, and coreference merging of the same claim in different wording) as a worked example for if our verdict vocabularies ever meet another agent's; the dataset's CC BY-NC-SA terms make it ideas-only under our licence discipline, and the RDF/SPARQL stack is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Washington Post "Bottomless Pinocchio" + repeater tracking
good: A claim already rated 3–4 Pinocchios and repeated at least 20 more times escalates to a Bottomless Pinocchio — repetition after correction is itself tracked and escalated rather than silently re-corrected each time.
bad: The escalation threshold is deliberately high and late: a claim must already have earned three or four Pinocchios and been repeated at least 20 times before it qualifies, so repetition is only flagged after it has already become, in the Post's own words, a form of propaganda. It is also a single newspaper's editorial rating for US politicians, not a published reusable standard or dataset.
took: Corrections taxonomy + repetition counter — built 2026-10-20, Phase 2 — source/inspiration: PolitiFact / WaPo pattern (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Corroboration — the Bottomless Pinocchio rule (repetition after a settled correction is itself tracked and escalated) confirms our corrections taxonomy + repetition counter, built from the PolitiFact / WaPo pattern; the Post's rating itself is editorial content, not something to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PolitiFact / Washington Post corrections taxonomy
good: A three-way taxonomy — update, correction, new rating (with the old version archived and a public corrections listing) — proposed as a refinement of our built corrections ledger, with the silent-fix class written narrowly.
bad: The documented loophole: PolitiFact classified a genuine factual error (a "recall" election that was a "runoff") as a typo-class "small error", escaping any correction notice — "The carve-out swallowed the rule."
took: Corrections taxonomy + repetition counter — built 2026-10-20, Phase 2 — source/inspiration: PolitiFact / WaPo pattern (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Corroboration — the three-way taxonomy (update / correction / new rating, old version archived, public corrections listing) confirms our built corrections ledger, with the silent-fix 'small errors' class written narrowly so the carve-out cannot swallow the rule. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: IFCN Code of Principles
good: Five written commitments including transparency of sources and methodology and an open corrections policy, with independent assessment and expiry — compliance is re-earned on a schedule, and readers must be able to replicate the work from its sources.
bad: External accreditation is meaningless for a private one-owner wiki; only the five-line code plus a scheduled self-audit transfers.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — a five-line written code (nonpartisanship/fairness, transparency of sources, of funding/organisation, of methodology, and an open corrections policy) plus a scheduled self-audit, as an idea for our private wiki; the external accreditation and independent-assessor machinery itself does not transfer to a one-owner corpus. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NewsGuard "Nutrition Labels"
good: Each source carries a short, structured, evidence-backed label on nine published practice criteria — who is behind it, whether it corrects itself, its rating history — written before you need it. The label block (not the score) fits our source pages.
bad: The file states the 0–100 numeric score itself would be theatre for a one-owner corpus and is not proposed.
took: Source trust labels (evidence-backed block per source page; no numeric score) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 1 — source/inspiration: NewsGuard pattern (score rejected) (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Corroboration — the evidence-backed Nutrition Label block confirms our source trust labels as built (a structured label per source page, written before it is needed); NewsGuard's 0-100 numeric score was explicitly rejected for our corpus. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: The Trust Project — 8 Trust Indicators
good: Two indicators transfer directly: Type of Work labels saying what kind of thing an item is, and Methods notes attached to the item itself explaining why it was pursued and how it was built. Our pages lack a kind-of-page axis.
bad: Adoption is gated to news organisations: only established outlets producing a majority of original journalism can join, through a multi-step approval process, training programme and compliance check before they may show the Trust Mark, and rechecks are ad hoc — so the scheme as a whole is a newsroom consortium standard, most of whose indicators (author expertise, locally sourced, diverse voices, actionable feedback) are written for published journalism rather than a private wiki.
took: Type-of-work labels (record / synthesis / advice / speculation, with methods note) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 1 — source/inspiration: Trust Project pattern (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Corroboration — the Type of Work labels and Methods notes confirm our built type-of-work labels (record / synthesis / advice / speculation, with a methods note attached to the item itself); the trademarked Trust Mark and consortium membership are not applicable to a private wiki, so only the disclosures were borrowed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SIFT + lateral reading (Mike Caulfield)
good: Fact-checkers leave the page: check previous work first, judge the source by what others say about it (never its own About page), and trace claims upstream to original context. Maps directly onto a written pre-ingest check (search the wiki before the web).
bad: SIFT is deliberately quick and shallow: Caulfield's own post frames it as a narrow list of things to do rather than things to consider and rate, warns that tracing to the original may lead to something worse (a junk journal or an unsubstantiated tweet), and that investigators can get sucked into an increasingly confusing maze of pages. It provides no citation-locking, scoring, abstention or record-keeping machinery of its own.
took: SIFT as the written research protocol — built 2026-10-20, Phase 0 — source/inspiration: Caulfield (SIFT method, CC-BY), as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md.

It is a MediaWiki editorial practice for a fiction-canon wiki, with no citation locking, scoring, verification or abstention machinery.

name: Genealogical Proof Standard (GPS)

Its 'reasonably exhaustive research' element is also a heavy, genealogy-specific bar for calling a conclusion proven, not a lightweight per-claim check for a general wiki.

name: Mills' Evidence Analysis Process Map
good: Every citation is classified on three independent axes — source (original/derivative/authored), information (primary/secondary/undetermined), evidence (direct/indirect/negative) — assessed per citation at ingest, saying mechanically how far a claim sits from a firsthand original.
bad: The lesson itself limits the map: the analysis is 'only the first step toward a conclusion', repeated as research progresses, and conclusions must be based on the whole body of evidence assembled — classification alone settles nothing. It also notes derivative records frequently contain errors, and that for many sources the informant's involvement remains undetermined.
took: Genealogy proof bar for claims (five-element Genealogical Proof Standard; Mills' 3×3 citation classes; independent-corroboration test; research log) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 1 — source/inspiration: Genealogical Proof Standard / Elizabeth Shown Mills (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Adopt/build — Mills' 3×3 citation classes (source / information / evidence) as the per-citation classification in our genealogy proof bar for claims, built 2026-10-20 Phase 1 (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Independent-corroboration test (Mills, QuickLesson 17 worked cases)
good: Before counting two sources as independent support, trace each to its informant/origin; agreement between records with a common origin counts once, and provenance (where the record physically was) is part of the test. Directly transferable to two agent filings deriving from one source.
bad: In the first worked case corroboration is refused because an unidentified informant may be the same person behind both records.
took: Genealogy proof bar for claims (five-element Genealogical Proof Standard; Mills' 3×3 citation classes; independent-corroboration test; research log) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 1 — source/inspiration: Genealogical Proof Standard / Elizabeth Shown Mills (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Adopt/build — the independent-corroboration test (trace each record to its informant/origin before counting two sources as independent support), built as part of the genealogy proof bar for claims, 2026-10-20 Phase 1 (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Negative evidence vs negative findings + research logs
good: Logging every search (date, scope, exact terms, result — positive or negative) makes "we found nothing" a checkable statement, and an absence becomes evidence only after mundane causes (record loss, incomplete coverage, indexing error) are ruled out.
bad: A negative finding alone is routine and carries no evidentiary weight.
took: Genealogy proof bar for claims (five-element Genealogical Proof Standard; Mills' 3×3 citation classes; independent-corroboration test; research log) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 1 — source/inspiration: Genealogical Proof Standard / Elizabeth Shown Mills (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Adopt/build — the research-log component of the genealogy proof bar, with the negative-evidence vs negative-findings distinction (an absence counts only where the record should not be silent), built 2026-10-20 Phase 1 (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Layered citation — "we do not cite sources we have not used" (Mills)
good: Two-layer citations distinguishing seen from seen-through, with the consulted source always first, so pages can honestly carry "reported by X, not yet consulted" instead of silently upgrading secondhand references.
bad: Borrowing another writer's citation as if you had seen the original is "both unethical and risky" — you inherit blame for their errors.
took: Nothing taken.

name: Evidentia
licence: Proprietary — commercial desktop software sold by Evidentia Software; no open-source licence stated at the vendor site opened

took: Nothing taken.

name: Persona vs conclusion-person — correlation (Gramps / FHISO Better GEDCOM / Centurial)
good: Each source yields personae (the person-as-described-in-this-record) kept separate from the conclusion person, joined by a reversible, non-destructive judgement called correlation — identification is an explicit, undoable link with its reasoning, never a merge.
bad: The file judges it heavier machinery than a one-family wiki needs today.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — persona vs conclusion-person separation, with identification as a reversible, non-destructive correlation link rather than a merge, as an idea for entity/person resolution if the wiki's people pages ever need it (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GEDCOM QUAY
licence: Apache License, Version 2.0 — FamilySearch states the GEDCOM specification and any code available from FamilySearch based on the specification are subject to the Apache License, Version 2.0
good: A graded certainty value attached to each source citation — one use of one source for one fact — because the same source is reliable for one claim and weak for another, aiding ranking of conflicting information.
bad: The spec itself states the grade "is not intended to eliminate the receivers' need to evaluate the evidence for themselves", and the file notes Mills' three axes carry more information than a 0–3 grade.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected — a single 0–3 certainty grade per citation is coarser than the Mills three-axis classification already built into our proof bar, and the specification itself warns the grade is not intended to eliminate the receiver's need to evaluate the evidence (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ʿIlm al-rijāl — biographical evaluation of transmitters
good: Trust as a standing registry entry per transmitter, graded on two disjoint axes — ʿadālah (uprightness) and ḍabṭ (precision) — in a fixed graded vocabulary (six levels of praise, six of criticism), kept as a durable reference separate from the reports it judges.
bad: The article shows the grades are not mechanical: the evaluation terminology varied in usage between individual evaluators and al-Suyūṭī had to reconcile differing level schemes (four levels, then five, then six), and the Companions were traditionally exempted from evaluation altogether — so a registry entry's meaning depends on which critic's vocabulary produced it.
took: Two-axis source grading (integrity and precision kept separate; matn content check beside the chain check) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 1 — source/inspiration: the rijāl pattern (ʿilm al-rijāl) (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Adopt/build — two-axis source grading keeping integrity (ʿadālah) and precision (ḍabṭ) as separate axes, built 2026-10-20 Phase 1 from the rijāl pattern (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Chain-continuity and hidden-defect checks (hadith criticism)
good: Provenance verified link-by-link for possibility (birth/death dates, when and where a narrator could have met his teacher) and separately audited for hidden defects (ʿilal) that only cross-comparison with established transmitters reveals.
bad: A claimed hearing after the teacher's recognised death breaks the chain — continuity failures are fatal to the report.
took: Two-axis source grading (integrity and precision kept separate; matn content check beside the chain check) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 1 — source/inspiration: the rijāl pattern (ʿilm al-rijāl) (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Adopt/build — chain-continuity checking beside the content check (verify each provenance link could actually have transmitted to the next, and audit for hidden defects), built as the chain side of the two-axis source grading, 2026-10-20 Phase 1 (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Matn criticism
good: Dual verification — a narration is also criticised when its content contradicts established principles or more established narrators (shudhūdh, anomaly); a sound chain does not rescue an anomalous text. It completes the pair with chain checking.
bad: Its trigger is narrow: a shādh ruling requires a trustworthy narrator contradicting a more reliable one, and the definition explicitly does not include a hadith that is unique in its matn and narrated by no one else — so anomalous content with no competing narration escapes the check entirely.
took: Two-axis source grading (integrity and precision kept separate; matn content check beside the chain check) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 1 — source/inspiration: the rijāl pattern (ʿilm al-rijāl) (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Adopt/build — the matn content check beside the chain check (a claim is also criticised when its content contradicts more established sources, so a sound chain does not rescue an anomalous text), built 2026-10-20 Phase 1 (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

bad: The close is not system-enforced: the source states closing the books is optional and usually unnecessary in Beancount because reports are date-aware and balances do not spill over, a formal close is only a simple year-end transaction when compliance or shareholder reporting requires it, and the Wrap-up step itself is framed as optionally performing a closing entry and archiving a copy.
took: Balance assertions + periodic close — built 2026-10-20, Phase 2 — source/inspiration: Beancount pattern (as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Adopt/build — a fixed periodic close checklist for the wiki sweep, with corrections as new entries and the period archived as it stood, re-implemented from the Beancount pattern; GPL-2.0 code itself is ideas-only and was not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

bad: The guide itself limits its own authority: it states twice that retention periods vary by state and situation, that the figures are general guidelines and not a guarantee for specific circumstances, and that a document tied to real money, an open loan, an active claim or an asset still owned should be confirmed with a tax professional before shredding — so its tables cannot be applied mechanically.

didnt: Adopt/build — retention as a property of the record class, with the clock starting at a defined life-event and a destruction date labelled at filing, as built in Phase 2. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

licence: Proprietary — subscription-only on Lexis+ / LexisNexis; no open licence stated at source

licence: Proprietary — available exclusively on Westlaw by subscription; no open licence stated at source
good: Flags attach to points of law (headnotes), not whole documents — a case can be dead for one point and good for another — and every citing reference gets a four-level Depth of Treatment grade plus a verbatim-quotation marker.
bad: Paywalled like Shepard's; verified through Thomson Reuters' own "KeyCite at a Glance" and library guides.
took: Citation treatment signals (followed / questioned / caution / negative, with transitive weakening) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 1 — source/inspiration: Shepard's / KeyCite pattern (as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md).

name: KeyCite Overruling Risk
licence: Proprietary commercial — no open licence stated at source; KeyCite Overruling Risk is a Thomson Reuters feature available exclusively on Westlaw (Westlaw Edge / Westlaw Advantage).
good: Flags an authority with no negative treatment of its own purely because something it relies on has fallen — transitive weakening. A one-hop version is "the difference between a wiki that is locally consistent and one that is globally honest".

took: Citation treatment signals (followed / questioned / caution / negative, with transitive weakening) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 1 — source/inspiration: Shepard's / KeyCite pattern
didnt: Adopt/build — citation treatment signals with transitive weakening, built 2026-10-20 (Phase 1) per lane 8; the proprietary Westlaw service itself is not used (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

bad: Verified through an official adopter's handbook (CDC ACIP, ch. 7) rather than the Working Group's own book-form handbook.

licence: No licence stated at source — MAGICapp is the MAGIC Evidence Ecosystem Foundation's hosted platform; its site describes free sign-up but states no open licence for the platform or its content.

It is also a hosted web platform, so guideline custody sits with MAGIC rather than locally.

name: Living systematic reviews — retirement triggers (Murad et al.)
good: Four explicit retirement triggers (evidence conclusive, question less pertinent, no new studies anticipated, resources unavailable) with the decision and rationale stated in the final iteration — the missing exit half of re-verification scheduling.

name: Persian-language PKM literature (1pezeshk)

name: ARK (Archival Resource Key)
licence: Specification / practice, no code to copy.
good: Identifier independent of hostname/protocol, with ?info inflections returning a metadata record plus a commitment statement, opaque shoulders/blades, and tombstone-by-design for withdrawn objects.
bad: The scheme itself guarantees nothing: the draft states persistence is purely a matter of service, neither inherent in an object nor conferred by a naming syntax, and that no identifier scheme has any direct impact on the funding, political and stewardship failures that actually break persistence; maintaining the indirection/mapping table is an unavoidable ongoing cost for the provider. The cited specification is also an expired 2008 Internet-Draft, described in its own status memo as a work-in-progress document valid for a maximum of six months.
took: FOR US as internal naming discipline — opaque, checkable, location-independent name per registered object whose lookup returns a small metadata record including a commitment line.
didnt: We would mint nothing publicly and register no NAAN.

name: DOI/DataCite tombstone practice + DOI states
good: DOI name and metadata continue after content is retracted; three-step ritual moves DOI to registered state, repoints to a tombstone page with last citation metadata, and records a Withdrawn date.
bad: A DataCite DOI can never be deleted, so withdrawal is irreversible and only partial: the DOI still resolves in Registered state and its metadata remains retrievable by authenticated users via the Member API. The tombstone itself is entirely the repository's own burden — DataCite states it does not currently provide any tombstone pages automatically, offering only a single generic fallback URL for members without the resources to build a specific page.
took: FOR US — erased/retracted wiki object should leave a tombstone record in its register (identifier, last metadata, withdrawn date, reason) rather than a gap.
didnt: No DOI registration is proposed; internal only.

name: DataCite relation types + name-identifier schemes
good: Closed relationType list with inverse pairs (Cites, HasVersion, IsDerivedFrom, Obsoletes, etc.) makes relations checkable, and nameIdentifier uses scheme+value pairs (ORCID, ISNI, ROR) instead of bare names.
bad: The vocabulary sits inside a large, XML-oriented registration schema built for DOI deposit, not for local records: relationType is mandatory only if RelatedIdentifier is used, nameIdentifierScheme becomes mandatory whenever nameIdentifier is used, and the page notes DataCite infrastructure supports only about 8,000–10,000 names per record, pushing larger lists out to linked related metadata. Taking the relations therefore means extracting a subset from the kernel rather than adopting the schema as-is.
took: FOR US — adopt the relationType list/subset as controlled vocabulary for source manifest cross-record relations and page-source frontmatter links, and scheme-qualified IDs for people/agents.
didnt: Adopt/build — the relationType list/subset and scheme-qualified nameIdentifier pairs (ORCID, ISNI, ROR) as controlled vocabulary for source-manifest cross-record relations, page–source frontmatter links, and people/agent identifiers; the full DataCite XML kernel and DOI registration are not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PURL and partial redirection (incl. w3id.org)
licence: Service pattern; the public services are free to use but public by definition.
good: Partial redirection lets one registered prefix redirect a whole subtree, appending the unmatched remainder, so one rule fronts a hierarchy whose files move underneath.
bad: Public services are unusable for us — privacy-absolute; a registered PURL is a public record.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — public services rejected; pattern recorded as reference design for an owner-controlled redirect table if stable addresses are ever needed.

name: URN (RFC 8141) and ni:/nih: hash names (RFC 6920)
good: URN contributes governance shape and non-reassignment commitment; ni: names are self-verifying hashes of content, and nih: adds grouping separators and a Luhn check digit for dictation/typing.
bad: Adopting either wholesale would renumber the corpus for no reader-visible gain; we already hash content and keep IDs in registers.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — recorded as standards reference for a private urn:-style namespace and for the nih: check-digit trick, not adopted wholesale.

name: Public PID registration for the wiki itself
good: Public registration would give the wiki persistent, citable identifiers: under DataCite's policy a DOI resolves through the global Handle System to a publicly available landing page carrying open metadata, so a registered object stays findable, identifiable and citable by outsiders even when its location changes, while the underlying content itself does not need to be publicly available.
bad: Registration is a publication act: a DOI must resolve to a publicly available landing page and its metadata must be open/public, creating a permanent public artefact.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "privacy-absolute ends the discussion: a public registry entry for a private family corpus is a disclosure".

name: CiTO (Citation Typing Ontology)
good: Citations typed by relationship in a factual × rhetorical grid (23 properties, positive/negative/neutral valence), plus a local vs global citation-frequency split.
bad: Nothing here justifies an OWL stack; batch 3.1 already infers typed edges into our own closed set.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — recorded as reference vocabulary to check our edge set against, not adopted.

name: Trusty URIs
good: Hash computed over a canonicalised representation, not file bytes, with an artifact code naming what was hashed, so the same statement keeps the same identifier across serialisations; verification extends over the reference tree.
bad: The paper's own caveats limit the guarantee: permanence is only assumed if search engines and web archives crawl and cache the artifacts, verifiability helps only when the correct trusty URI is already known (a manipulated artifact simply arrives with a different trusty URI), and an author can change an artifact and its URI and claim it was always so if the original URI has not yet been picked up and linked by third parties. Only three modules (FA, RA, RB) are defined in the specification.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — filed as deepening evidence for the queued converter-identity item; Trusty URIs themselves not adopted, and nanopublications not re-proposed.

name: Nanopublication signing + registry mechanics
licence: Toolkit open source (Rust/Python/npm); licence text not re-verified on the page opened.
good: Claims signed at creation with RSA key, introduction nanopublications bind a key to an identity, registry lets consumers filter by trusted agents/types, and retrieval returns only items whose Trusty URI verifies.
bad: The trust-network layer is explicitly not wanted: one owner admits agents, no endorsements graph.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — reference implementation for signed filings if wanted; trust-network layer rejected.

name: Crossmark update metadata
good: Correction is a separate publication with its own DOI, the original is never modified, and <updates> metadata on the original names the update with a closed update-type vocabulary.
bad: The mechanism is narrow by design: Crossref states updates should only be deposited for editorially significant changes likely to affect the interpretation or crediting of the work, not for minor corrections. Each update also costs a separate publication with its own DOI and metadata, deposited as Crossmark XML (or via Crossref's tools) inside a Crossref member/publisher workflow, and the original record's metadata and landing page still have to be amended separately (e.g. a 'RETRACTED:' title prefix) for readers to notice.
took: Filed as vocabulary refinement for the existing corrections ledger — closed update-type vocabulary as candidate kind values, and the corrected page should carry a pointer to its correction in its own metadata.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms our corrections-ledger design of corrections as separate records that point back to the corrected page, and supplies a closed update-type vocabulary as candidate kind values plus the rule that the corrected page carries a pointer to its correction in its own metadata; the Crossref/DOI deposit machinery itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CSL (Citation Style Language) + CSL JSON
licence: Styles/spec CC BY-SA historically; schema relicensing to MIT agreed, texts in transition.
good: Separates the bibliographic record from rendering: one canonical CSL JSON record per source, renderable in any style by citeproc processors, with styles as versioned, validatable files.
bad: The wiki has no bibliography to render today, so no processor is needed.
took: A CSL-JSON sidecar via Citation.js — Tier B; boarded by the coordinator in Round 3, Waiting — as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md (Round-4 research candidates bundle bullet).
didnt: IDEA ONLY — CSL JSON field set recorded as interchange shape for external-source records, not queued as a build.

name: CFF (Citation File Format 1.2.0)
good: One small human-writable YAML file at a repo root declares how to cite the thing, validated against a schema and consumed by GitHub/Zenodo without scraping prose; precedence rule decides in advance which metadata file wins.
bad: Scope is deliberately narrow: one CITATION.cff file at a repository root declaring citation metadata for software or datasets only, with no provenance, history, or integrity mechanism documented on the homepage. Its value depends entirely on consumers that choose to parse it — the homepage lists support only from GitHub, Zenodo, and Zotero — so a file consumed by nothing is inert.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — CFF-shaped record recorded as natural citation block for wiki exports/tools; precedence lesson applies to frontmatter vs manifest vs lockfile.

name: BibLaTeX/Biber inheritance
licence: LaTeX Project Public License (documentation/practice; no code proposed).
good: Metadata inheritance with explicit override and field-level granularity: crossref inherits/remaps fields, xref points without inheritance, @xdata holds reusable bundles with granular references, cascading, and cycle detection.
bad: The clean inheritance semantics depend on the Biber backend: the manual's caveats say BibTeX's crossref uses symmetric field mapping that 'tends to bloat database files and corrupt the data model', requiring duplicated fields and empty-field workarounds in the child entry. Traditional BibTeX also brings static-memory capacity limits with cryptic overflow warnings and ASCII-only sorting — and the whole mechanism lives inside a LaTeX/Biber toolchain.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — recorded as reference semantics for a future manifest parent-record mechanism; no .bib tooling proposed.

name: SKOS (Simple Knowledge Organization System)
good: Concepts have identity separate from words, with prefLabel/altLabel/hiddenLabel tiers, definition/scopeNote/changeNote, broader/narrower with transitive expansion, and graded mapping properties (exactMatch, closeMatch, etc.).
bad: SKOS is deliberately lightweight and semi-formal: the Primer describes concepts as semantically related in 'informal hierarchies', and states SKOS offers only limited support for containment of KOS information in a concept scheme — there is no mechanism to record that a specific statement such as a skos:broader assertion pertains to a specific concept scheme. Full use also presumes concepts identified by URIs and published as RDF, which is heavier than a plain registry file.
took: FOR US — as data model for the registered tag vocabulary: keep registry as a wiki file but give each tag the SKOS field set and let search use broaderTransitive expansion; not an RDF migration. Additionally: Built (marathon records): SKOS tag registry (tag vocabulary formalised as data in a wiki file)
didnt: Adopt/build — the SKOS field set (prefLabel/altLabel/hiddenLabel tiers, definition/scopeNote/changeNote, broader/narrower with broaderTransitive expansion, and graded mapping properties) as the data model for our registered tag vocabulary, kept as a wiki file with search using transitive expansion; no RDF migration or SPARQL stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SKOS governance tooling (Skosmos, VocBench, Skosify/qSKOS)
good: Treats a controlled vocabulary as code with a test suite — Skosmos browses/searches it, VocBench edits it, and Skosify/qSKOS validators detect orphans, label clashes, missing symmetric relations, and unreachable roots.
bad: We will not run a SPARQL endpoint for a few dozen tags.
took: The check battery transfers — port qSKOS-style integrity rules into the lint lanes as the tag registry's own lane.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — tools recorded as references/off-the-shelf option only, not adopted.

name: Dublin Core application profiles (Singapore Framework)
good: Schema-as-contract with graded obligation — every term has definition, refinements, encoding schemes, and an M/MA/R/O obligation grade, with dumbing-down designed so values stay human-useful without the scheme.
bad: It is a heavy documentation regime, not a lightweight schema format: a conforming profile is a packet requiring mandatory functional requirements, a domain model, and a Description Set Profile — and the page itself notes the DSP model was still being developed and put forward as a Working Draft, and that there were no stable, published examples of full-blown conforming application profiles. Its terms and constraints are also grounded in the DCMI Abstract Model and RDF, so conformance pulls in that whole stack.
took: FOR US — formalise AGENTS.md schema with per-field obligation grades and named encoding schemes, and let the validator report by grade (errors for M, warnings for MA/R). Additionally: Built (marathon records): Schema as application profile (Dublin Core obligation grades; validator reports by grade)
didnt: Adopt/build — formalising our schema as an application profile with per-field obligation grades (M/MA/R/O) and named encoding schemes, with the validator reporting by grade (errors for mandatory, warnings for recommended); the full Singapore Framework documentation packet and its RDF/DCAM/DSP stack are not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: schema.org Claim
good: Distinguishes where a claim has appeared (appearance) from where it first appeared (firstAppearance), enabling provenance answers and detection of a repeated claim mistaken for corroboration.
bad: Schema.org itself states on the Claim page that it 'does not define any types of relationship between claims' — appearance and firstAppearance only link a Claim to CreativeWorks, with no claim-to-claim relations, no truth verdict and no supersession link. The page also warns that many claims are better understood in the context in which they appear, so ambiguity risk remains even with a full Claim description.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — recorded strictly as internal field discipline (appearances list with first_appearance pointer); no JSON-LD, no markup, nothing outward.

name: Frictionless Data Package
good: One descriptor file (datapackage.json) per bundle, with identity (name/id) separated from version, sources as a first-class array, contributors with closed roles, and resources checkable mechanically.
bad: Most wiki sources are documents, not datasets, and the source manifest already covers the general case.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — datapackage-style descriptor recorded for dataset-shaped ingests; name/version separation could be adopted for snapshot naming.

name: DID Core (W3C)
good: Self-sovereign identity — control of the identifier is proven cryptographically by whoever holds the keys in the DID document, without a central registrar.
bad: Resolution is public by design, and method fragmentation (a registry of incompatible resolution rules) buys nothing at one-owner scale.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "a DID document for any family agent would be a public artefact about a private system"; agents' identities are internal and owner-issued.

name: W3C Web Annotation selectors
good: Redundant heterogeneous anchoring — TextQuoteSelector (quote plus prefix/suffix) plus TextPositionSelector plus a State recording which representation was selected against — survives reflow and proves a passage moved.
bad: The specification itself warns that the Text Position Selector is 'very brittle with regards to changes to the resource' — any edits or dynamically transcluded content may change the selection, so a State should additionally be used to identify the correct representation. The model also prescribes no transport protocol for creating, managing and retrieving annotations, leaving that to a separate specification.
took: FOR US — as extension format for citations into unstable sources (PDFs, HTML captures): keep #Lstart-Lend primary, add quoted passage with prefix/suffix as second anchor.
didnt: Adopt/build — add a TextQuoteSelector-style quoted-passage anchor (exact text plus prefix/suffix, with a State recording the representation) as a second anchor alongside the primary #Lstart-Lend line range for citations into unstable sources, because position-only anchoring is brittle to edits. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: IIIF fragment addressing
good: A region of an image/recording is addressed as #xywh=… or #t=… — human-readable, machine-actionable, and copy-safe, with the original never cropped or duplicated.
bad: We run no IIIF server and need none.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — fragment syntax recorded as citation form for image/media sources if media citations become common; full Presentation/Canvas stack not proposed.

name: URL text fragments (#:~:text=)
good: Browser-native deep-linking to a cited sentence with quote as address; directive is stripped from document.URL after parsing and never sent to the server.
bad: Works on HTML renderings only, not markdown sources, and support is a browser feature — the link must still be correct without it.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — recorded as a Lens nicety for citation links in Ask answers/briefings, not infrastructure.

name: OKF spec (Open Knowledge Format)
good: Bundle is a directory of Markdown files, one concept per file, YAML frontmatter with type the only required field; §4.1 round-trip clause requires consumers preserve unknown keys and not reject unrecognised fields, and §11 conformance is permissive.
bad: Spec has not moved past v0.2; §13 records breaking v0.1→v0.2 changes, and runtime protocol/attester parts are deferred — nobody should build against those yet.
took: FOR US — §4.1 clause as a conformance test for our own exporter and any consumer of our bundles: unknown keys survive a round trip or the tool fails.
didnt: Adopt/build — the §4.1 round-trip clause as a conformance test for our own exporter and any consumer of our bundles: unknown keys survive a round trip or the tool fails; the OKF conformance export and the bundle audit step are already built, and the spec's deferred runtime/attester parts are not built against. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Stashpad (namespacing pattern)
licence: open source, free (author's statement); repo licence not re-verified
good: Keeps OKF fields namespaced in the working vault (okfType etc.) so they never collide with user fields, maps to standard keys only at export, and keeps original namespaced fields in the bundle so it round-trips losslessly.
bad: Caveats stated by author: alpha; export targets v0.1 shape and already lags the now-current v0.2 spec.
took: FOR US (the pattern) — native frontmatter never renamed in place; OKF mapping lives in the exporter; native keys ride along in the bundle beside mapped ones.
didnt: Adopt/build — the namespacing pattern only: native frontmatter is never renamed in place, the OKF mapping lives in the exporter, and native keys ride along in the bundle beside the mapped ones so exports round-trip losslessly; Stashpad itself is alpha and lags the v0.2 spec, so no product or code is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-export (zoni)
good: CLI converts an Obsidian vault to CommonMark, resolving wikilinks/embeds, with partial export, tag filters, .export-ignore, and explicit recursive-embed cycle handling.
bad: Its README states it "supports most but not all of Obsidian's Markdown flavor" — even the best dedicated converter publishes a remainder.

didnt: IDEA ONLY — no dependency; we don't run Obsidian and the Lens build already emits exports.

licence: AGPL-3.0 (GNU Affero General Public License v3.0)

bad: Markdown export omits block-link details entirely, losing block references, page/block attributes and {{components}}; full-fidelity JSON is bulky (102 MB for one Bible translation).

didnt: NOT FOR US as a target.

name: Pandoc
good: Reads/writes dozens of formats with every Markdown extension individually switchable — the field's boundary normaliser between Markdown flavours that disagree on links, tables, footnotes and metadata.
bad: Licence noted as fine as an invoked tool; do not vendor its code into MIT/Apache-shaped tooling.
took: FOR US (the rule) — pin one canonical flavour inside the system and normalise only at the boundary, with a converter whose loss behaviour is documented.
didnt: Adopt/build — the boundary rule Pandoc embodies: pin one canonical Markdown flavour inside the system and normalise only at the boundary, with a converter whose loss behaviour is documented; Pandoc itself is used, if at all, only as an invoked tool — its GPL-2.0-or-later code is ideas-only and is never vendored into our MIT/Apache-shaped tooling. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Djot
good: Clean-slate markup by Pandoc/CommonMark's creator: ~95% identical to Markdown but parsing is local/unambiguous, with definition lists, footnotes, tables, attributes on any element and generic containers built in.
bad: Switching dialects would break every tool we own (Lens renderer, search, validators, agents' habits) for benefits already patched by house convention.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — valuable only as a diagnostic checklist of what CommonMark lacks.

name: MyST Markdown
good: Extends CommonMark (strict superset) with directives and roles kept in plain text, plus named targets for cross-references; proof at ecosystem scale that a directive grammar can stay diff-able and renderer-independent for a decade.
bad: Much of MyST's extended syntax is optional and disabled by default, enabled only via the Sphinx conf.py myst_enable_extensions setting, so a plain MyST file is not self-describing about which extensions it needs. The documentation also states that directive syntax such as {image} will not show the image in common Markdown viewers (for example when the files are viewed on GitHub), unlike standard Markdown syntax.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — do not adopt the syntax; keep as prior art if the Lens live-block grammar ever needs a v2.

name: mdformat + mdformat-myst
good: Formats Markdown to one canonical style, with plugins per dialect, and formatting is proven per construct against round-trip test fixtures.
bad: Running a formatter over the corpus now would produce enormous cosmetic diffs and fight agents' hand formatting.
took: Borrowable point recorded: fixture discipline — a converter/formatter is trustworthy exactly where it has round-trip fixtures.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — not worth a corpus-wide pass.

name: Jupytext
good: Bidirectional conversion between Jupyter notebooks and text formats so notebooks can live in git as diff-able text, with paired notebooks as the documented pattern.
bad: Cell outputs are NOT stored in text representations and are lost on refresh; paired notebooks are the workaround, each format holding only the half it can hold losslessly.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — wiki holds no notebooks today; paired-format pattern and round-trip-test acceptance shape recorded if executable evidence pages arrive.

name: Quarto (.qmd)
good: One source format rendered to HTML, PDF, Word, slides, websites and books via Pandoc after executing code chunks; .qmd ⇄ .ipynb conversion built in, notebook as peer not rival; outputs regenerated at render, never stored in source.
bad: A .qmd file is not a finished document on its own: Quarto's own site says it uses knitr to execute R code (with Jupyter/Julia engines for other languages) and Pandoc to convert the result, so rendering requires the Quarto CLI plus a working language runtime and Pandoc pipeline, and a failing code chunk breaks the render. The executable-document model also means the source alone does not show the outputs a reader will see.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — our pages are not executable documents and shouldn't become so; Quarto recorded as standing reference if a page ever needs a computed table/figure.

name: Maildir + notmuch
licence: notmuch is GPL-3.0+ (practice reference; no code proposed)
good: Maildir stores one file per message with state in filename flags, readable by any tool forever; notmuch indexes it into Xapian with tags, and notmuch dump exports the whole tag layer as a plain-text batch file that restore can replay.
bad: notmuch's tags live only in its database, requiring interfacing with notmuch, whereas mu's approach is more interoperable; mbox is hostile to diffs, dedupe and per-message addressing.
took: FOR US (as practice) — split Takeout mbox to one-file-per-message in raw/, keep original mbox sealed, treat any index as rebuildable, and export tag layers as plain-text sidecars.
didnt: Adopt/build — the Maildir practice: split a Takeout mbox to one file per message in raw/ with the original mbox kept sealed, treat any index as rebuildable, and export tag layers as plain-text sidecars; this is practice only — no GPL-3.0 notmuch code is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OPML 2.0
licence: OPML 2.0 specification copyright (UserLand Software, Inc. / Scripting News, Inc., all rights reserved): the specification document may be copied and furnished to others with the copyright notice included but may not be modified, while the format it describes may be implemented by any party for commercial or non-commercial purposes without royalty or licence fee.
good: Universally importable for feed subscription lists — every reader already speaks OPML for exchanging subscriptions.
bad: Spec allows arbitrary attributes but type/attribute meanings are undefined with no mechanism to learn them; as a knowledge container it is strictly weaker than Markdown and cannot carry a page, frontmatter or citations.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY narrowly; NOT FOR US as a knowledge format — only shape proposed is a "sources we follow" subscription list.

name: Data Transfer Project
good: Portability as shared common data models plus per-service adapters for direct service-to-service transfers, underlying Google Takeout's direct transfers.
bad: It is infrastructure for platforms (service-scale Java); privacy-absolute local files are not a platform.
took: Borrowable architecture recorded: portability = a shared model + thin adapters + transfers that are actually exercised.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — nothing to run.

name: Exit drills (Notion exit playbook / migration post-mortems)
good: Worked ritual: export, re-import into a scratch target, run a written validation checklist against the imported copy, file the loss list, repeat the delta after a freeze window — losses are discovered at re-import, never at export.
bad: The playbook itself is heavy and loss-prone in practice: it estimates 1-3 weeks end-to-end, warns teams consistently underestimate database mapping, and lists friction the drill must absorb — DB relations flatten, embeds are lost, formulas arrive static, links break post-import, workspace ZIP exports can take 24h+ and partial exports miss nested subpages, and long Notion titles can exceed filesystem limits. It is also a single-author newsletter post with no tooling, tests or guarantees behind the checklist.
took: FOR US — periodic round-trip drill over OKF bundle and llms exports into a scratch wiki, re-running validator + citation lockfile + search benchmark, filing the diff as the drill report.
didnt: Adopt/build — run the drill as a periodic round-trip over our own exports (export, re-import into a scratch wiki, run the written validation checklist, file the loss list, repeat the delta after a freeze window), because the playbook's central finding is that losses are discovered at re-import, never at export. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Notion (export loss profile)
licence: Proprietary — no open-source licence; use is governed by Notion's Master Subscription Agreement / Personal Use Terms of Service, under which Notion retains all right, title and interest in the Services and customers receive only the limited rights expressly granted.
good: Official export preserves text and basic tables.
bad: Database relations/rollups are flattened, formulas export as values not logic, linked-database views arrive as disconnected CSVs, synced blocks export as static copies, and deep subpage trees are easily truncated.
took: General rule recorded: anything computed exports as its value — live blocks/computed views must never be the only copy, underlying data lives in pages/frontmatter and computation is re-runnable.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — we would never target Notion.

name: OAIS reference model (ISO 14721 / CCSDS 650.0)
