good: Reference model every preservation system is measured against: SIP → AIP → DIP packages, designated community, and six archive responsibilities / five functions; discipline is vocabulary + responsibilities, not software.
bad: Adopting OAIS wholesale means package ceremony a one-person markdown+git archive doesn't need; full text is paywalled.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — value is two specific ideas split out as finds 2 and 11, and the shared vocabulary.

name: OAIS representation information + designated-community test
good: Bits alone are not preservation: a data object is only information with representation information, and the archive must ensure it is understandable by the Designated Community without the producers.
bad: The understandability test proved hard to apply consistently: OAIS v3 had to clarify the relationship between Preservation Description Information and the Content Data Object and introduce Preservation Objectives to allow 'Independently Understandable' to be more consistently testable. It also imposes a continuing burden — representation information must be kept sufficient for a Designated Community over an indefinite long term, instead of a one-time recording.
took: FOR US — name the designated community (owner, family, agents, 30 years out) and preserve a representation bundle with the corpus: format specs depended on plus tooling build/run documentation.
didnt: Board — naming the designated community (owner, family, agents, 30 years out) and preserving a representation bundle of format specs plus tooling build/run documentation with the corpus, as the understandability test for our local-first archive (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NDSA Levels of Digital Preservation v2.0 (2019)
good: Tiered maturity matrix (five functional areas × four levels) with a lightweight self-assessment spreadsheet scored 0/1/2 per cell, designed to show where you are and what's next.
bad: Scope is deliberately narrow: the DPC RAM v3 model notes the NDSA Levels are primarily technical and limit their scope to a subset of preservation considerations, so organisational viability and succession are outside them. The NDSA page also shows v2.0 already superseded by v2.1 (March 2026), and that the files live in OSF, whose navigation the NDSA itself publishes extra guidance to help with.
took: FOR US — one-page annual scorecard in the wiki; lowest cells name next year's preservation work.
didnt: Adopt/build — the one-page annual NDSA Levels scorecard, recorded in lane8 as built 2026-10-20 in Phase 3, with its lowest cells naming the next year's preservation work (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DPC Rapid Assessment Model (RAM) v3 (2024)
licence: no licence stated at source — the v3 PDF states the model is freely available for anyone to use
good: Maturity model over 11 capabilities (six organisational, five service) rated 0–4, explicitly not a strict certification tool, basic assessment under two hours; covers organisational viability/succession that NDSA excludes.
bad: Heavier than the NDSA scorecard and aimed at organisations.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — keep as reference for the succession question, not as a second scorecard to maintain.

name: POWRR
good: Named counterweight to gold-plating for restricted resources: the 4 Ds and an M — Decision, Description, Duplication, Distance, Monitoring.
bad: No specification, criteria or tool at source: the 4 Ds and an M exist at source as a presentation mnemonic, and its author records that audiences can usually state only two of the four Ds. POWRR itself is a grant-funded programme for small and mid-sized institutions with restricted staff, IT infrastructures and budgets, so its guidance is institutional advocacy and training, not a testable standard a personal archive can be scored against.
took: FOR US (as doctrine) — adopt the 4 Ds + M as the wiki's stated preservation doctrine, the checklist every preservation choice is checked against; zero build cost.
didnt: Corroboration — the 4 Ds + M as stated preservation doctrine for checking preservation choices, corroborating the Phase 3 scorecard build whose lane8 record credits NDSA Levels / POWRR doctrine as its source (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BagIt (RFC 8493)
licence: Copyright (c) 2018 IETF Trust and the document authors, subject to BCP 78 and the IETF Trust's Legal Provisions Relating to IETF Documents (RFC 8493 Copyright Notice)
good: Hierarchical file-layout convention with data/ payload, manifest-<algorithm>.txt checksums, optional tagmanifests and fetch.txt holey bags; a bag is complete when every file is present and valid when every checksum verifies, with in-place algorithm agility and direct file access.
bad: Informational, not a Standards Track specification, and its integrity guarantee is corruption-only by its own text: sections 1.1 and 5.4 state BagIt is not designed to be secure against active attacks, with digital signatures out of scope. Implementers must also defend against special directory characters in manifests and fetch.txt (sections 5.1-5.2) and against filename case and Unicode-normalisation differences that can make a present file fail a manifest check (section 6.1.1).
took: FOR US — make the nightly take-home export a proper bag before zipping (manifest-sha256.txt + bag-info.txt) so the Drive copy is self-verifying.
didnt: Adopt/build — the nightly take-home export made a proper self-verifying BagIt bag (manifest-sha256.txt + bag-info.txt) before zipping, recorded in lane8 as BagIt take-home packaging built 2026-10-20 in Phase 3 from RFC 8493 (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CLOCKSS trigger-event doctrine
licence: Creative Commons — CLOCKSS states it assigns Creative Commons Open Access licences to all triggered publications; no licence stated at source for the archive service itself
good: Dark archive whose release conditions are written down in advance as a short enumerated list of trigger events (publisher ceased, content withdrawn, catastrophic failure).
bad: By design there is no access at all until a trigger event occurs, so it cannot serve as a working archive, and release is a Board decision, not the owner's. It is also a governed, fee-based service for libraries and publishers operating 12 archive nodes, not a tool or doctrine a personal archive can run or direct on its own.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — for us a one-paragraph succession note (who may restore, on what events), not a system.

name: LOCKSS polling & repair
licence: BSD-3-Clause (3-Clause BSD License, LOCKSS Program FAQ software licence statement)
good: Many copies plus a protocol: peers poll each other and vote on a hash; a disagreeing peer repairs from the original/proven peer, and an inconclusive poll raises an alarm for a human instead of guessing.
bad: Operationally heavy for a personal archive: the FAQ recommends a minimum of four copies to allow majority consensus, expects content retrievable over HTTP for ingest, requires a traditional POSIX filesystem (LOCKSS cannot yet interface directly with back-end object storage such as S3), and warns that regularly reading data may not align with cloud cost structures. Alliance participation and technical support are also fee-based.
took: FOR US — scheduled cross-copy fixity poll across Azure/Drive/local: hash canonical tree and each copy, report agreement, re-make the outvoted copy, escalate split votes to the owner.
didnt: Adopt/build — the scheduled cross-copy fixity poll across Azure, Drive and local copies, re-making the outvoted copy and escalating split votes to the owner, recorded in lane8 as built 2026-10-20 in Phase 3 from LOCKSS doctrine (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PREMIS preservation metadata
good: Standard data dictionary with five entity types (Intellectual Entities, Objects, Events, Agents, Rights) and the rule that objects are immutable — a change creates a new, related object.
bad: Full PREMIS (let alone PREMIS-in-METS) is institutional metadata machinery.
took: Borrowable part recorded: PREMIS event vocabulary as closed set of event types for our preservation record.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — vocabulary and immutability rule only, no PREMIS XML adoption.

name: METS
good: XML schema encoding descriptive, administrative and structural metadata — a machine-readable map of a complex object's files and relationships (verified via Archivematica).
bad: Our corpus structure is already a human-readable directory tree under git; METS would add a second XML map to keep in sync, read by tools we don't run.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — earns its keep for complex multi-file objects in repository platforms; a markdown wiki is not one.

name: OCFL 1.1 (Oxford Common File Layout)
licence: Spec is CC-BY (as recorded in the file: "Spec is CC-BY")
good: Application-independent storage layout for versioned objects with inventory.json (digest → paths, forward-delta version history) so a repository can be rebuilt from the storage root alone, with no database.
bad: Git already gives content addressing and version history; re-laying the repo as OCFL objects would fight git for no gain.
took: Borrowable idea recorded: the rebuildability test — could the wiki be fully reconstructed from the take-home bag alone?
didnt: IDEA ONLY — test kept, layout not adopted.

name: PRONOM registry + PUIDs
good: The field's technical registry of file formats keyed by PUIDs, built to support preservation risk assessment, migration pathway planning, object identification and validation.
bad: PRONOM is a data store, not an identification or validation tool itself — the overview presents it as supplying information on formats, products and support lifetimes for others to use. Sampled entries show observable gaps: Format Risk and Supported-by fields left blank and some entries last updated years ago, so coverage and currency depend on registry maintenance.
took: FOR US — slow-cadence format-risk watch over the few non-markdown formats we depend on, and record the PUID in the source manifest when a binary source is ingested.
didnt: Corroboration — the PUID-keyed format registry confirms our format-risk watch and recording the PUID in the source manifest at ingest; there is no separate system here to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DROID / Siegfried (identify-at-ingest)
licence: DROID three-clause BSD; Siegfried Apache License 2.0
good: Signature-based format identification by magic number, reporting format ID and basis for the match, with an EXTENSION_MISMATCH flag when extension disagrees with signature; Siegfried is a single Go binary, faster, DROID-compatible.
bad: Identification is only as good as the signature set: Siegfried's README marks its Library of Congress FDD and Wikidata identifiers as beta, and says by default it uses the latest PRONOM signatures without buffer limits, so it may do full file scans. DROID is a platform-independent Java application requiring Java 21 to build/run, a heavier runtime than Siegfried's single Go binary.
took: FOR US — at ingest, record identified format and basis for every non-text source in the source manifest and flag extension lies.
didnt: Corroboration — signature-based identify-at-ingest reporting format ID, basis and extension mismatch, with the PUID recorded in the manifest, confirms the pattern already recorded in took; no new tool adoption is decided here. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: JHOVE
good: Validates files format-by-format with a two-tier verdict — well-formed (syntactically conforms) and valid (also semantically conforms) — plus characterisation.
bad: LGPL makes it ideas-only under licence discipline, covers ~15 formats with no markdown module, and format specialists advise against using JHOVE for PDF/A validation.
took: Borrowable mechanic recorded: two-tier verdict as pattern for our own gates ("parses" vs "conforms").
didnt: IDEA ONLY — tool not adopted.

name: veraPDF + PDF/A policy checking
licence: MPLv2+/GPLv3+ per consortium release announcement (as recorded, from search)
good: Industry-standard open-source PDF/A validator with implementation checker, policy checker for custom institutional rules, reporter, and metadata fixer; PDF/A doctrine is self-contained (fonts embedded, no external dependencies).
bad: Licence makes the tool ideas-only to embed; running an installed validator over our own files is use, not incorporation, as noted in the file.
took: FOR US — veraPDF pass over generated reports and PDF/A's self-containment doctrine as target profile for delivered reports.
didnt: Adopt/build — run veraPDF as an installed validator over our generated reports and adopt PDF/A's self-containment doctrine (fonts embedded, no external dependencies) as the target profile for delivered reports; running the tool is use, not incorporation — its MPLv2+/GPLv3+ code is ideas-only to embed and is never embedded. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Library of Congress sustainability factors + Recommended Formats Statement
good: Scores every format against seven sustainability factors (disclosure, adoption, transparency, self-documentation, external dependencies, patents impact, technical protection) and classifies formats per category as Preferred or Acceptable.
bad: The RFS page itself limits the scope: it is primarily geared towards published content as opposed to personal papers or archival acquisitions. Its Preferred/Acceptable verdicts are also determined from both global/community criteria and the Library's own local/institutional criteria, and the statement is revised annually, so the labels are LC-specific judgements rather than a portable score.
took: Borrowable mechanic recorded: a one-page format policy for the wiki scored on the seven factors, with preferred/acceptable verdicts per category held.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — a document, not a system; filed as an idea for the owner's queue.

name: Migration on significant properties (Smithsonian preservation strategy)
good: Settled field practice: bit-level preservation of every original always; migration based on named significant properties with the migrated format stored together with the original (original always retained); emulation reserved for when the original environment is the content.
bad: The Archives' own page states the limits: bit-level preservation 'does not guarantee future accessibility', migration is performed only 'when required and if possible', and accessions arrive intermingled, unique and often 10-15 years old (up to more than 30) with copies or backups rarely included — so the strategy rests on per-object significant-properties judgement rather than an automatic rule.
took: FOR US (as standing rule) — any format migration must name significant properties first, keep the original alongside, never migrate-and-discard, and be recorded as a preservation event.
didnt: Corroboration — migration on named significant properties with the migrated format stored together with the always-retained original, and emulation reserved for when the original environment is the content, confirms our standing never-migrate-and-discard rule. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WACZ 1.2.0 (Web Archive Collection Zipped)
licence: Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) for the individual specification; the webrecorder/specs repository itself carries no licence file
good: Self-contained verifiable web-archive package: ZIP with WARC data, CDXJ index, pages.jsonl, datapackage.json manifest with sha256 per resource, and datapackage-digest.json hashing the manifest itself; optional signing with RFC 3161 timestamping; replay needs no server.
bad: Our web captures are reading copies, not evidence; spec itself notes it is a draft with no formal standards-body standing.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — upgrade path if a capture ever needs to be provable; not needed today.

name: Archivematica
good: Reference open-source OAIS implementation with ingest-to-access microservices, PRONOM-integrated Format Policy Registry, and METS/PREMIS/BagIt AIPs; storage service requires justification + approval for deletion.
bad: An institutional platform to install, operate and feed — opposite of a one-owner markdown+git corpus — and AGPL puts its code in ideas-only class regardless.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — borrowable ideas already filed separately (format policy registry, deletion ceremony).

name: COPTR (Community Owned digital Preservation Tool Registry)
good: The field's shared, community-maintained registry of preservation tools organised by OAIS function — the place practitioners check before building anything.
bad: Currency depends entirely on community upkeep: the main page says COPTR needs users' help to update existing records as tools change, and editing requires an account that must be requested by email because of spam problems. It is a descriptive registry (664 tools and 41 workflows at opening), not a tested or evaluated catalogue.
took: FOR US (as standing reference) — COPTR-first habit: check the registry before writing a preservation tool.
didnt: Corroboration — a shared, community-owned registry organised by lifecycle/OAIS function confirms our COPTR-first habit of checking the registry before building a preservation tool; it is an external reference to consult, not a system to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Repository audit & certification (CoreTrustSeal / ISO 16363)
good: External certification (16 CoreTrustSeal requirements, peer review with public evidence) that a repository actually does what OAIS/RAM describe, with succession planning explicit.
bad: Certification buys trust from strangers; our designated community is one family, privacy is absolute, no external audience to convince.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — only the succession question inside it is worth keeping, already carried by RAM and CLOCKSS finds.

name: Sigsum
good: Transparency log accepting only a signed checksum (hashes and signatures, never data), with witness cosigning (k-of-n quorum) against split views, and a monitor that enumerates every signature a key has ever logged so key theft is discoverable.
bad: Project itself states submitter privacy is "mostly preserved" — rate-limiting via DNS reveals submitter's domain to the log operator, and every entry is publicly linkable to one key, so submission cadence is public metadata.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — revisit the day agent filings carry signatures; today filings aren't signed and the public cadence/key linkage leaks against privacy-absolute.

name: C2SP checkpoint format + witness cosigning (transparency-dev/witness)
good: Checkpoint is a signed note (origin, tree size, Merkle root, signature lines); a witness cosigns only after verifying a consistency proof that the new tree extends the old, refusing same-size different-root forks (ErrRootMismatch).
bad: The witness's first checkpoint for a log is trusted on first use (TOFU), so a fork already present at first contact is not caught by consistency proof. The witness repo also ships no releases (0 releases, 0 tags on the repo page), and a witness only countersigns checkpoints — it stores no log entries itself.
took: FOR US — emit the Black Box head/provenance root as a C2SP checkpoint signed by Mehmed's key and cosigned by one witness we control, converting the Black Box into a witnessed chain with no public log.
didnt: Adopt/build — the C2SP checkpoint plus one self-controlled witness pattern for emitting the Black Box head/provenance root as a witnessed chain with no public log, as recorded in took; the witness code is Apache-2.0, so code use is permitted, not ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Rekor / Sigstore
good: Public append-only log binding artifact hash + signer key/certificate + signature with integratedTime, inclusion proof, and SET (Signed Entry Timestamp) allowing offline verification; Fulcio issues ~10-minute certificates from OIDC login.
bad: Log is public by design and the signer's email identity is permanently, publicly visible in every Rekor entry — a permanent public activity feed for a private wiki.
took: The SET pattern is noted as genuinely good design, already captured privately in the C2SP witness find.
didnt: NOT FOR US — public-by-design identity and timing metadata.

name: Certificate Transparency (RFC 9162)
licence: IETF Trust copyright, subject to BCP 78 and the IETF Trust's Legal Provisions Relating to IETF Documents; the RFC's Copyright Notice states that Code Components extracted from the document must include Revised BSD License text and are provided under the Revised BSD License.
good: RFC's own security model is the find: logs do not detect misissuance — monitors do, by comparing signed tree heads (gossip); a hash chain nobody compares against an independent copy detects nothing.
bad: CT itself is public logs of X.509 certificates for browsers; parties not covered by gossip stay unprotected, and the RFC deliberately leaves gossip undefined.
took: Mechanic recorded: the Black Box needs a named monitor role periodically comparing its head hash against a head recorded elsewhere.
didnt: IDEA ONLY as a practice; CT itself is NOT FOR US — nothing in our system issues public certs.

name: Trillian
good: General-purpose verifiable append-only Merkle log engine (inclusion + consistency proofs, signed tree heads) under CT and Rekor-class logs.
bad: It is only a core — every deployment must write its own personality — and it is a database service to operate (MySQL, gRPC, signer) built for millions of entries and public verifiers.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "run our own Trillian" is a platform, not a small step; file-scale Merkle provenance already suffices at our size.

name: Sunlight
good: CT log redesigned around static files — tiles of the Merkle tree + checkpoints servable from plain object storage/static host/CDN, no database or dynamic server.
bad: Software itself is CT-specific (entries are X.509 certificates), so nothing is installable for us.
took: Borrowable idea recorded: files-not-a-service shape — publish checkpoints + tiles as static files if Black Box heads ever need public checkability.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — architecture proof, not a tool.

name: OpenTimestamps
licence: Protocol is an open specification; Python/JS clients LGPL-3.0; Go implementation public domain
good: Proof-of-existence anchored in Bitcoin with no trusted authority and no per-timestamp cost; only a digest leaves the machine, calendars aggregate digests into one Bitcoin transaction, and the upgraded proof is self-contained and verifiable forever against any Bitcoin node.
bad: Block-header time is coarse (within a few hours, almost certainly within a day) and proves existed no later than, never created at; fresh proof is initially only a calendar's PendingAttestation promise.
took: FOR US — stamp the Black Box head hash or the nightly zip's SHA256 manifest once a day; proof ages better than any service. Additionally: Built (marathon records): Dual timestamp anchoring (Black Box head hash anchored via two independent authorities)
didnt: Adopt/build — stamp the Black Box head hash, or the nightly zip's SHA256 manifest, once a day via OpenTimestamps, because only a digest leaves the machine and the upgraded proof is self-contained and verifiable forever against any Bitcoin node; dual timestamp anchoring is already built. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RFC 3161 timestamping practice (TSAs)
licence: Copyright (C) The Internet Society (2001), all rights reserved; the RFC's Status section states 'Distribution of this memo is unlimited' and the document states no other licence name at source.
good: TSA receives only a hash (message imprint) and returns a signed token binding it to trusted UTC time; TSA must only timestamp the hash, never examine data, and the token must not identify the requester; openssl ts is already on any Linux VM and free public TSAs exist.
bad: A TSA is a trusted party that could in principle lie about its clock; free hobbyist staple FreeTSA is marked "Credible: No" (not on EU trusted lists).
took: FOR US — second anchor for the same Black Box head from a different trust root than Bitcoin, stamping a salted head hash via openssl ts and a free TSA.
didnt: Adopt/build — RFC 3161 timestamping as the second, independent anchor for the Black Box head hash (a salted head stamped via openssl ts against a free TSA), because the TSA sees only a hash, never the data, and its trust root differs from the Bitcoin/OpenTimestamps anchor; lane 8 records dual timestamp anchoring as built 2026-10-20. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: C2PA / Content Credentials
licence: Specification under a royalty-free licence; reference implementation c2pa-rs/c2patool dual MIT / Apache-2.0
good: Signed provenance manifest embedded in a media file: chain of assertions bound by hard binding (SHA-256), ingredients preserve predecessors through editing, all certificates travel inside the manifest so validation works offline.
bad: Spec's own honesty: C2PA proves a signer made a claim and the file hasn't changed — it does not prove the claim is true; valid ≠ trusted (trusted requires chaining to the C2PA Trust List via a conformance-gated CA), and manifests strip easily.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — adopt only if media provenance ever needs to convince a third party; self-signed manifests add nothing over existing hashes, and becoming trusted needs an outside gatekeeper.

name: did:key
licence: W3C Software and Document License for reports; specification contributions under the W3C CLA; software and sample implementations under Apache-2.0 (per the spec repository's LICENSE.md).
good: Identifier is the public key itself (multicodec, base58btc); resolution is pure local computation, offline forever, with no registry, server or ledger.
bad: Spec's own security considerations: a did:key can never change — no rotation, no revocation, no deactivation; a compromised key is impersonable permanently.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — right identifier format the day agent filings are signed, paired with an in-wiki key page for retirement; never for a long-lived identity.

name: did:web
licence: W3C Software and Document License for reports; specification contributions under the W3C CLA; software and sample implementations under Apache-2.0 (per the spec repository's LICENSE.md).
good: DID resolves over HTTPS to a did.json file on a domain you control; create = publish the file, rotate = edit it, deactivate = remove it — the only DID method whose lifecycle one person can operate with tools already in hand.
bad: Document is public by design (publishes agents' public keys and listed service endpoints — a small accurate map of our setup), and resolution trusts the host's TLS at read time.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — right long-lived identity shape if an outside verifier ever needs it; publishing that map is an owner disclosure decision, not a default.

name: Verifiable Credentials Data Model 2.0 + Data Integrity (EdDSA) proofs
licence: W3C Software and Document License (W3C Recommendation; implementations carry royalty-free licensing commitments under the W3C Patent Policy, per the specification's Status section).
good: Standard envelope for a signed claim (issuer asserts about a subject, holder presents, verifier checks without contacting issuer); Data Integrity EdDSA cryptosuite signs canonicalised claims with Ed25519, verifiable offline against a did:key/did:web.
bad: Today our certificates are internal records in a private repo; wrapping them in VC format now would be ceremony without an audience.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — standard envelope to adopt at a boundary if a boundary audience ever exists; not infrastructure to run today.

name: Git SSH commit signing + in-repo allowed_signers file
good: Since Git 2.34, commits/tags sign with ordinary SSH keys through the SSH agent, and verification is fully local via an allowed_signers file that can live inside the repository — any clone carries its own trust root and verifies offline, with no external service.
bad: Verification is entirely local and manual: git refuses SSH signature verification unless a gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile is configured and exists, and trust, rotation and revocation are all hand-maintained edits to that allowed_signers file (plus an optional revocation file) — there is no central registry, expiry or distribution mechanism in the feature itself, and a compromised SSH key signs as its owner until every verifier's file is updated.
took: FOR US — first build in the lane: Grok/Hark branch commits and Mehmed's merges signed, allowed_signers in-repo stating which keys may sign for which identities.
didnt: Adopt/build — Git SSH commit signing with the allowed_signers file kept in-repo for agent branch commits and Mehmed's merges, because verification is fully local and offline and the trust root travels with every clone; Git is GPL-2.0 code but is used as a tool, not embedded, and lane 8 records the signing pack as built 2026-10-20. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Gitsign (keyless git signing via Sigstore)
good: No long-lived keys — each session does an OIDC login, Fulcio issues a ~10-minute certificate, and the commit is signed.
bad: Every signature is recorded in Rekor (public — signer identity + timing for every commit, forever), and plain git verify-commit checks only cryptographic integrity + that a Rekor entry exists, not who signed; identity is only checked by gitsign verify.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — public logging of a private workflow, plus identity theatre at the point verification should be strictest.

name: Signed pushes (git push certificates)
good: git push --signed signs the push itself (full ref-update list) covering a server-issued nonce, defeating replay, and the server can store the push certificate as a permanent attestation of who moved which refs, when.
bad: Mechanism only exists where the server supports it (rare, mainly self-hosted git); no Azure DevOps documentation found mentions push certificates — our host — recorded as absence-of-evidence, not a tested refusal.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — right idea, wrong host; recorded so it isn't re-proposed without a hosting change.

name: age
licence: Reference implementation BSD-3-Clause (Go); Rust implementation (rage) also exists
good: Small file-encryption format: X25519 recipients, scrypt passphrase mode, existing SSH keys work directly as recipients/identities, plugin recipients extend to hardware, ~200 bytes overhead per recipient, no config/keyserver/ceremony.
bad: It is encryption, not signing — proves nothing about origin; an SSH recipient stanza embeds a public-key tag, so an age file reveals which key can open it (wrong for a deniable hand-off).
took: FOR US — sealed-copy tool for offline backups of signing keys and sealed exports, encrypted to a key the owner already holds.
didnt: Board — age-sealed key backups for the signing keys: age fits as the sealed-copy tool for offline backups of signing keys and sealed exports, encrypted to a key the owner already holds, but this use touches the signing keys' custody and stands as a Tier C item awaiting the owner's ruling, so the idea is boarded rather than built. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Minisign
good: Tiny Ed25519 file signer whose trusted comment is covered by a second signature (default timestamp + filename, documented for version numbers to prevent downgrade attacks), with an 8-byte KeyId defeating key-substitution, secret key encrypted under a passphrase, and public keys short enough to print.
bad: Signify cannot verify minisign signatures, because it expects no trusted comment (one-way compatibility only).
took: FOR US — signer for artefacts that leave: nightly take-home zip's SHA256 manifest, shipped PDFs/exports, and the erasure-certificate register, verifiable offline from the public key.
didnt: Adopt/build — Minisign (ISC-licensed) as the signer for artefacts that leave the system (nightly zip manifests, shipped PDFs/exports, the erasure-certificate register), because its public keys are short enough to print, verification is fully offline, and the signed trusted comment gives downgrade protection; lane 8 records minisign over artefact manifests in the signing pack built 2026-10-20. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Signify (OpenBSD)
good: Minimal Ed25519 sign/verify tool; OpenBSD's release practice is the find — one SHA256 manifest covering every file, and one signature over the manifest, verifies an entire directory.
bad: As a tool it adds nothing on our Linux VM that minisign lacks, and it cannot verify minisign's trusted comments.
took: Its manifest-signing doctrine is adopted inside the Minisign find: never sign N files — sign one manifest of hashes.
didnt: IDEA ONLY as a tool.

name: TUF (The Update Framework)
good: Signing authority split across four roles (Root, Targets, Snapshot, Timestamp) with separate keys, thresholds and expiry, designed assuming keys will be compromised; root rotation must be signed by both old and new root thresholds with version incrementing by exactly one.
bad: Over-engineering as software for one owner, not a software-distribution network.
took: Borrowable discipline recorded: separate the root key (offline, owner's) from operational keys (agents', short-lived), and let the root cross-sign every rotation.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — design discipline for when the key registry outgrows a single wiki page; no tooling now.

name: Drafts (Agile Tortoise)
licence: Proprietary (free tier; Pro subscription). Pattern only.
good: Opens to a blank page with keyboard up and no folder/title/filename before typing; capture surfaces everywhere (Siri, widgets, share extension, watch, floating Mac capture window), a staging Inbox with exactly three verbs (Tag, Flag, Archive), and scriptable Actions as the dispatch layer.
bad: Apple-ecosystem only — the official site lists iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple Watch, with no Windows, Android or Linux version. The dispatch layer that makes it useful is paywalled: creating/editing Actions, Workspaces, themes and enhanced widgets/share options require the Drafts Pro subscription.
took: FOR US — as interface spec for any wiki capture surface: open on blank, save on one keystroke, file later, dispatch rules separate from the capture act.
didnt: Board — the blank-first capture, staging Inbox with Tag/Flag/Archive, and separate scriptable dispatch Actions as an interface spec for a wiki capture surface; the proprietary Apple-only app itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Obsidian iOS Quick Capture + Share Sheet Locations
licence: Proprietary app; placeholder/location specifications are documented conventions, free to mirror.
good: Named Capture Locations bind a behaviour to an optional template; templates fill provenance via placeholders (content, date, time, location, author, domain, published, url, wordCount, etc.), and the Share Sheet flow includes a review-or-edit step before Save, with Full Text vs URL-only as a per-location choice.
bad: Version- and platform-gated: the native Share Sheet is only on iOS/iPadOS 18+ and the described features require Obsidian 1.13.0 or later, and every Location is bound to an existing Obsidian vault, folder, daily note or bookmarked note — there is no capture independent of the proprietary app and a pre-configured vault.
took: FOR US — mirror the shape for wiki capture doors: short list of named destinations, each with a template stamping provenance automatically; full-text vs link-only explicit per location, never a global default.
didnt: Board — named Capture Locations, each with an optional template stamping provenance placeholders and an explicit Full Text vs URL-only choice, as the shape for wiki capture doors; Obsidian itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Org-mode org-capture + org-protocol
good: Templates as small grammars with %-escapes including %a, a link to the exact place capture was invoked from; prompts (%^{...}) ask only for what the harness cannot know; org-protocol routes a browser page into the same named template system.
bad: Capture outside Emacs only works if a running Emacs server, emacsclient and a correctly registered org-protocol URL handler are all set up per operating system/desktop — the orgmode.org setup page documents that multi-step registration and known handler breakage. The system is Emacs-only, so the grammar is unusable without adopting the Emacs ecosystem.
took: The lane's single most valuable idea recorded: adopt this grammar as the specification for our own capture templates (implemented in our own code).
didnt: IDEA ONLY — grammar adopted as spec, Org itself not adopted.

name: jrnl
licence: Free & open source per project site; exact licence not confirmed — treated as ideas only.
good: One shell line is a capture interface: natural-language date prefix parsed from the owner's words, first sentence promoted to title, @tags inline, multiple named journals, storage in plain-text files "that will still be readable in 50 years".
bad: Entry-grammar details partially verified (from PyPI/docs text in search); exact licence not confirmed.
took: Mechanic recorded for a terminal-side wiki capture door: one command, timestamp and title derived from the text itself.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — nothing here needs jrnl itself.

name: Superwhisper (Modes)
licence: Proprietary (free tier; Pro from $8.49/mo per vendor page).
good: System-wide dictation on Whisper models running on-device by default ("audio never leaves your machine"), with Modes — named profiles (faithful, cleanup, custom prompt formats) chosen before speaking — plus a personal vocabulary taught once.
bad: Cloud models are opt-in via the owner's own API key (noted as a choice, not a default).
took: FOR US — as pattern to generalise: voice capture should offer named modes (raw thought / structured note / message draft), each a stored prompt chosen at trigger time, on-device default, cloud only as explicit per-mode choice.
didnt: Board — the Modes pattern for voice capture: named modes (raw thought / structured note / message draft), each a stored prompt chosen at trigger time, on-device by default with cloud only as an explicit per-mode choice; Superwhisper itself is proprietary, so the pattern is boarded as an idea and no product or code is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Just Press Record
good: Every surface is a record button (Lock Screen, Control Centre, Action Button, Shortcuts, Siri, widget, Watch complication) with built-in transcription in 30+ languages and App Store privacy label "Data Not Collected"; transcript is stored within the audio file itself so text and audio travel as one artefact.
bad: Apple-only and paid: the App Store listing covers only iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple Watch at $6.99, with sync/storage through iCloud Drive or the device itself, so there is no Android, Windows or Linux capture surface and no self-hosted sync path.
took: FOR US — two defaults copied: trigger on lock screen/wrist via a deliberate Shortcuts/Action-Button door, and voice capture landing in git as one self-describing artefact (audio + transcript, timestamped name).
didnt: Board — one-tap record from Lock Screen/Control Centre/Action Button/Watch and storing the transcript inside the audio file as one self-describing artefact, as defaults for wiki voice capture; the proprietary Apple-only app itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Wispr Flow
good: Polished cloud dictation: hold-to-talk on every platform, live auto-editing of filler/grammar, per-app context awareness, spoken edit commands.
bad: Context awareness sends audio and periodic screenshots of the active window to its cloud; disabling screenshots measurably reduces accuracy, and there is no offline mode at all.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "a dictation layer that must watch the screen to work inverts our privacy rule".

name: Zotero Connector
licence: Open source, copyleft (AGPL family per the project) — ideas only.
good: Per-site translators recognise what a page is and populate typed metadata in one click; the toolbar icon changes shape before clicking to signal what was detected, a folder icon opens an item picker, degradation to a Web Page item is designed, and Add Item by Identifier captures by ISBN/DOI/PMID.
bad: For an unrecognised page, remaining fields are filled in by hand (docs note this frankly).
took: Translator architecture recorded: per-site extractors, a capture button declaring detected type before committing, and identifier-paste as a first-class capture path.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — architecture is the find, tool not adopted.

name: Hypothes.is (capture)
licence: Hosted service (open-source client); annotations live on hypothes.is servers by default.
good: Marginalia as a separate layer over an unchanged document, anchored to the exact selection (W3C Web Annotation model, quote plus context, not just offset), public/private/group-scoped, embeddable by publishers. Additionally: Capture unit is the anchored selection — mark passages on the live page or PDF with tags, private/group/public, reappearing in place — so the owner's judgement about which sentences matter is the capture.
bad: Storage is wrong for us by default: margin notes must land in git as markdown, or they become a second, unsynced memory. Additionally: Hosted service itself is not adopted (annotations must live in the repo, not a third party's cloud).
took: Mechanic recorded: for web material deliberately not ingested whole, an anchored-selection record (quote, URL, note, date) landing in git as our own file. Additionally: Pattern recorded: Lens margin-notes layer writing notes into the repo as a per-page annotations sidecar, not an embed of the hosted service.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — hosted service/embed not adopted.

name: Glasp
good: Highlighting works well — select, colour, note, tag, export to Markdown/CSV/JSON, AI summaries over highlights.
bad: Default visibility is public: vendor lists "Private highlights" as a Pro feature and states "Highlights are public by default", with a social layer and an offer to publish an AI built from your reading.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "a capture tool whose default is to publish the owner's reading trail fails privacy-absolute at the first setting".

name: Evernote email-in
licence: Proprietary service; the grammar is a convention, free to adopt.
good: Subject line is a routing grammar in fixed order — [Title] ![reminder] @[notebook] #[tag] — and a trailing + appends to the most recent note with that title, so one deliberate send carries destination, tags, date and create-vs-append intent.
bad: Unmatched names fail silently (note lands in default notebook, tag skipped); the article also documents filter-based automatic forwarding, which is the rejected auto-ingest pattern.
took: FOR US — as routing grammar for a wiki mail-in door (@section #tag, + for append), with unmatched names bouncing back a correction prompt, never failing silent; deliberate single sends only.
didnt: Automatic forwarding mode explicitly excluded from the find.

name: OmniFocus Mail Drop
licence: Proprietary service; the addressing pattern is a convention.
good: Multiple private send-to addresses (username + random string) minted per purpose/person, deletable at any time — revoking one touches no other — with a restore window; subject → item name, body → note, forwarded mail keeps a link to the original.
bad: Contrast in the file: Things' single mail address offers no way via email to set tags/metadata, ignores attachments, and truncates body at 4,000 characters.
took: FOR US — if wiki accepts mail-in from anyone but the owner, use per-sender, per-purpose revocable capability addresses, never one shared inbox address.
didnt: Adopt/build — per-sender, per-purpose revocable capability addresses for any mail-in route into the wiki, never one shared inbox address; built 2026-10-20, Phase 7 as email-in capture at the gateway inbox, as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Flameshot
licence: Open source (GPL family per the project; licence not stated on the man page opened).
good: Annotation happens in the capture overlay on the frozen screen before any file exists (arrows, text, highlight, blur/pixelate for redaction, pin-to-screen), then save/copy/discard; fully scriptable via subcommands, flags, raw PNG to stdout, D-Bus and ini config.
bad: Wayland capture is fragile: on GNOME Wayland Flameshot must obtain screenshot permission through the desktop portal and can fail with 'Unable to capture screen', with some features limited compared with X11. The repo also notes Windows code signing is manual, so not every patch release is signed.
took: Pattern recorded for a wiki screenshot door: region → annotate/redact → name → land in raw/ with a caption, as one gesture (upload-to-Imgur stays off).
didnt: IDEA ONLY — pattern adopted as idea, tool not proposed.

name: ShareX
good: After-capture task chains as an explicit ticked list running in order per capture, different hotkeys carrying different task sets, and a filename-pattern grammar stamping source application name + timestamp with monthly subfolders; since v19.0.1 automatic upload is off by default.
bad: Windows-only: ShareX runs on Windows 10 or later and, by the project's own statement, cannot be made multi-platform — its .NET stack, hundreds of native calls and UI prevent it running on Linux or Mac even via Mono. That excludes it from our Linux VM workflow entirely.
took: Two grammars recorded to adopt: a declared post-capture chain per capture type, and provenance-bearing filenames (sourceapp_YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS) as default for wiki captures; upload steps never in our chains.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — tool not adopted.

name: Rocketbook (destination symbols)
good: Seven printed symbols per page each assigned once to a destination; the owner marks an X in pen while writing, and scanning routes the page to that symbol's destination — filing decision made on the artefact, at writing time; QR carries page identity, bundling/format per symbol.
bad: Cloud destinations and proprietary notebook are not for us; vendor's own site was not opened this pass (manual + review only).
took: Transferable mechanic recorded: routing marked on the capture medium itself — a paper-notebook symbol/code convention the scan-ingest step reads.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — product not adopted.

name: reMarkable (handwriting conversion)
good: Conversion is a deliberate, selection-scoped act: select pages/lasso a region, convert to typed text as a new artefact, original handwritten pages stay untouched as source of truth.
bad: Conversion requires Wi-Fi and a signed-in reMarkable account — recognition happens in reMarkable's cloud, not on the device.
took: Interaction shape recorded (owner selects → convert → original preserved, conversion filed alongside).
didnt: IDEA ONLY — product not adopted; cloud recognition breaks privacy-absolute, so any wiki pen capture must convert locally with the scan in raw/ first.

name: ScanSnap profiles (Ricoh/PFU)
good: Profiles bundle scan settings, destination and follow-on action (up to 30 on device, 100 in software), so capture is load paper → pick profile → one button; the Quick Menu profile offers the decide-after alternative as a named switchable mode.
bad: Hardware- and software-locked: profiles are tied to the computer that created them — PFU help states the Scan button is disabled and settings cannot be modified for a profile not created on the connected computer — and the ScanSnap-specific driver provides no TWAIN/ISIS support on Windows and no TWAIN on macOS, so the scanner only interfaces directly with PFU's own software.
took: FOR US — as operating pattern for paper ingest: a tiny set of named scan profiles whose destination is a wiki inbox folder with naming/OCR steps attached; decide-after scan is the fallback, not the default.
didnt: Board — a tiny set of named scan profiles bundling settings, destination and follow-on action behind one button, with a named decide-after mode as fallback, as the operating pattern for wiki paper ingest; the proprietary ScanSnap hardware/software itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ABBYY FineReader Verification
licence: Proprietary product; the workflow is a practice, free to adopt.
good: OCR treated as guilty until verified: low-confidence words highlighted and queued in a Verification dialog beside a magnified image of the original, with suggested variants, Skip as explicit "checked, kept as-is", and Add to Dictionary so confirmed names stop being flagged.
bad: Proprietary and subscription-priced (FineReader Standard $99/year, Corporate $165/year on ABBYY's own page, with automated processing capped at 5,000 pages/month), and verification remains a manual operator queue. The FineReader guide also warns that sending a document to the OCR Editor loses attachments, bookmarks, comments and annotations.
took: FOR US — as quality practice for OCR ingest: OCR'd sources that will be quoted/compiled from carry a low-confidence word list presented as a verification queue, with confirmed words feeding a project dictionary.
didnt: Board — OCR treated as guilty until verified: low-confidence words highlighted in a verification queue beside a magnified original, explicit Skip for checked-as-is, and a project dictionary fed by confirmed words, as quality practice for wiki OCR ingest; the proprietary product itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Open Library Books/Covers APIs
licence: Open data/API (Internet Archive), free without a key.
good: Identifier-first capture: supply the ISBN printed on the artefact and the harness fetches title, authors, publisher, date, page count and cover; records available as .json/.rdf/.yml, and etiquette is shaped for deliberate per-item human capture.
bad: Strictly throttled and deliberately not a backend: 1 request/second by default, 3/second only for identified requests carrying a User-Agent and contact email, caching is required, bulk download via the API and use as a high-traffic commercial backend are expressly prohibited on pain of aggressive rate limiting or blocking, and the Legacy JSON API is deprecated.
took: FOR US — back end for a book-capture door: scan ISBN → fetch metadata + cover → land a source record in the wiki with fetch URL and date as provenance.
didnt: Board — an identifier-first book-capture door (scan ISBN, fetch Books/Covers metadata and cover, land a wiki source record with fetch URL and date as provenance), used within the stated per-item, non-bulk rate limits. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ambient AI wearables (Limitless pendant; Bee; Omi; Friend)
good: Hands-free, always-on capture removes the friction of starting a recording: the Limitless Pendant remembers what you say throughout the day from meetings to impromptu conversations, then delivers Smart Summaries of the whole day, replayable Perfect Recall audio, automatic speaker recognition from a 20-second sample, reminders and meeting prep, across 100+ languages.
bad: There is no capture act — devices record by default, transcripts/summaries accumulate in the vendor's app/cloud, the owner's role is reviewing/muting/opting out after the fact, and Limitless's Consent Mode shipped off by default at launch.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "the category is the owner's rejected pattern in hardware form: auto-capture of life, cloud-held, with deliberateness as an opt-out".

name: Firefox Reader View + Mozilla Readability.js
good: One toggle re-renders a page as a clean single column with exactly five persistent controls (font, size, content width, line spacing, theme); Readability scores DOM nodes by text/link density to extract title, content, excerpt, byline and length.
bad: Heuristic and unsafe by itself: isProbablyReaderable is described in its own README as quick-and-dirty and likely to produce both false positives and false negatives, parse() mutates the DOM unless you pass a clone, the bundled JSDOMParser is restricted to XML-compatible markup and not recommended for general use, and sanitising output is explicitly not Readability's job — a sanitiser such as DOMPurify plus CSP is strongly recommended for untrusted input.
took: FOR US — Lens needs the same contract: a "Read" toggle re-rendering any compiled page in one column under the owner's saved typography profile, with chrome/graph furniture gone.
didnt: Board — the Reader View contract for the Lens: a 'Read' toggle that re-renders a compiled page in one clean column under the owner's saved typography profile, with extraction heuristics treated as fallible and any extracted output sanitised. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Readability Consortium / Readability Matters
good: Controlled experiments (386 adults, 16 fonts) found changing to a reader's best font yielded +38 WPM on average and +93 WPM for the top quartile, comprehension unchanged; personalised formats also improved child outcomes, with inter-letter spacing most effective for dyslexia.
bad: 80% of readers believed their preferred font was their most effective; it was true only 18% of the time — familiarity predicted neither preference nor effectiveness.
took: FOR US — build the Lens reading profile as a calibration (timed self-test with comprehension checks recommending the fastest preset), not a settings page.
didnt: Adopt/build — the Lens reading profile as a timed calibration with comprehension checks that recommends the fastest preset, not a settings page (preference does not predict effectiveness, per the study); built 2026-10-20, Phase 8, as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Atkinson Hyperlegible (+ Next)
good: Designed for low-vision readers by maximising letterform distinction so homoglyphs (I/l/1, O/0, rn/m) cannot collide; legibility is in the glyphs and survives screen, PDF, print and e-ink; Next adds variable weights, 150+ languages and a monospace version.
bad: Narrow scope and a thin original release: the Institute frames the family solely around low-vision letterform distinction, the original 2019 font shipped only four styles in two weights with accent support for 27 languages (the gaps Next was created in 2025 to fill), and the official download is gated behind a required email-address form; the page offers no spacing, line-height or layout guidance to go with the glyphs.
took: FOR US — add Atkinson Hyperlegible (and its Mono for IDs/hashes/citation locators) as a candidate in the reading-profile calibration and as PDF fallback face.
didnt: Adopt/build — Atkinson Hyperlegible and its Mono (for IDs, hashes and citation locators) as candidate faces in the Lens reading-profile calibration and as a PDF fallback face, matching the reading profile built 2026-10-20 with Atkinson recorded as a candidate face. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Lexend
licence: SIL Open Font License via Google Fonts
good: Variable font whose axis is character expansion, treating spacing as a prescription chosen by measured Words Correct per Minute; demonstration study reported 17 of 19 third-graders scoring better than in Times New Roman (+19.8 WCPM, p = 0.014).
bad: Headline study is creator-run, n = 20 children reading aloud, not independently replicated at scale.
took: The axis idea recorded: one continuous "expansion" slider (letter-spacing + scale) inside the reading profile.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — skip the font adoption decision until calibration can judge it like any other candidate.

name: WCAG 2.2 §1.4.8 + §1.4.12
good: Numeric, testable reading targets: line width ≤80 characters, no full justification, line spacing ≥1.5×, paragraph spacing ≥1.5× line spacing, resize to 200% without horizontal scroll, and §1.4.12 override values with no loss of content.
bad: Limited reach as a standard: 1.4.8 is Level AAA, applies only to blocks of text, and requires only that a mechanism be available — which may be relied on from the user agent, with scaling described as primarily a user-agent responsibility — rather than that the default presentation meet the numbers; the Understanding text also carves out small-screen devices and very long words/URIs from the no-horizontal-scroll expectation.
took: FOR US — adopt as typography gate for both the Lens stylesheet and WeasyPrint PDF templates, each number converted into a CSS assertion/smoke-test.
didnt: Board — converting the 1.4.8/1.4.12 numbers (≤80-character measure, ≥1.5× line spacing, 200% resize without horizontal scroll, and the 1.4.12 override values) into CSS assertions/smoke tests acting as a typography gate for the Lens stylesheet and the PDF templates. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BDA dyslexia-friendly mode (Smashing Magazine implementation)
licence: article content; the technique is unencumbered practice
good: Complete code-level recipe as a body-class toggle, with the honest negative that font choice shows little benefit — spacing matters (letter-spacing 0.35ch, word-spacing 1.225ch, ligatures off, line-height 2.0, cream background, ≥4.5:1 but not maximum contrast, zebra striping).
bad: Self-acknowledged limits in the article itself: it builds only on English-language research generalisable to Latin and Cyrillic scripts, with other languages/scripts needing the guidelines tailored or ignored; its ch-based spacing values are an approximation that needs adjusting for fonts with a narrow or wide zero glyph; and it admits no dyslexia-specific research was found for its zebra striping, which was added on one dyslexic reader's request — as was the increase of paragraph spacing from 3em to 3.5em.
took: FOR US — implement as the Lens's "Comfort" preset inside the reading profile: one class toggle, ~40 lines of CSS, values already evidence-checked.
didnt: Board — a Lens 'Comfort' preset inside the reading profile: one body-class toggle applying the article's spacing values (letter-spacing 0.35ch, word-spacing 1.225ch, ligatures off, line-height 2.0, cream background), treated as a preset to calibrate rather than settled evidence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: W3C COGA "Making Content Usable"
good: Design-pattern library for cognitive/learning disabilities (explicitly covering ADHD) with personalisation as a key mechanism: clear purpose at top, summary of any long document, chunked content with descriptive headings, consistent furniture, multiple ways to understand content.
bad: Guidance, not a standard, with acknowledged gaps: W3C states Making Content Usable is an informative Working Group Note (not a W3C standard), that following the supplemental guidance is not required to meet WCAG, that some cognitive accessibility user needs are not addressed in existing W3C standards, and that the personalisation standards COGA treats as a key mechanism are still in development.
took: FOR US — as a checklist delta: every long compiled page opens with purpose + summary + contents, uses one consistent layout, and never makes the reader hold state across a scroll; COGA asks for added summaries/structure, never removal of the rigorous layer.
didnt: Board — a COGA checklist delta for compiled pages: purpose and summary at the top of every long page, chunked content under descriptive headings, one consistent layout, and no requirement for the reader to hold state across a scroll — added structure, never removal of the rigorous layer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: axe-core
good: Accessibility rules engine (inside Lighthouse/Accessibility Insights) running WCAG 2.0/2.1/2.2 rule sets against a live DOM with structured violations; zero-false-positives is its stated design goal, making it gate-able.
bad: README's own bound: it finds on average 57% of WCAG issues automatically, returning the rest as "incomplete" for manual review.
took: FOR US — add an axe lane to the Lens smoke suite over Briefing, a compiled page, Ask results and graph view in both themes and the Comfort preset.
didnt: Adopt/build — an axe-core lane in the Lens smoke suite (WCAG rule sets run over Briefing, a compiled page, Ask results and graph view, in both themes and the Comfort preset), as recorded in this row's took field; MPL-2.0 permits using the engine itself, and its zero-false-positives design goal is what makes it gate-able (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Microsoft Immersive Reader (Line Focus)
licence: Service is proprietary (Azure Cognitive Services); the mechanic is a CSS mask + scroll handler, re-implementable
good: Line Focus darkens everything except a moving window of one, three or five lines, externalising place-keeping; panel also groups Column Width, Page Color, Text Spacing, Syllables and Read Aloud — adjustments that survive contact with real readers.
bad: A proprietary cloud service, not a component: it is an Azure Applied AI Service embedded via a single API call, metered beyond 3M free characters per month on the pricing page, and it builds on other Azure AI services (Translator, text-to-speech, Computer Vision) — so using the service itself means sending reading content to Microsoft's cloud, against local-first custody, even though the Line Focus mechanic is simple to re-implement.
took: FOR US — implement Line Focus natively as a Lens reading-profile option (1/3/5 lines, keyboard-advanced), alongside column-width steps.
didnt: Board — Line Focus re-implemented natively as a Lens reading-profile option (a 1/3/5-line moving window via CSS mask and scroll handling, keyboard-advanced), while rejecting the Azure Immersive Reader service itself on custody and proprietary-service grounds. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NN/g on dark mode (Kohler & Zhang, 2023)
good: Survey + usability study findings: preference splits roughly in thirds, users set preference at system level and often don't notice app violations, and dark-first design does not improve usability.
bad: Aesthetically pleasing design cannot compensate for poor usability fundamentals (as reported in the study).
took: FOR US — standing rule: Lens defaults from prefers-color-scheme with manual override, dark theme as a real palette (never inversion, never pure-black behind long text), light remains default for long-form reading and PDFs.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms the Lens theming rule recorded in this row's took field: default from prefers-color-scheme with manual override, dark theme as a real palette (never inversion, never pure black behind long text), and light kept as the default for long-form reading and PDFs (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Andy Matuschak's stacked notes
licence: System is not released (author's own note); pattern is public and re-implementable, MIT Obsidian Sliding Panes plugin re-implements it
good: Clicking a link opens the note beside the current one in a stacking deck, earlier notes visible as titled spines; the trail is serialised in the URL (?stackedNotes=id,id,…) so a reading path is addressable, restorable and shareable, with hover previews before committing.
bad: Not a product anyone can adopt: the author states plainly that he has not made the system available for others to use and that it is still an early research environment; the notes are written for himself by default, may seem confusing or under-explained to other readers, and the site offers no index or navigational aids beyond following links from a starting point.
took: FOR US — build a Lens "Trail" mode: following a link appends the page to a visible stack encoded in the URL, so a session is resumable and a trail can be handed to another agent as a link.
didnt: Adopt/build — a Lens 'Trail' mode re-implementing the public pattern (following a link appends the page to a visible stack serialised in the URL, so a reading path is resumable and shareable), matching the Trails work built 2026-10-20 with Matuschak's stacked notes recorded as its source/inspiration. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TiddlyWiki (Story River)
licence: TiddlyWiki is open source (BSD-style licence); pattern in any case
good: Every opened tiddler joins one vertical "story river" column in open order, with a sidebar Open tab listing everything in the river (jump, close, close all) — you always know what your current reading set is.
bad: The river gets unwieldy as it grows, by its own documentation: when both the story river and the sidebar extend below the screen there are two competing scrollbars, closing tiddlers one by one to find one is described as a clunky approach many new users try, and closing a tiddler in the middle of the river makes everything below it slide up to take its place.
took: Open-tab mechanic recorded as companion piece if Trail mode ships: a visible, reorderable, closable list of what is in this reading session.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — river fits sequential surfaces better than compiled-page reading, where stacked notes win.

name: GOV.UK contents list
licence: GOV.UK design resources openly published (OGL); component pattern is public practice
good: User-researched contents component (navigation landmark, announced item count, current part indicated); research found users "chapter-scan and hop" via contents links, and streamlining a long list from 10 items to 5 measurably reduced confusion.
bad: A long contents list itself became the obstacle in the May 2024 project.
took: FOR US — compiled pages and PDF reports get a contents list under the summary, generated from H2s only, held to roughly ≤7 items, carried into PDFs with page numbers.
didnt: Adopt/build — a contents list under the summary on compiled pages and PDF reports, generated from H2s only, held to roughly seven items or fewer, and carried into PDFs with page numbers, as recorded in this row's took field; the pattern is openly published GOV.UK practice, so nothing proprietary is taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LiquidText
good: Pairs every document with an infinite workspace: drag a passage out and it becomes a movable, groupable, connectable excerpt object while remaining live-linked to its exact source location; pinch collapses a document so distant passages/hits sit side by side.
bad: Proprietary and app-bound: excerpts, links and workspaces are created and viewed inside LiquidText projects, and the official pages document no plain-file, API or self-hosted custody route for that synthesis. The vendor's current company page also narrows the product's presented focus to lawyers, legal teams and enterprise deployments.
took: Pattern recorded as long-horizon form of the citation-viewer delta: excerpts as cite-anchored markdown blocks, not a proprietary canvas.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — not a build now.

name: Readwise Reader (triage states delta)
good: Queue discipline: deliberate saves and automatic arrivals are different streams (Library vs Feed), and every item sits in exactly one explicit state (new / later / shortlist / archive / feed, feed split unseen/seen), with triage as a first-class keyboard-speed activity.
bad: Hosted subscription service with no permanent free tier shown on its official pricing page — free for the first 30 days, then $9.99/mo billed annually ($12.99 billed monthly). Its own docs also state a hard content limit: for copyright reasons it cannot import the full content of externally purchased books (e.g. Kindle or Apple Books), and an EPUB uploaded instead will not retain the highlights taken on the original platform.
took: State machine recorded as design for a Lens-visible ingest queue (states as frontmatter on raw items, surfaced in the Briefing), distinct from the approved annotation layer.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — not the service, and not a new build ahead of the wave-3 queue.

name: SuperMemo incremental reading
good: Most developed reading-queue system extant: priority queue with graceful overflow and auto-postpone, extracts becoming independent schedulable items with inherited priority, and reading position/re-read scheduling in the same system.
bad: A SuperMemo extract is a free-floating fragment; imported as-is it would violate our discipline that every kept fragment become a cited claim or stay in raw — "the extract button without the citation step is exactly how a wiki rots".
took: Part (a) recorded: a priority/overflow scheduling candidate for the owner's reading, companion to the ingest-queue find.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — extract mechanic must not cross over as-is.

name: Paged.js / CSS Paged Media practice
good: JavaScript polyfill implementing CSS Paged Media/GCPM in the browser: @page margin boxes, running headers via string-set, page counters, and target-counter cross-references resolving to real page numbers with TOC leaders — numbers computed at layout time so they can never go stale.
bad: WeasyPrint already implements most of GCPM natively, so Paged.js itself is not a pipeline replacement.
took: FOR US — as a gap audit on PDF deliverables: running section heads, "§x, page N" cross-references, TOC leaders, widow/orphan control, and WCAG type numbers in the print stylesheet.
didnt: Corroboration — the GCPM feature set Paged.js polyfills (running section heads, '§x, page N' cross-references resolved by target-counter, TOC leaders, widow/orphan control) serves as the gap-audit checklist for our WeasyPrint PDF deliverables; Paged.js itself is not adopted, since WeasyPrint already implements most of GCPM natively (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Vivliostyle
licence: Core/Viewer/CLI AGPL v3; VFM and Pub code Apache-2.0 — AGPL = ideas only
good: Single-source markdown → web, PDF and EPUB (SSMO) from shared CSS, with a Viewer paginating in-browser (paged view as a reading mode, not an export) and npm-packaged themes as versioned artefacts; proves the shape at production scale in Japanese commercial book publishing.
bad: The core engine, Viewer and CLI are AGPLv3: the project's own FAQ states that modifying and distributing Vivliostyle (web use counts as distribution) requires publishing the modified source, and a program incorporating it as a single combined program must be published under AGPL. The FAQ also records concrete typesetting gaps, e.g. citing issue #522 that 'reset-counter: page;' does not work properly with web publications.
took: Confirmation and the VFM lesson recorded: a small set of publishing extensions to markdown, formally specified.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — AGPL engine not adopted; WeasyPrint already covers the PDF leg.

name: KOReader
good: E-ink document viewer treating reading position as data (stored per document, synced, resumable anywhere), reading statistics feeding time-remaining estimates from measured speed, and an e-ink design mode (no animation, paginated menus, adjustable contrast), plus highlights export and OPDS/Wallabag.
bad: Scope is e-ink/Android/Linux only in the README — no iOS version is listed, and desktop use is a developer emulator on Linux and MacOS rather than a general desktop app. Installation is model-specific (separate steps for Android, Cervantes, Kindle, Kobo, Linux, PocketBook and reMarkable), and the README states the project is developed and supported by volunteers, with Liberapay as the only donation route.
took: Trio recorded as e-ink/offline direction: EPUB digest of briefing/key syntheses, reading position as a Lens sidecar, and time-remaining estimates from calibrated reading speed.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — format, not an app, is the way in; no code copied.

name: Speed-reading displays (RSVP) — Rayner et al. 2016 review
good: Authoritative synthesis of what the scientific community knows about the reading process and its implications for speed-reading courses and apps: it explains normal reading (200–400 wpm for good readers, language skill at the heart of speed), evaluates RSVP — words presented one at a time, freed from eye movements — and other presentation technologies, and identifies the legitimate faster route as practice and becoming a more skilled language user (e.g. increased vocabulary), with skimming available when moderate comprehension suffices.
bad: Standing scientific review: a hard trade-off between speed and accuracy; doubling/tripling speed without comprehension loss is not achievable (bottleneck is language processing/foveal span), RSVP removes regressions comprehension uses, and trained speed readers' gains are in substance trained skimming.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "no RSVP/'speed mode' in the Lens, ever: on a corpus whose entire value is verified comprehension, a feature whose measured effect is less understanding per page is anti-aligned".

name: Bionic Reading
licence: n/a (assessed via journal literature, as recorded)
good: As presented on its official site, Bionic Reading revises texts so the most concise parts of words are highlighted, guiding the eye over the text so the brain remembers previously learned words more quickly; it works through the interplay of 'Fixation', 'Saccade' and 'Opacity' visual stimuli, is individually adaptable to each reader, and aims at faster, better, more focused reading, including for the more than 15% the site says have serious reading difficulties (ADHD, dyslexia).
bad: Controlled eye-tracking test (Spear et al. 2025) found first-half bolding claims "were not supported", with costs relative to regular unbolded reading and no subgroup benefiting on speed or eye-movement measures, replicating earlier null results.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — do not add a "bionic" toggle; treated as the lane's cautionary tale that a formatting that feels faster is not faster.

name: Hearst, Search User Interfaces ch. 1 — hierarchical faceted metadata + query previews
licence: Book (commercial publisher; full text readable free at the source). Pattern/practice only.
good: Hierarchical faceted metadata lets a searcher start from any facet and narrow in any order; query previews show the count selecting each value would yield, and the vocabulary problem (~11–12% same-word agreement) is documented empirically.
bad: Parametric interfaces that hide counts until execution are called out as the failure mode, producing empty result sets users cannot anticipate.
took: FOR US — filter rail on Lens search results showing each facet value with its result count, zero-yield values greyed, all computed at build time from existing frontmatter.
didnt: Adopt/build — the filter rail on Lens search results showing each facet value with its result count, zero-yield values greyed, all computed at build time from existing frontmatter; built 2026-10-20, Phase 8 as facets on the Lens search, as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Morville & Callender, Search Patterns — faceted navigation layout
licence: Book excerpt on a magazine site. Pattern only.
good: Concrete layout rules worked out on a federated academic-library catalogue: collapsible facets, top four/five most populated values per facet, counts beside values, selected values restated as stacking breadcrumbs, filters independent and removable in arbitrary order.
bad: Anti-pattern named: Snooth-style interfaces revealing no counts until after execution are "hard on people but soft on hardware".
took: FOR US — these are the acceptance criteria for the facet rail: collapsed-by-default, top-5 by population, counts always visible, active filters as a removable chip stack above results.
didnt: Adopt/build — these layout rules as the acceptance criteria for the Lens facet rail: collapsed by default, top five values by population, counts always visible, active filters as a removable chip stack above results, filters independent and removable in arbitrary order; built 2026-10-20, Phase 8 with the Lens facets, as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tunkelang, Faceted Search (2009)
good: First comprehensive treatment; abstract states user studies demonstrate faceted search provides more effective support than best-first search even though users are more familiar with the latter; frames the known-item vs exploratory split and Endeca's "no dead ends" design goal.
bad: By its own description it is a short, deliberately non-exhaustive treatment — 79 pages, published June 1, 2009, stating 'Although we cannot hope to be exhaustive' and offering a self-contained introduction with an extensive bibliography rather than an implementation or evaluated system. Its examples and commercial practice are those of its era, centred on e-commerce and site search.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — recorded as evidence anchor for the facet finds; no separate build follows from the book itself.

name: Elasticsearch suggesters
licence: Documentation of a commercially-licensed engine (Elastic License / SSPL family) — pattern only, nothing copied
good: Term, phrase and completion suggesters draw every candidate from the indexed corpus's own term dictionary, never a general dictionary — so a suggestion is guaranteed to be a term that returns results, frequency-weighted, with phrase corrections ranked by a corpus n-gram model.
bad: Heavy, server-side machinery with sharp limits documented on the page itself: the term suggester's max_edits can only be 1 or 2, min_word_length defaults to 4, the term suggester does not take the request's query into account and leaves suggestion selection to the API consumer, and the phrase suggester 'requires special mapping up front' (custom trigram and reverse analyzers) to work at all.
took: FOR US — a "did you mean" for Lens search and the Ask door whose dictionary is the wiki itself (titles, tags, headings, body tokens), implementable over our own token index.
didnt: Elasticsearch itself is NOT proposed — a server engine for a static build is the wrong shape.

name: Algolia retrieval pipeline (preprocessing)
licence: Proprietary SaaS; blog post. Pattern only.
good: Four transferable moves: typo tolerance as retrieval with typo-count as a ranking criterion, one-way synonyms with direction, facet-tagging the query (detecting facet values in the query text), and a relaxation ladder that relaxes precision rules one by one rather than returning empty.
bad: The vendor's own post exposes the trade-offs: performing queries with all terms optional produces a large increase in matched records and pollutes faceting (any 'black' item matches 'iphone black case'), typosquatting is called 'a complex and difficult challenge', ranking depends sensitively on the order of criteria in the ranking formula, and proximity is capped at 8 so distances beyond that are indistinguishable. It is also a proprietary hosted engine, so the pipeline cannot be inspected or run locally.
took: FOR US — as checklist against our pipeline: facet-tagging is the standout, and the relaxation ladder's engine-side rule (relax one constraint at a time and say which was relaxed).
didnt: Rejected — the Algolia engine itself: proprietary SaaS and a hosted server shape, wrong for a local-first, static-build wiki; only its preprocessing moves are kept, as the checklist pattern already recorded in took. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Baymard Institute — "no results" page strategies
licence: Research institute article (free summary of premium research). Practice only.
good: Large-scale usability findings with five ordered strategies: related categories, alternative searches with previewed results (auto-apply if exactly one works, with notice), personalised recommendations, a direct human/help route, and popular content as the floor.
bad: Nearly 50% of sites fail to provide effective recovery from a no-results search, and generic "search tips" text is rarely read and doesn't work as the only help.
