took: FOR US — translated to our surfaces: nearest wiki sections, relaxed-query alternatives with previews, recently viewed pages, "Ask instead" carrying the query, and most-linked pages as the floor.
didnt: Adopt/build — the designed zero-results surface plus save-the-failed-search, translating the five strategies to our surfaces (nearest wiki sections, relaxed-query alternatives with previews, recently viewed pages, 'Ask instead' carrying the query, most-linked pages as the floor); built 2026-10-20, Phase 8, as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Algolia InstantSearch conditional display
good: Treats no results, no query yet, and search error as three different conditions with three different surfaces; on the no-results surface it puts the reset (ClearRefinements) control on the zero page itself.
bad: Conflating the three states (a spinner that is actually an error, an empty-query state that looks like a failure) is the bug the guide exists to prevent.
took: FOR US — every Lens zero state should say which state it is, show the active refinement stack, and offer one-click clearing from the zero page; Ask abstention display disciplined the same way.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms the discipline for every Lens zero state: say which state it is (no results, no query yet, or error), show the active refinement stack, and offer one-click clearing from the zero page itself, with the Ask abstention display disciplined the same way, as recorded in this row's took field (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Prefixbox — no-results page examples roundup
good: Worked survey of 12 production zero-results pages, plus two mechanics Baymard lacks: eBay's save-the-failed-search (save and alert when it matches) and GAP's auto-correct-and-show (corrected results immediately, correction visible, no interstitial click).
bad: A vendor's e-commerce roundup, not evaluated evidence: every example is a retail product search, several showcased pages are weak by the post's own account (Disney's 'isn't very helpful'; Costco misses offering alternative results based on popularity or user behaviour), and the guidance rests on anecdote and a cited Baymard statistic rather than any test of the mechanics. Nothing in it addresses knowledge search or a citation contract.
took: Two mechanics recorded as variants to choose between: save-the-failed-search as bridge to standing queries, and auto-correct-and-show as the aggressive end of the did-you-mean spectrum.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — general guidelines duplicate Baymard; auto-correct must never fire silently on the Ask door, where it would break the citation contract.

name: NN/g Heuristic 9 poster
good: Canonical heuristic — error messages in plain language, precisely indicating the problem and constructively suggesting a solution — with a no-search-results page as its worked example prescribing popular topics as help.
bad: The source itself frames the heuristics as "broad rules of thumb and not specific usability guidelines": Heuristic 9 is a single sentence plus a note on visual treatment, with no thresholds, test procedure, or implementation detail, so it can judge an error message but cannot specify or verify one.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — filed deliberately thin as corroboration from the canonical source; no build follows that the Baymard/InstantSearch finds don't already specify.

name: A Survey of Conversational Search (Mo, Mao, Zhao et al. 2024)
good: Organises conversational search into four load-bearing modules (reformulation → clarification → retrieval → response generation); clarification's contract is to proactively ask rather than directly answer when intent is unclear.
bad: The survey is explicit that the hard problem is accurately and efficiently identifying when clarification is necessary and generating appropriate questions — asking is cheap, knowing when not to answer yet is the research problem.
took: FOR US — a clarification turn for the Ask door when evidence genuinely splits (2–3 candidate interpretations as tappable chips before answering), triggered by a measurable evidence split, not a model's mood.
didnt: Corroboration — the survey's four-module organisation (reformulation, clarification, retrieval, response generation) and clarification's ask-rather-than-answer contract confirm the Ask door's design; our clarification turn is recorded in lane8-dispositions.md under the ClariQ pattern, and the survey adds the trigger discipline — clarify on a measurable evidence split (2–3 candidate interpretations as tappable chips), not a model's mood (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ClariQ / Qulac / MIMICS (clarification datasets)
licence: Research datasets (licences vary; none needs to be copied)
good: Benchmark layer showing clarification need is gradable, not binary (ClariQ annotates need on a scale, enabling a threshold policy), and that good clarifying questions are mostly facet keywords — "which facet value did you mean?" — with MIMICS derived from Bing's production clarification pane and real engagement signals.
bad: Scale and provenance limit all three: ClariQ's train/dev set is only 187/50 topics extended from Qulac's TREC Web Track data over ClueWeb09/12, its roughly 1 million multi-turn conversations are synthetic, and MIMICS is Bing-log-specific (clarification panes with up to five candidate answers, only ~2k manually labelled queries) with its GitHub repo archived.
took: Implementation sketch recorded for the clarification find: facet-generated clarification chips plus an evidence-split trigger (below threshold answer, above it ask once).
didnt: IDEA ONLY — design lesson is the find, datasets not copied.

name: Algolia InstantSearch performance guide
licence: Vendor documentation. Numbers are Algolia's guidance for its hosted engine — design targets, not measurements of our system
good: Published latency budget: 200 ms preferred debounce (over 300 ms degrades experience), stalled-search indicator appearing only on stall (default 200 ms), preconnect at page load, and session caching with explicit discard guidance.
bad: The guidance is tied to Algolia's hosted engine: it assumes a preconnect handshake to an Algolia domain, and the guide's own QPS section notes every keystroke in a SearchBox counts as one operation against the plan's maximum QPS and operations limit, with extra widgets adding more operations per keystroke — so the budget is inseparable from a metered hosted service, not a local index.
took: FOR US — as budget sheet for any as-you-type surface and the pending instant-lane decision: results feel continuous at ~200 ms, stall signalled at ~200 ms, nothing may degrade past ~300 ms.
didnt: Corroboration — the published 200 ms preferred / 300 ms degrading debounce budget confirms our instant-lane design targets; Algolia's hosted engine itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Scatter/Gather (Cutting, Karger, Pedersen & Tukey, SIGIR 1992)
good: Founding paper of result clustering as a visible interface: scatter a result set into a few clusters with short summaries, gather selected groups and re-scatter finer — keyword search as the book's index, Scatter/Gather as its table of contents, suited to queries retrieving too many documents.
bad: The paper itself records the standing objections it must answer: document clustering is often too slow for large corpora (running times often quadratic in the number of documents) and cluster search is not markedly superior to near-neighbour search and in some situations inferior; the method also targets vague, hard-to-formulate browsing needs rather than a specific query, and depends on cluster descriptions that are revealing yet short enough to scan together.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — at our scale a ranked list plus facets answers the need; clustering earns its complexity at thousands of hits.

name: Carrot2
licence: Not stated on the page opened (project is open source); nothing proposes copying code
good: Groups hits on the fly with human-readable labels ("dynamic facets" per query), runs clustering on query-focused highlights, and treats an explicit "Other Topics" bucket as a first-class output rather than force-filing leftovers.
bad: Docs insist clustering "requires at least a few dozen documents in order to make sense" and a fetch window of at least ~100 — the technique publishes its own operating range.
took: One morsel recorded as applicable today: any grouping over results should carry an explicit "unclustered / other" remainder rather than silently absorbing leftovers.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — same scale verdict as Scatter/Gather.

name: Hearst, Search User Interfaces — result surrogates, previews and sitelinks
good: Defines what a result entry owes the searcher: previews/surrogates supporting a judgement before any click (matched passage in context), and sitelinks/deep links exposing a hit's important sub-pages so the searcher can jump in at the right depth.
bad: Plain Lens search results, by contrast in the file, are essentially title pointers.
took: FOR US — Lens result entries should show the matched passage with terms marked, and long pages should expose section headings as deep-link sub-entries under the hit.
didnt: Adopt/build — Lens result entries showing the matched passage with terms marked, and long pages exposing their section headings as deep-link sub-entries under the hit; built 2026-10-20, Phase 8 as passage-level search results, as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: My NCBI / PubMed saved searches and alerts
licence: Public documentation of a public service. Pattern only.
good: Standing query perfected: one click turns a search into a named durable object with save-only or alert modes (daily/weekly/monthly), capped digest delivery shape, and central management (edit, pause, delete) — the searcher's own query re-run against new material.
bad: Official NLM help page failed to fetch in this pass; mechanics verified via a library guide to the official flow.
took: FOR US — owner-saved queries stored as a small wiki file, re-run at build/sweep, Briefing gaining a named "since you last looked" capped line per standing query.
didnt: Adopt/build — owner-saved standing queries stored as a small wiki file, re-run at build/sweep, with the Briefing gaining a named, capped 'since you last looked' line per standing query; built 2026-10-20, Phase 8 as standing queries + a ⌘K palette, as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Hearst, Search User Interfaces — search history and revisitation
good: Evidence base: over a year, 40% of search-result clicks were on previously clicked pages and 71% of revisits used the identical query; 17% named not being able to return to a once-visited page among their biggest problems. Two tiers: automatic chronological recent queries, and deliberate named saves, with per-facet breadcrumb elements.
bad: The chapter is a 2009 synthesis and concedes the support is patchy: devising interfaces for the search process as a whole is "much less well-understood", "not many interfaces support all of this functionality", most of the worked systems are 1990s research prototypes, and it notes thumbnails in page history are useful while thumbnail search-results displays at best do not improve on text.
took: FOR US — a "recent & frequent" strip on Lens search kept client-side/local to the owner's browser: recent queries one tap to re-run, frequently-opened pages pinned by use.
didnt: Corroboration — the revisitation evidence (repeat clicks and identical re-queries) confirms keeping search history as a first-class, local feature; it is a book pattern only, with no code or system taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Command K bars (Maggie Appleton pattern analysis)
licence: Essay (pattern is public practice); cmdk/kbar MIT if ever used
good: Keyboard-summoned bar searching commands and content in one grouped, fuzzy-subsequence-matched list, with recents before typing and shortcuts shown at the right edge teaching themselves; core put at ~60 lines of vanilla JavaScript in a circulating teardown.
bad: The essay is an anecdotal pattern survey with no evaluation or usage data, and it surfaces the pattern's own weaknesses: the summoning shortcut is not standardised (CMD+K, CMD+E and CMD+/ are all contenders), the keyboard-first bar inherits the CLI's hiddenness the essay describes for command lines, and pre-built bars make it "easy for product teams to pop one of these in without thinking too much about it" despite stuffing in tabs, forms, menus and grids.
took: FOR US — a ⌘K overlay over the existing merged search index (pages, modes, a handful of actions) unifying surfaces already built instead of adding another.
didnt: Corroboration — the pattern confirms a single keyboard-summoned bar unifying content search and actions (a ⌘K palette was built in Phase 8, recorded in lane 8 under a different source pattern); the essay itself contributes the pattern analysis only, no library is adopted on its strength. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Bates's berrypicking (1989, via IXD@Pratt discussion)
licence: Academic discussion of a journal article. Theory/practice only.
good: Founding correction to one-query-one-answer: real searching is evolving berrypicking where the need changes as fragments are picked up, with named cheap transitions (footnote chasing, citation searching, area scanning, journal runs, mid-session pivots).
bad: The 1989 primary text itself was not reachable in this pass; the find rests on Pratt's academic discussion quoting/diagramming it.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — recorded as the model explaining why history/standing queries/palette matter, and as a speculative resumable search trail; no build proposed.

name: Algolia search analytics
licence: Vendor documentation; the service is not proposed in any part. Pattern only.
good: Owner-facing log surface as triage: popular searches with CTR/click position, Searches without Results, Searches without Clicks, Filters used, and rates as trends; zero-result/zero-click lists are work queues with diagnosis-matched remedies, and popular data aligns user vocabulary with the database's.
bad: The metrics only exist inside Algolia's hosted dashboard and only if the site sends events to Algolia: click-through rate, click position and searches-without-clicks all require sending click (and conversion) events, users are distinguished by IP address by default, as-you-type searches are aggregated within 30 seconds, and revenue and filter analytics are optional features — so the triage view means exporting a personal query log to a vendor, against local-first custody.
took: FOR US — as interface spec for a periodic "search health" review over the existing query log: top zero-result and zero-click queries pre-diagnosed as missing page / missing words / ranking bury, filed sweep-shaped in the owner's own wiki.
didnt: Corroboration — the zero-result / zero-click lists as diagnosis-matched work queues confirm a periodic search-health review over our own query log; Algolia's hosted analytics service is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TimelineJS — group rows (Knight Lab)
licence: MPL-2.0 (library, stated on its own page)
good: The group property assigns each event to a named row, turning a single timeline into labelled swimlanes over the same clock; free, from spreadsheets or JSON.
bad: Knight Lab guidance caps a readable timeline at ~20 slides, and its privacy FAQ is blunt: the spreadsheet route requires the sheet to be public.
took: FOR US — grouping mechanic as the Lens timeline's next shape: lanes by record type (decisions, claim lifecycle, filings, corrections) derived at build time; self-hosted-JSON route only.
didnt: The public-spreadsheet route is rejected inside this find as a disclosure; the tool itself is not adopted (Lens has a Timeline mode).

name: LifeFlow / EventFlow (UMD HCIL)
licence: Tool: UMD-licensed, not open (EventFlow distributed via UMD OTC, commercial licensing). Aggregation form is a published research design.
good: Aggregates thousands of event sequences sharing a prefix into one icicle flow — width = how many records pass through an event, position = typical time gap — so what usually happens after X, and how often, is visible, with rare paths visibly thin.
bad: The tool is not adoptable (commercial/review-copy distribution).
took: FOR US (the form, not the tool) — render claim lifecycles LifeFlow-style across lifecycle-bearing pages to show which paths the corpus uses and which states are dead ends, with one claim's history highlightable as a path.
didnt: Adopt/build — the LifeFlow aggregation form (not the UMD-licensed tool, which is not open) for rendering claim lifecycles across lifecycle-bearing pages, showing which paths the corpus uses and which states are dead ends, with one claim's history highlightable as a path; built as part of the state-shaped views in Phase 8. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Histography
licence: Closed web artwork; no reusable licence.
good: Award-winning, self-updating timeline of ~15,000 Wikipedia events, one dot per event with density swelling into a waveform, category filters and per-dot drill-down; widely praised as "hypnotic".
bad: Density measures how much was written down, and the eye reads it as how much mattered — on our corpus it would render Mehmed's busiest days as the wiki's most "significant" periods.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "coverage masquerading as importance. Beautiful, and a lie of emphasis."

name: EPPI-Mapper (evidence-and-gap maps)
licence: Free for EPPI-Reviewer users; the method is published Campbell/EPPI practice.
good: Renders a standalone interactive HTML matrix from coded records (mosaic squares or bubble counts), every cell/header click-through to its records, filters recomputing the matrix, and an empty cell as a first-class result — the gap the map exists to expose; the method states the map shows what evidence is available, not what it concludes.
bad: Bubble view is explicitly not adopted in the file: area ∝ count is the weaker encoding.
took: FOR US — a Lens coverage matrix (topics/entities × verification state) computed at build time, mosaic-style, every cell click-through, empty/stale-heavy cells surfaced as the work list; called the strongest find in this lane.
didnt: Bubble view not adopted.

name: Palladio (Stanford Humanities + Design)
licence: Open source per the project page (specific licence not stated there — flagged, not assumed).
good: Four coordinated views over one table (Map, Graph, List, Gallery) with a timeline/timespan filter brushing all views at once, data processed locally in the browser.
bad: Its Map view needs literal latitude/longitude columns and shows at most two attributes at a time.
took: Coordination pattern recorded: one shared filter state across Lens modes, especially a time brush shared by Timeline/Graph/Cards.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — the tool itself does nothing our build doesn't.

name: StoryMapJS (Knight Lab)
licence: Free tool (Knight Lab); hosted editor is a service, not a library we can wall off.
good: Narrative cartography: a slide deck pinning text/media to map locations panned between in story order, plus gigapixel deep-zoom image stories.
bad: Our compiled layer carries almost no coordinates (places are names in prose), so a map would plot a handful of pins as decoration; and a story map imposes one authored order on reference knowledge — the opposite of a wiki's job.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — both data and form reasons stated; honest first step if coordinates accumulate is a plain pin layer, not a narrative.

name: RAWGraphs
good: Maintained catalogue of unconventional chart forms with working d3 implementations (alluvial, streamgraph, treemap, sunburst, circle packing, dendrograms, matrix plot, Gantt, horizon, bumpchart, parallel coordinates), each chart a module with a declared data shape.
bad: RAWGraphs will happily draw any of these from any table — the honesty gate must decide which forms our numbers may use.
took: FOR US — as reference catalogue and implementation source for Lens forms (build-time SVG from our own JSON, no runtime dependency), e.g. streamgraph/alluvial for state flows, treemap/sunburst for corpus composition, matrix plot for the coverage matrix.
didnt: Adopt/build — RAWGraphs as the reference catalogue and implementation source for Lens forms (build-time SVG from our own JSON, no runtime dependency), e.g. streamgraph/alluvial for state flows, treemap/sunburst for corpus composition and a matrix plot for the coverage matrix, with the honesty gate deciding which forms our numbers may use; Apache-2.0. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Skosmos (National Library of Finland)
good: Browses SKOS vocabularies as a place: SPARQL-backed alphabetical index, concept hierarchy tree (jsTree), concept pages with broader/narrower/related, REST API, and new/changed concepts as their own list.
bad: PHP + a SPARQL endpoint is a platform our static build neither needs nor should grow.
took: Rendering idea recorded: if the tag registry outgrows a flat list, a build-time Lens hierarchy page (tree + alphabetical index + per-tag page counts) in Skosmos's form.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — Skosmos itself not adopted; delta on the wave-6 SKOS registry, not a re-proposal.

name: Argdown
good: Lightweight argument syntax designed to live inside Markdown ([Statement], <Argument>, + / − support/attack, #tags, {source:} metadata) compiling to an argument map (SVG/PDF/DOT/GraphML/JSON or embeddable web component); the diagram is derived from text that stays readable as text.
bad: Argdown's own syntax documentation states the parser will not check consistency: "Currently the Argdown parser will not check if the derived relations are consistent with the explicitly defined relations. It is possible to create 'nonsense' relations", and it likewise can not and will not check that members of an equivalence class really are logically and semantically equivalent — so a map can be well-formed and still incoherent, with no lint to catch it.
took: FOR US — optional Argdown block inside a claims/synthesis page, compiled at Lens build time to inline SVG, as a per-page opt-in for genuinely argumentative pages, not a corpus-wide conversion.
didnt: Adopt/build — an optional Argdown block inside a claims/synthesis page, compiled at Lens build time to inline SVG, as a per-page opt-in for genuinely argumentative pages (MIT-licensed; argument maps from Argdown are recorded as built in Phase 8 in lane 8), not a corpus-wide conversion. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Kialo
licence: Proprietary hosted platform (free tiers; Kialo Inc.).
good: Tree discipline: a thesis at the root, recursive Pro/Con claims (under 500 characters, sources linkable) with a sunburst mini-map, and an edit-proposal workflow handling move/archive/clarify per claim — every objection attaches to the exact claim it attacks.
bad: Impact votes sort arguments by the crowd's averaged rating; the platform is unusable for a private wiki regardless.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY for the tree discipline (already substantially our design); impact voting recorded as an anti-pattern — it would put a number that looks like evidence-weight on claims decided by citations and the owner, with exactly one voter.

name: AIF (Argument Interchange Format)
good: Argument graphs as typed nodes (I-nodes, RA-nodes for inference applications, CA-nodes for conflict, PA-nodes for preference) with argumentation schemes as first-class, queryable structure; AIFdb holds 4,000+ maps.
bad: AIF is an ontology, not a usable tool: its extended form AIF-RDF is expressed in the RDFS semantic language and its reifications span MySQL schema, RDF, Prolog and JSON, so using it means importing RDF/OWL-style machinery; and its infrastructure has decayed — the format's own website and the AIFdb site linked as its data home no longer resolve/serve (404).
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — design reference only; "No RDF/OWL machinery enters a markdown wiki on the strength of this find."

name: CmapTools / Novak concept-mapping practice (IHMC)
licence: CmapTools is freeware (IHMC), not open source; the method is published practice.
good: Concept maps as networks of propositions — concept → linking words → concept — hierarchically arranged under a focus question with cross-links; the software demands linking words, because the label on the edge is the knowledge.
bad: The method is entirely manual and author-dependent: the IHMC theory paper stresses working memory processes only a few units at once (relationships among two or three concepts are about the limit), that large knowledge structures must be built up piece by piece through orderly iterations, and that meaningful learning depends on the author's prior knowledge and motivation — and the paper documents no automatic validation that a linking phrase forms a true proposition, so map quality rests wholly on the mapper.
took: Focus-question habit recorded for synthesis pages (a map/synthesis answers one stated question).
didnt: IDEA ONLY — batch 3.1 typed edges are the same medicine in stronger, lintable form; CmapTools stands as comparison point against freehand diagram pages.

name: Kumu
good: Causal-loop diagram notation: directed connections with labels and polarity (+/−), and named feedback loops annotated R (reinforcing) or B (balancing) as first-class objects.
bad: Platform is disqualified on privacy alone (a private wiki's maps cannot live in someone else's cloud, free-public or paid).
took: Notation recorded: CLD polarity + R/B loop labels as the disciplined way to draw causal claims, as an Argdown-style text-first artefact, not a Kumu embed.
didnt: IDEA ONLY — platform not adopted.

name: Anki statistics (Future Due forecast + review calendar)
licence: Anki is GPL-3.0-family open source; design borrow, not code.
good: Future Due draws two scenarios at once (due load if you keep up, shaded due load if you do nothing), plus a calendar heatmap of past activity; the community Review Heatmap extends the calendar both directions.
bad: Manual states the chart's own blind spot: it does not count currently-overdue items, so a backlog is invisible in it; streak framing is explicitly not adopted in the file.
took: FOR US — delta on the FSRS item: Lens Briefing renders a 90-day calendar with exact due counts, scheduled-load bars, do-nothing scenario shaded, and — correcting Anki's flaw — overdue pages as their own visible block.
didnt: Streak framing explicitly not adopted.

name: Bullet graphs (Stephen Few)
licence: Published design specification (a form, not software).
good: Replacement for gauges: one bar = value, a tick = target/comparison, single-hue background bands = qualitative ranges, all on honest linear scales from zero — a complete claim (what it is, what it should be, what "good" means) in one line of ink.
bad: Each bullet carries exactly one featured measure with at most one or two comparative markers and two to five qualitative ranges, so the form cannot show distributions, uncertainty, or trends over time; and the bands are only as honest as the thresholds someone declares for them — the form supplies no data labels or performance-gap readout of its own, which is why practitioners (e.g. the Clearly and Simply alternative design) add labels and an explicit gap display the original specification lacks.
took: FOR US — Briefing health numbers should be bullets, not bare counts: value bar, baseline tick, and bands whose edges are our own declared thresholds/policy.
didnt: Adopt/build — bullet graphs as the Briefing's health-number form (value bar, target tick, bands edged by our own declared thresholds); recorded in lane8-dispositions.md as built on 2026-10-20 in the Phase 8 briefing honesty stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sparklines and small multiples (Tufte; Few)
good: Word-sized sparklines embedded in text/tables, and small multiples — the same small chart repeated for many items always on the same scale — so differences between panels are differences in data, never framing; the form structurally forbids rescaling each panel to flatter its subject.
bad: A sparkline without its numbers is a mood, not a measure (as noted in the file).
took: FOR US — grammar for longitudinal numbers: one sparkline per lint lane/eval axis/graph headline in the Briefing, every panel same scale, labelled with first/last/exact current value in text beside it.
didnt: Adopt/build — sparklines and same-scale small multiples as the grammar for longitudinal numbers in the Briefing: one sparkline per lint lane, eval axis and graph headline, every panel on the same scale and labelled in text with its first, last and exact current value, so a sparkline is never left as an unnumbered mood. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Alberto Cairo, How Charts Lie
licence: A book (W. W. Norton, 2019); checklist discipline transfers.
good: Standard catalogue of chart deception (truncated axes, dual axes, 3D, area-for-value, dubious/insufficient data, concealed uncertainty, correlation as causation) as a checklist with named failure modes; portable rules include bars start at zero, no dual axes, length > area > angle, and captions stating what a chart cannot show.
bad: A general-audience trade book written to teach readers to read charts critically — Publishers Weekly calls it 'a valuable guide to reading charts with a critical and nuanced eye' — not a producer-side standard: its evidence is media-chart examples, and it ships no checklist in checkable form, no tooling, and no conformance test, so any build gate has to be distilled from prose.
took: FOR US — adopt as a chart-honesty gate in the Lens build checklist: every new visual ships with data source, encoding ranked against length>area>angle, zero baseline where bars are used, and an explicit "this view cannot show X" line.
didnt: Adopt/build — Cairo's failure-mode catalogue as the chart-honesty gate in the Lens build checklist; recorded in lane8-dispositions.md as built on 2026-10-20 in the Phase 8 briefing honesty stack, with Cairo named as the chart-honesty source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Vanity-metrics literature (Ries, The Lean Startup, et al.)
licence: Practitioner literature; the test is a sentence, free to use.
good: Portable admission test for dashboard numbers — if this number moved 20% next week, here is exactly what I would do — with the fix usually the nearby rate, ratio or per-segment figure, which can go down and therefore can inform.
bad: Cumulative totals (registered users, downloads, total pages) grow by inertia, flatter by construction, and imply no action.
took: FOR US — Briefing admission rule: actionable figures (citation-lock coverage %, open Cases, pages past verified_until, MRR vs baseline) get prominent slots; corpus-growth figures that fail the 20% sentence print small as context or not at all.
didnt: Adopt/build — the vanity-metrics admission test as a Briefing admission rule: figures that pass the 20% sentence (citation-lock coverage %, open Cases, pages past verified_until, MRR vs baseline) get prominent slots, while cumulative corpus-growth figures that fail it print small as context or not at all. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Word clouds (Voyant Cirrus pattern)
licence: n/a — a form, assessed via its evaluation literature
good: Cirrus visualizes a corpus's or document's top-frequency words as a cloud: the most frequent terms are placed centrally and sized largest, hovering over a word shows its exact frequency count, clicking a word drives Voyant's other tools in multi-tool skins, and a Terms slider (default 50) plus stopword/whitelist, font-family and palette options configure the view; it can also be restricted to a single document. The documentation itself states that word colour and absolute position are not significant.
bad: Evaluation literature is consistent: font size is a poor quantitative channel, perceived size scales with word length as much as frequency, there is no reading order, plain alphabetical lists beat clouds for finding/comparing values, and frequency masquerades as importance.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — fails the honesty gate on three counts (undecodable encoding, length confound, vanity signal); a sorted bar list is the same data in an honest form.

name: Gource
licence: GPLv3 (ideas only under licence discipline, in any case)
good: OpenGL visualiser rendering a git repo as an animated tree with contributor avatars darting between files as commits land, exportable as a growth video.
bad: Its visual rhetoric is growth = health: a busy tree looks alive, a quiet one dead — for a wiki whose doctrine is that a faster incorrect corpus is worse than a slower correct one, our best days (a correction, a retraction) would render as shrinkage.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — "an activity-is-progress animation is the precise inversion of the truth".

name: IIIF + Mirador
licence: IIIF is an open specification; Mirador is open source (per the IIIF site; licence text not re-opened in this pass — flagged).
good: Images become addressable objects via a JSON Manifest (metadata, canvases, annotation targets), so deep-zoom, side-by-side comparison in Mirador's tiled windows, and region-annotated notes become links, not instructions.
bad: Our raw/ is overwhelmingly text and image-bearing material is thin (homeschool images live in read-only GitHub repos), so IIIF serving would be infrastructure in search of a corpus.
took: Pattern recorded for a stated trigger: if image-bearing sources become a real ingest stream, manifest-per-source is the right shape and Mirador the right reference viewer.
didnt: NOT FOR US yet, with the revisit trigger stated in the file so the verdict can expire honestly.

name: The Collector's Fallacy — Christian Tietze (2014)
good: Names the core failure — knowing about a thing is not knowing it; collecting is self-rewarding and copies become an alibi. Prescribes short closed cycles: cap research, process to empty, review, repeat.
bad: Essay, not measured; authority is that later literature cites it as the name for the failure.
took: Adopt the cycle rule as an ingest habit: work a named backlog to empty in bounded passes before new bulk ingest, and report the raw-vs-compiled gap as a standing number.
didnt: Adopt/build — the short closed knowledge cycle (cap research, process to empty, review, repeat) as an ingest habit with the raw-vs-compiled gap as a standing number; lane8-dispositions.md records the backlog + never-retrieved audits it motivated as built on 2026-10-20, Phase 5. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Collecting material feels more useful than it usually is — Andy Matuschak
good: Shows accumulating tabs/PDFs/bookmarks feels like progress but systematically overrates value and buries important material; note-writing itself gives weak feedback with no test of quality.
bad: Essay from a researcher's working notes, no measurement.
took: Keep existing feedback loops (Ask eval, cite-lock) and treat never-retrieved/cited pages as the weak-feedback blind spot to instrument.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms two standing design rules: a collected/mirrored source is not knowledge until it is worked into notes (our raw-vs-compiled distinction), and note-writing's weak feedback makes never-retrieved pages the blind spot to instrument; the note itself prompts no separate build. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Save Now, Read Never — Glasp read-it-later study
good: Audits its own genre: saving relieves pressure to read, queues grow monotonically; debunks the viral "82% of saved articles are never read" claim as sourceless.
bad: Vendor blog essay; verified platform numbers are modest and bounded (some authors ~10% opened, others >80%, ~37-day active period).
took: Adopt queue rule — no queue without a stated exit (processed/decision date) and maximum healthy size; keep the phantom statistic as the standing example for why uncited numbers never enter the wiki.
didnt: Adopt/build — the queue discipline the article argues for (a queue is legitimate only when small, time-boxed, and feeding a scheduled reading slot) as the rule for our capture inboxes — no queue without a stated exit and a maximum healthy size — and its debunked, sourceless '82% of saved articles are never read' statistic kept as the standing example for why uncited numbers never enter the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Digital Hoarding research roundup — Sweeten / Neave / Sedera et al.
licence: Subscription journal article (Elsevier, Computers in Human Behavior) with no open licence stated at source; the DHQ instrument's PsycTESTS record is held by the APA, all rights reserved.
good: Measured distinction: accumulating and difficulty deleting are separable; harm tracks felt loss of control/findability, not volume. Digital Hoarding Questionnaire separates the two subscales.
bad: Field contradicts itself on harm (positive, null, and negative performance links); all cross-sectional, no longitudinal or intervention trial exists.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — the DHQ's two separable subscales (accumulating vs difficulty deleting) and its finding that harm tracks felt loss of control/findability rather than volume, as a diagnostic lens for our own backlog and never-retrieved audits. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: My second brain became a mausoleum — JA Westenberg
good: Firsthand mechanism of deferral — the future self who would sort/distill never arrived; a 7,000-item reading list became a shrine to an imagined self. Deleted 10,000 notes after seven years and reported relief.
bad: Firsthand account, n=1, generalises beyond one vault.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the deferral mechanism (the future self who would sort, tag and distill never arrives) confirms process-to-empty, approval-gated ingest over total capture; her remedy — deleting the whole archive — is rejected for a citation-locked, custody-first wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: I Kept a 'Perfect' Second Brain for Three Years — Elena Rivera
good: Strongest abandonment evidence in the lane: maintenance cost scales with surface area while capacity stays flat, so the system goes quietly wrong while still trusted — "a second brain that's 80% current is arguably worse than none, because you trust it." Poses the Monday Morning Test.
bad: Firsthand, n=1; author builds a product (Locul) in the category argued for — diagnosis used, prescription vendor-adjacent.
took: Adopt the Monday Morning Test as a standing weekly sweep check, and flag any page quoted in an answer that has passed verified_until or sits on the drift list, in that answer.
didnt: Adopt/build — the Monday Morning Test as a standing weekly sweep check, with staleness surfaced at the moment of use; lane8-dispositions.md records 'staleness surfaced at the moment of use (verification state travels with the answer)' as built on 2026-10-20, Phase 5, with Rivera named as source/inspiration. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Why I'm Giving Up on a Second Brain — Sudo Science
good: Names false-productivity linking/tagging/plugin work, and abandoned intermediate artefacts (Forte's intermittent packs made handful, mostly abandoned).
bad: Firsthand, n=1, ~3.5 years BASB use; linking critique is one user's reasoning.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the false-productivity trap (linking, tagging, appearance and plugin work that feels like progress) confirms keeping wiki maintenance agent-side and minimal rather than owner-performed; a firsthand n=1 account, so it stands as evidence, not as the basis for a build. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tool-hopping cycle — Jessica Lin; Ella New
good: Describes the six-month arc — architecture, friction, backlog anxiety, graveyard, return to Apple Notes — and the addiction frame: changing systems gives a euphoric high while procrastinating real work.
bad: Essay synthesising forum accounts, no sample/counts, plus one firsthand account; pattern, not a measured rate.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the system-hopping cycle (excitement, friction, neglect, chasing the next system) confirms our settled-stack discipline: churn and re-architecture are procrastination, not progress, so the wiki's tooling stays fixed unless the owner rules otherwise (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: The Tyranny of the Note Taking Industrial Complex — Herbert Lui
good: Diagnoses system-envy as a marketed product: courses sold on enrolment numbers, never student outcomes; guru photographed switching to the paper notes his course replaced.
bad: Essay / curated scrapbook; merchant anecdote anonymised and unverifiable; absence-of-evidence argument.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms judging note-taking systems and courses by user outcomes rather than sales and marketing claims, the same standard our programme applies to tools and research (results verified at the source, never vendor promises) (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: The Notes I Stopped Taking — SystemsAndFlow (diagnosis)
good: Names note graveyards precisely: "The capture is easy; the return on capture is almost zero"; making notes a system made taking and returning more expensive.
bad: Firsthand, n=1 over four years and five apps; "almost zero" stated as general law from one experience. Carries a disclosed affiliate link.
took: Adopt the return-on-capture question as a metric habit: every capture class must point at its retrieval path; a class with zero retrievals over a long window is a graveyard bed to stop planting in.
didnt: Corroboration — the diagnosis confirms the return-on-capture metric habit already adopted from this piece (see took): capture classes that are never retrieved are graveyards, so our wiki measures retrieval, not volume captured (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Stuff goes into the computer and doesn't come out — Boardman & Sasse (CHI 2004)
good: Foundational cross-tool PIM study: information diligently stored in silos (files, email, bookmarks) and then not retrieved; filing driven by tool at hand, not retrieval plan.
bad: Filed secondary in the source (ACM 403, PDF 404); 20 years old, pre-cloud/pre-agent — silo shape transfers, tooling does not.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the foundational finding that information filed per-tool into silos is then not retrieved confirms our single canonical wiki with retrieval-first, citation-locked design instead of per-tool filing driven by whichever tool is at hand (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: The Blogging Iceberg — Perseus Development Corp. (2003)
good: Measured base rate: of 4.12 million hosted blogs, 66.0% not updated in two months, 1.09 million one-day wonders, abandoned blogs lasted on average 126 days.
bad: Blogs are not wikis and 2003 population is not this owner; number transfers as a prior, not a prediction.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the measured 66% abandonment base rate confirms designing the wiki for neglect and drift (nightly sweeps, verified_until dates, drift lists) rather than assuming steady tending; the figure is used as a prior, not a prediction for this owner (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques — Dunlosky et al. (2013)
licence: © The Author(s) 2013 (SAGE, Psychological Science in the Public Interest); no open licence stated at source — reprints by permission
good: Systematic review: highlighting/underlining and rereading rated LOW utility; practice testing (retrieval) and distributed practice are the only HIGH utility techniques. Fluency/confidence masks absence of learning.
bad: Filed secondary (full text paywalled, quotes verified via secondary sources); population is students, transfer to wiki rereading is an analogy.
took: Adopt principle: prefer test-shaped checks (eval, cite-lock, reverify-against-source) over review-shaped checks (rereading, skim audits); a page only ever reread has not been checked.
didnt: Corroboration — the high-utility rating for practice testing over rereading confirms the test-shaped verification principle already adopted from this review (see took); a synthesis paper offers no code or method to adopt beyond that principle (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tags Networks Narrative tagging experiment — De Montfort University
good: Measured vocabulary inflation: 1,396 unique tags for 40 sites mapping to 721 WordNet words — folksonomy used ~60% more terms than an official taxonomy; distinguishes indexers vs describers.
bad: Small study, n=30, social-bookmarking era; 19 of 24 who expressed a preference wanted no standardisation.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — tag governance by suggestion rather than constraint: the measured folksonomy inflation (1,396 tags mapping to 721 taxonomy words) plus users' rejection of standardisation is an ideas-board candidate for wiki tag suggestions that nudge toward existing terms without forbidding new ones (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Fake Progress — Christian Tietze (2016)
good: Names deciding/planning as soothing false accomplishment chained to the Collector's Fallacy: "You have to act."
bad: Essay, aphoristic, unmeasured.
took: Adopt reporting discipline: progress reports lead with counts finished and verified, with filed/planned counts stated separately and never summed into the headline.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms the reporting discipline already adopted from this piece (see took): deciding, planning and filing are not progress, so our reports headline only work finished and verified (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Digital Gardening Follow-up — Noah Wright
good: Honest six-month follow-up: gardening still easy to neglect; neglect produces binge-reclaim pressure ("write 3 blog posts right now") rather than steady debt.
bad: Firsthand, n=1, six months; verified search-rendered, direct fetch 404'd.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the neglect-then-binge-reclaim pattern confirms steady small maintenance (nightly sweep, continuous rounds) over periodic binge reclaiming for our wiki; an n=1 follow-up is a warning shape, not a rule (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Digital Gardening — Tom Gagor
good: States the compounding cost in one line: reclaiming a neglected garden becomes exponentially harder; maintenance debt compounds like legacy software.
bad: Essay, software analogy; "exponentially" is rhetorical, not fitted to data.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the compounding cost of reclaiming a neglected garden confirms continuous tending of the wiki (nightly sweeps, same-session ingest) over deferred maintenance; the software analogy states the shape, our own sweep record supplies the evidence (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: A Brief History & Ethos of the Digital Garden — Maggie Appleton
good: Founding history shows the garden metaphor hides a labour contract — WikiGardeners/WikiGnomes were jobs; unplanned sprawl is wilderness.
bad: Essay/history, reading of the movement's own texts.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the founding history confirms our design assumption that a garden/wiki is a labour contract, not a self-tending metaphor: caretaking roles (WikiGardeners/WikiGnomes) were real work, and unplanned sprawl becomes wilderness, which is why our wiki treats tending, sweeping and retrieval checks as named, scheduled work rather than expecting the corpus to stay healthy on its own. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Weekly Review: Key to GTD — Leo Babauta / GTD literature; Asian Efficiency
good: Practitioner consensus that the weekly review is load-bearing and most skipped: without it the system atrophies, trust decays, and users return to memory/inbox.
bad: Essay/practitioner consensus, no controlled study.
took: Keep paced owner-review as a protected mechanism (weekly-five-decisions); treat two consecutive unopened weekly-fives as a system health signal to surface plainly, not as a backlog to double up.
didnt: Corroboration — the practitioner consensus confirms the mechanism already adopted in the took field: a paced, protected owner review is what keeps a trusted system trustworthy, and skipped reviews are a health signal (system going stale, users reverting to memory/inbox) rather than a backlog to be doubled up later. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Review debt — Expertium on Anki; Eshan Ramesh; iandanforth
good: Arithmetic of review debt: unbounded intake with no input rate limiting makes reviews overwhelming and users quit; pausing an app does not pause forgetting. Ramesh lived version: 400–500 reviews/day, burnout, quit at 2,000 cards.
bad: Essay plus firsthand accounts; no dropout-rate study exists.
took: Adopt input rate limiting for every obligation queue (reverify, caveats, adjudication): cap new obligations per cycle at demonstrable clearing capacity; shed or escalate when due-count crosses cap. Also named in wave10-synthesis.md queue items 42.
didnt: Corroboration — the review-debt arithmetic confirms the input rate limiting already adopted in the took field: every new obligation creates future review load, pausing does not pause decay, and an uncapped queue predictably becomes a wall users abandon, so capping intake at demonstrable clearing capacity is the correct control. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Commonplace-book scholarship — Blair; Darnton; Yeo
licence: Copyrighted scholarship, all rights reserved — Blair's Too Much to Know is © 2010 Yale University, no open licence stated at source
good: Historical practice was storing, sorting, summarizing, selecting under headings designed in advance for retrieval/composition — copying was the least of it; Locke's indexing method exists because retrieval was the hard part.
bad: Scholarship, historical/archival, not measurements of modern tools; Yeo filed abstract-level/secondary.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the scholarship confirms our index-first, retrieval-first design: historical commonplacing was storing, sorting, summarising and selecting under headings designed in advance for retrieval and composition, and Locke's indexing method exists because retrieval, not copying, was the hard part — the same reason our wiki is built around its index and compiled pages rather than raw capture. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Folgezettel is More than Mechanism — Bob Doto (counterpoint)
good: Corrects over-application of the Collector's Fallacy: it applies only if a maker lacks engagement with collections over time; friction at import (folgezettel) separates collecting-with-engagement from hoarding.
bad: Essay, practitioner rebuttal, no measurement; concedes the fallacy is real.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — the import-context trail for the ideas board: folgezettel's bird's-eye record of how a note was first contextualised when it entered the system, and its import-time friction forcing at least one explicit connection, as a possible provenance/engagement signal for our ingest — an idea only, since the essay carries no licence for reuse. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: A Metabolic Workspace — Joan Westenberg
good: Coherent design for a thinking workspace: treat information like food, ideas have a half-life, no inbox/read-later/archive, single daily note, ideas enter only in own words from memory.
bad: Essay/design proposal, work in progress, no follow-up outcome data found.
took: not recorded in this lane
didnt: Expiry-by-default and no-archive design rejected — this wiki is a record of decisions, corrections, and a hash-chained log; expiry would destroy auditability. Also listed as negative N4 in wave10-synthesis.md.

name: Too many documents, not enough readers — Marcus Obst
good: Only find written about this exact shape (agents producing for one reader): production cost collapsed, reading/verification cost has not; proposes a three-question audit — opened in 90 days, actually read, changed thought/informed a decision.
bad: Essay/talk transcript; the 1–5% hit rate is the speaker's estimate, not a measurement.
took: Adopt the audit as periodic measurement in sweep reporting: pages retrieved in answers, pages cited onward, pages that informed a recorded decision, and pages never retrieved since creation with oldest named. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 44.
didnt: Corroboration — Obst's audit confirms the measurement already adopted in the took field: production cost has collapsed while reading/verification cost has not, so a corpus written by agents for one reader must periodically measure pages retrieved, pages cited onward, pages that informed a recorded decision, and pages never retrieved since creation, rather than assuming retrieved-not-read is working. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Capture less, trust your memory — SystemsAndFlow (remedy)
good: Friction half applies: capture must be near-zero-effort, simplest tool that lets you write and find a thought.
bad: Firsthand, n=1, for a person whose unaided memory was not the failing component; premise "important thoughts come back" varies between people.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected as a remedy for this setup — the wiki exists because a glitch cost ~3 months of memory and the owner's ADHD stream requires catching every dropped idea; "if it doesn't come back, it probably wasn't important" is indistinguishable from losing it here. Also negative N4 in wave10-synthesis.md. ## Wave 8 — Dead systems

name: Nupedia
licence: GNU Free Documentation License (GFDL) — switched January 2001 from the initial Nupedia Open Content License
good: Expert encyclopedia with a seven-step editorial process requiring true experts/PhDs — the quality-gate ideal stated in full.
bad: Throughput collapse: 2 full articles by Nov 2000, 21 in first year vs Wikipedia's 18,000, final tally 24 approved articles; funding withdrawn, server crashed 26 Sep 2003.
took: Adopt throughput test for any new gate/review/approval stage: state expected cost per item and effect on ingest volume, or don't build it. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 1 and negative N10.
didnt: Corroboration — Nupedia's throughput collapse under a seven-step expert gate (24 approved articles in three years, then funding withdrawn and the server lost) confirms the throughput test already adopted in the took field: any new gate in our system must state its cost per item and its effect on ingest volume before it is built. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Citizendium
licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 Unported for original articles (Wikipedia-derived articles also under GFDL 1.2)
good: Fork restoring real names, credentialed experts, peer-reviewed approved articles, and constables — Nupedia's formula as governance.
bad: Zombie death: fewer than 100 active members by Oct 2011, foundation never registered, managing-editor office vacated 2016 and not refilled, article count shrinking (17,956 in 2023 to 16,440 in 2025) while technically "active."
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected — Citizendium repeats Nupedia's formula (real names, credentialed experts, approved articles, constables) and died the same zombie death, with a shrinking article count and unfilled governance offices; an expert-gated, multi-contributor governance model does not fit a single-owner personal wiki whose gates are owner rulings, and its CC BY-SA content terms are in any case ideas-only for our system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Google Knol
licence: Content licence CC-BY-3.0 by default (authors could instead choose CC-BY-NC-3.0 or traditional copyright protection); the Knol service itself was a closed commercial Google product with no open licence
good: Exit pattern was good: announced Nov 2011, service to Apr 2012, download/migrate window to Oct 2012, Google co-built Annotum WordPress migration target with redirects.
bad: Never gained traction, Google never promoted it — public-attention failure.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Death by public-market indifference cannot apply — private single-owner wiki has no public and no market. Exit pattern already covered in wave 6.

name: Wikispaces
licence: no licence stated at source — a closed, proprietary hosted wiki service (private company, fee-based tiers) with no open licence shown on its surviving record page
good: One of the largest wiki farms, education-focused, claiming over 1.5 million wikis and 10 million users.
bad: Killed in stages after TES acquisition because modernising infrastructure/code was "very substantial" and no longer viable; export door narrow, tiered, and lossy (MediaWiki import only for paid spaces).
took: Adopt invariant: for every hosted component, name where its state lands in the repo, or treat the component as a defect; no surface may hold the only copy of anything.
didnt: Rejected — a closed hosted wiki farm offers no adoptable mechanism; its failure mode (landlord modernisation cost, tiered and lossy export) is already captured in the took invariant that no surface may hold the only copy of anything (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Yahoo Groups
licence: no licence stated at source — a closed, proprietary Yahoo hosted service (commercial, owner-operated) with no open licence shown on its surviving record page
good: Twenty years of community memory for ~10 million groups — mailing list plus archive/files/photos/polls, much existing nowhere else. Archive Team rescued ~1.8 billion of ~2.1 billion public messages.
bad: All web content deleted 14 Dec 2019; official GetMyData export missed attachments, databases, polls, photos, and metadata; rescuers were actively blocked by Yahoo.
took: Adopt rule: an export is verified by content (counts, hashes, spot-opened attachments) or recorded as unverified, never as "backed up."
didnt: Rejected — a closed Yahoo service offers nothing adoptable; its landlord-deletion and lossy official export are already captured in the took rule that an export counts only when verified by content, counts and hashes (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Yahoo Answers
licence: no licence stated at source — a closed, proprietary Yahoo hosted service; answer content remained owned by its users, with Yahoo holding a non-exclusive royalty-free right to publish it, and no open licence shown on its surviving record page
good: Longest-running mass Q&A platform, ~60 million visitors/month near the end.
bad: Quality death before corporate death: points rewarded participation over accuracy, a chosen "best answer" could never be changed, factual quality decreased as users increased; ceased 4 May 2021, stored content deleted after 30 Jun 2021.
took: Adopt correctability invariant for stored answers — superseded visibly, never frozen — and check any future answer scoring against the points-for-participation failure.
didnt: Corroboration — its points-for-participation scoring and frozen, unchangeable best answers confirm our correctability invariant (answers superseded visibly, never frozen) and our scored-abstention design; the closed platform itself offers nothing adoptable (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GeoCities
licence: no licence stated at source — a closed, proprietary Yahoo hosted service (commercial, owner-operated) with no open licence shown on its surviving record page
good: First mass home-page host, tens of millions of homesteaders; outsiders preserved tens of millions of pages, rescue torrent 650 GB.
bad: All 38 million pages of the main English site erased Oct 2009 after Yahoo decided it was obsolete; only a fraction of ~10 TB hosted was saved.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Death by landlord deletion cannot occur here — no landlord; owner holds files on Azure, locally, and in nightly Drive zip.

name: Google Reader
licence: no licence stated at source — a closed, proprietary Google hosted service with no open licence shown on its surviving record page
good: RSS reader that was the sync backend for an entire ecosystem of third-party clients; subscriptions exportable via Takeout over four months.
bad: Retired 1 Jul 2013 for portfolio focus despite loyal following; when the backend died every client built on it was stranded; team had been pulled away years earlier.
took: Adopt design review question for every feature: "if this surface vanished tomorrow, what in the repo is poorer?" If the answer is the feature's accumulated value, redesign before building.
didnt: Corroboration — a whole client ecosystem stranded when its sync backend was retired confirms the took design-review question (if this surface vanished tomorrow, what in the repo is poorer?); the closed service itself offers nothing adoptable (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Google Code
licence: no licence stated at source for the service itself — a closed, proprietary Google hosted forge; the projects it hosted carried their own individual licences, none of which is the service's licence
good: Graceful-death pattern, first witness: announced 10 months ahead, read-only phase, tarballs of source/issues/wikis downloadable through 2016, archive kept accessible, exporter tools and staffed migration help.
bad: Died by supersession and spam/abuse load — "the service simply isn't needed anymore"; Google itself migrated ~1,000 projects away.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — its graceful-death pattern (announced about ten months ahead, read-only phase, downloadable tarballs, exporter tools and migration help) confirms our exit-drill and self-verifying packaging patterns; the closed service itself offers nothing adoptable (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CodePlex
licence: no licence stated at source for the service itself — a closed, proprietary Microsoft hosted forge; the projects it hosted carried their own individual licences, none of which is the service's licence
good: Graceful-death pattern, second witness: final complete backup before shutdown, permanent read-only lightweight archive with per-project downloads in Markdown/JSON, redirects and "I've moved" pointers honoured with no end date planned.
bad: Usage collapsed to fewer than 350 projects with a commit in last 30 days; 2015 spam epidemic; GitHub became de facto host.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — its graceful-death pattern (final complete backup, permanent lightweight read-only archive, per-project downloads and honoured moved pointers) confirms our exit-drill and archive patterns; the closed service itself offers nothing adoptable (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Delicious
licence: no licence stated at source — a closed, proprietary hosted bookmarking service (commercial, successively owner-operated) with no open licence shown on its surviving record page
good: Original social bookmarking service, inventor of mainstream tagging; final buyer kept over a billion bookmarks online as an archive so it wouldn't disappear.
bad: Death by serial acquisition — five owners in fourteen years; AVOS redesign removed features power users loved and triggered exodus.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected — mainstream tagging is already core to our wiki (SKOS tag registry built), and a defunct closed bookmarking service offers no further adoptable mechanism; its death by serial acquisition is a landlord risk our local-first, owner-held custody already removes (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ma.gnolia
licence: no licence stated at source for the service itself — a closed, proprietary hosted bookmarking service; only parts of its planned, never-completed M2 rewrite were announced as intended for an open source licence
good: Well-regarded social bookmarking service storing snapshots of bookmarked pages, nearly half a terabyte of user data.
bad: Canonical total loss in one night, 30 Jan 2009: database corrupted irretrievably, single on-site backup duplicated the corruption, no off-site copy, one-man operation; recovery failed and service closed permanently.
took: Adopt restore-verification as the standard: a backup counts only when a restore from it has been performed and hash-verified, on the exit-drill cadence. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 25.
didnt: Corroboration — its irretrievable single-night loss, with the on-site backup duplicating the corruption and no off-site copy, confirms the took restore-verification standard (a backup counts only when a restore from it has been performed and hash-verified); the closed service itself offers nothing adoptable (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Pocket
licence: Proprietary (freemium service; no open licence stated at source)
good: Leading read-later service for eighteen years, built into Firefox after Mozilla acquisition.
bad: Shut down 8 Jul 2025 for "focus"; export disabled 12 Nov 2025 and all user data queued for permanent deletion — even a well-run shutdown deletes the inattentive.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — a leading hosted read-later silo shutting down and deleting user data confirms local-first custody and export-by-default in our wiki; the service was proprietary, so there was no code to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Springpad
licence: no licence stated at source (closed commercial service)
good: Well-designed Evernote rival with smart notebooks, ~5 million registered users at peak, $7.3M raised; at shutdown provided JSON/HTML export and Evernote migration.
bad: Monetisation failure in a better-funded rival's shadow; 2013 pivot alienated core base; for much of its life offered no export at all.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Death by free-service economics cannot occur in a private, one-owner, non-commercial wiki; export moral carried by Yahoo Groups and Omnivore finds.

name: CiteULike
licence: Closed source (proprietary); user dataset released into the public domain
good: First social reference manager, folksonomy of whole research fields, reference manager of choice for a decade of open-science advocates.
bad: Closed 30 Mar 2019 in its own words due to costs and "none of us really has any time"; BibTeX exported clean, uploaded PDFs did not.
took: Adopt cost-and-hands line in the preservation scorecard/exit materials; treat rising maintenance load as a lint-worthy signal.
didnt: Corroboration — clean BibTeX export alongside unrecoverable uploaded PDFs confirms citation data must export cleanly while the files themselves stay in local custody; the service was closed source, so there was no code to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Athens
good: Open-source, local-first Roam alternative, community-built in the open; local-first markdown/DataScript data stayed usable and alumni landed softly in Logseq.
bad: Stopped by decision with money in the bank because founder no longer believed in a billion-dollar opportunity, had no interesting ideas left, and thought AI-native tools might leapfrog the paradigm.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected — the project is unmaintained by its founders' own decision and its graph-database stack duplicates our file-based wiki; its local-first data surviving into Logseq corroborates our custody design, but dead code is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TWiki → Foswiki
good: Foswiki fork kept compatibility with TWiki content, governed by a non-profit association, and is still releasing (2.1.11, Mar 2026).
bad: Founder's company imposed new governance in Oct 2008, locked developers out of twiki.org; brandholder kept the trademark/name and lost the project — "a fork of one."
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — fork-survival governance: keep code custody and community governance independent of any single trademark/brand holder, so the project survives a governance rupture as Foswiki did; GPLv2 code is ideas-only under our licence discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MoinMoin
good: One of the most-deployed wiki engines, file-based page storage like ours, ran the Python and Debian wikis.
bad: Stranding: MoinMoin 1.9 ran on Python 2 which reached end-of-life 1 Jan 2020; rewrite MoinMoin 2 spent a decade "not production ready," leaving large installations on an unmaintained stack with no migration target.
took: Adopt stranding question for tool adoption: for every tool the wiki depends on, name what strands if it reaches end-of-life; if the corpus becomes hard to read/serve, the tool doesn't get adopted.
didnt: Corroboration — file-based page storage like ours endured, while the Python 2 end-of-life stranding confirms the dependency end-of-life question already adopted in took; GPL code is ideas-only, none taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Trilium → TriliumNext
licence: AGPL-3.0 (TriliumNext, as recorded in the file)
good: Succession that worked: original developer gave the repo to the community project; no special migration steps, TriliumNext uses the existing database, versions compatible and downgrading possible.
bad: Original Trilium, built essentially by one maintainer, entered maintenance mode in 2024 — single-maintainer risk was the precondition.
took: Adopt periodic cold-start test as the succession check: a fresh agent given only the repo must answer from it, lint it, and rebuild the Lens; pass criteria are stable format, explicit public handover artefact, and successor running old data as-is. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 31.
didnt: Adopt/build — the succession lesson, not the AGPL-3.0 code: a periodic cold-start test as the succession check, where a fresh agent given only the repo must answer from it, lint it and rebuild the Lens, with pass criteria of a stable format, an explicit public handover artefact and a successor running old data as-is. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Postmortem Culture — Google SRE Workbook
good: Canonical anatomy of inert post-mortems with testable defects: action items without tracking bugs are forgotten, vague verbs are unmeasurable, equal priority is no priority, blame destroys information, ownership must be singular, timeliness is accuracy.
bad: Mitigative-only lists and "make humans less error-prone" items do not prevent recurrence, per the chapter itself.
took: Adopt as lint-grade checklist for the post-mortem register: every action item needs a tracking reference outside the register, a measurable end-state (no improve/make better), and a single named owner. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 40.
didnt: Corroboration — its testable postmortem defects (untracked action items, vague verbs, equal priority, blame, split ownership, late write-up) confirm the lint-grade register checklist already adopted in took; the CC BY-NC-ND text itself is not reused. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Blameless PostMortems and a Just Culture — John Allspaw (2012)
good: Origin of blameless/just culture in software: the person who made the mistake becomes the expert responsible for educating everyone else; post-mortem reconstructs why the action made sense at the time.
bad: Filed secondary — original returned 403 and was not read firsthand.
took: Register entries should close with the lesson in teachable form — the condition that made the error look right — not apology/self-flagellation.
didnt: Etsy's public-sharing norm rejected — wiki is private to owner plus admitted agents, never public.

name: Postmortems That Actually Change Something — mecanik.dev
good: Follow-through is the whole game: success metric is proportion of action items done in last six months (under half = meetings, not process); review open items at start of next post-mortem; "human error" is a description, not an explanation.
bad: Practitioner write-up, not a controlled study.
took: Register should carry a standing close-out metric (share completed, trailing window) and a rule that opening a new entry surfaces still-open items of prior entries; write entries from contemporaneous log within a day or two.
didnt: Corroboration — its follow-through test (share of action items done in the last six months), named owner and date in the normal tracker, and reviewing open items at the next postmortem confirm the register practices already adopted in took; with no licence stated at source the text is ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Stop Treating Postmortems as the Learning System — COEhub
good: Diagnosis that post-mortems optimise for completeness at write time, not retrieval at decision time; timeline reconstruction and hindsight bias distort, and action items tracked locally do not accumulate into system-level signals.
bad: Vendor blog selling an incident-memory product; diagnosis filed because it cites primary safety literature and is corroborated elsewhere.
took: Register entries need failure-mode tags so patterns aggregate across entries.
didnt: The vendor product (SaaS ingesting Slack/Meet/Zoom transcripts into a vendor cloud) rejected — Azure-only, privacy-absolute, transcript ingest unapproved.

name: Post-mortems collection — Dan Luu
good: Industry's standard curated collection of public incident post-mortems with failure categories and a minimal link + one-line format cheap enough to keep doing; Config Errors is the largest curated class (35+).
bad: Taxonomy decayed: "Uncategorized" holds 230+, an order of magnitude more than every curated category combined, because categorisation costs effort at ingest and nobody's job is the taxonomy.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the collection's cheap link-plus-one-line format confirms low-cost failure ingest, while its decayed taxonomy (Uncategorized dwarfing the curated categories in the README outline) warns that categorisation must happen at compile time, not be left to ingest goodwill; with no licence stated at source the list is ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NASA Lessons Learned Information System — GAO-02-195 (2002)
good: Audited lessons system that is the ancestor of every lessons database: managers were required to review LLIS, giving a mandated-use test case.
bad: LLIS was not managers' primary source (reviews and colleagues were); search drowned in irrelevance, negative lessons were withheld for fear of looking like bad managers, and NASA conceded it was not effective for agency-wide sharing.
took: Key lessons should be pushed into the pages where the decision recurs, not left waiting in the register for a pull; register must be findable at decision time and entries must not soften failures. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 40.
didnt: Corroboration — GAO's own recommendations (disseminate key lessons to users, easier search, solicit user input) confirm the design already recorded in took: lessons must be pushed into the pages where the decision recurs rather than left waiting for a pull, even under a mandated-review regime. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NASA LLIS audit — NASA Inspector General (2012)
good: Ten-year follow-up with a price tag, testing whether the system was worth its cost; JPL's living local practice was the outlier that fed the system.
bad: ~$750,000–782,000/year, managers rarely consulted or contributed, Glenn/Johnson averaged ~1 lesson/year vs JPL ~12, Glenn spent ~$94,000 per lesson; IG concluded LLIS as structured is not effective. Filed secondary, OIG PDF not opened.
took: Adopt viability test of cost per used lesson for our own machinery — machinery whose per-entry cost exceeds retrieval value gets marginalised.
didnt: Corroboration — the IG's viability question (whether ~$750,000 a year on a rarely consulted system is a prudent investment) confirms the cost-per-used-lesson test already recorded in took for our own machinery: per-entry cost above retrieval value gets marginalised. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Columbia Accident Investigation Board report (2003)
good: Examined the knowledge systems that should have carried prior lessons into a safety decision, including problem/waiver tracking and LLIS.
bad: Tracking systems were "extremely cumbersome"; LLIS was used "only on an ad hoc basis," so it was functionally absent at decision time; information existed fragmented and never reached a point of decision in integrated form. Filed secondary via trade-press reporting.
took: Consultation must be wired into the decision path by procedure (agent checklist before consequential build/deploy/ingest), not left to recollection — applies to the register and corrections ledger.
didnt: Corroboration — the Board's finding that physical and organisational causes played an equal role, with knowledge fragmented and never integrated at a decision point, confirms the rule already recorded in took: consultation must be wired into the decision path by procedure, not left to recollection. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Factors Impeding Wiki Use in the Enterprise — MITRE case study
good: Case study identifying behavioural, not technical, impediments: reluctance to share (extra cost, desire to share only "finished" content, openness sensitivity) and heavy reliance on non-wiki tools.
bad: Filed opened (abstract) only; full paper not retrieved.
took: Capture rules must keep accepting unfinished fragments as first-class ingest — compilation is the agent's job, not a precondition; any capture surface demanding polished input re-imports the failure.
didnt: Corroboration — the case study's central behavioural finding, that staff withhold anything not 'finished', confirms the capture rule already recorded in took: unfinished fragments are first-class ingest and compilation is the agent's job, never a precondition the contributor must meet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: A Synthesis of Knowledge Management Failure Factors — Hajric
licence: CC BY (Creative Commons Attribution, as stated in the paper itself)
good: Reference taxonomy separating causal factors (no performance indicators, inadequate management support, improper planning, inadequate skill, culture, structure) from resultant symptoms (no widespread contribution, lack of relevance/quality/usability, loss from staff defection/retirement).
bad: Failure judgements are expectation-relative and the field lacks a shared definition, so "KM failure" claims across studies are often about different systems; overemphasis on formal systematisation is itself a failure factor.
took: Use as reference taxonomy; weigh its warning against letting the wiki schema grow more elaborate than the use it serves whenever a new lint lane/field is proposed.
didnt: Corroboration — the causal/resultant taxonomy and its own resultant factor 'overemphasis on formal learning, systematisation, and determinant needs' confirm the use already recorded in took: a reference taxonomy, and a standing warning to weigh any new schema field or lint lane against the use it serves. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Gartner enterprise social assessment — via Formtek
good: Purpose test: a working purpose names who participates, what issue, what value they gain, what value the organisation gains, is measurable, and feeds results back.
bad: ~70% adopted enterprise social, only ~10% succeeded under "provide and pray" deployment; filed secondary, Gartner release not opened, and statistic is about multi-user communities.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — Gartner's purpose test (name who participates, the specific issue, the value participants gain, the value the organisation gains, measurability, and results fed back to the community) as a gate question for any new wiki surface or community feature, so nothing is launched on a 'provide and pray' basis. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: The Rise and Decline of an Open Collaboration System — Halfaker et al. (2013)
licence: © 2012 SAGE Publications — no open licence stated at source (reprints/permissions via the publisher)
