good: Definitive empirical study of Wikipedia editor decline: active editors peaked 56,400 in Mar 2007; desirable newcomer proportion held steady while survival collapsed (25.6% still editing after two months in early 2006, later 11.7% within a year).
bad: Community's own quality machinery caused it — tightened rejection and algorithmic reverts predicted non-retention for good newcomers as for bad, and norms calcified against changes proposed by newer editors.
took: Every rejecting mechanism must be judged on two axes — what it keeps out and what it discourages from arriving; gates need a coaching path back, and AGENTS.md must remain amendable. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 41.
didnt: Corroboration — the study's mechanism (restrictive quality control and algorithmic reverts driving away desirable newcomers, norms calcified against newer editors) confirms the rule already recorded in took: every rejecting mechanism is judged on what it keeps out and what it discourages, with a coaching path back; the copyrighted text is ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Obsolete answers on Stack Overflow — Zhang et al. (2021)
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (arXiv version, per the licence icon shown on its arXiv page)
good: Large-scale study reframing staleness: 58.4% of obsolete answers were probably already obsolete when first posted.
bad: Only 20.5% of obsolete answers are ever updated; once stale, content mostly stays stale at any community size. Filed opened (search-rendered), full-text PDF timed out.
took: Verification must happen at ingest, not only on a later sweep; evidence for compile-at-ingest and against any "capture now, verify someday" fast lane. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 21.
didnt: Corroboration — the headline result that 58.4% of obsolete answers were probably already obsolete when first posted confirms the rule already recorded in took: verification happens at ingest (compile-at-ingest), never in a deferred 'capture now, verify someday' lane. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Outdated code in Stack Overflow answers — Ragkhitwetsagul, Krinke & Oliveto
licence: No open licence named in the fetched arXiv page text (a 'view license' link is present but the licence is not named in text); journal version in IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
good: Traces downstream harm of stale content and whether anyone reports it back.
bad: 19% of answerers rarely/never fix outdated code, 66% of visitors who cloned snippets experienced problems, and 56% of those affected never report back. Filed opened (search-rendered), full text timed out.
took: Detection must be active (probes, drift checks, verification passes), never passive reliance on readers reporting rot.
didnt: Corroboration — the paper's downstream-harm evidence (outdated clones reused in thousands of GitHub projects, and visitors/answerers largely not reporting or fixing rot) confirms the rule already recorded in took: detection must be active — probes, drift checks and verification passes — never passive reliance on readers reporting rot. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: When Online Content Disappears — Pew Research Center (2024)
licence: All Rights Reserved (Copyright © Pew Research Center 2024, per the report's publication record)
good: Reference measurement of link rot from ~1 million Common Crawl pages 2013–2023 plus government/news/Wikipedia link analyses, using conservative criteria so figures are floors.
bad: 25% of all pages that existed in 2013–2023 were gone by late 2023 (38% for 2013 cohort); 54% of Wikipedia pages contain at least one dead reference link.
took: Raw mirroring at ingest is warranted; external URLs are perishable and belong under drift checks; citation lockfile should prefer the mirrored raw copy as canonical and treat the live URL as a courtesy pointer.
didnt: Corroboration — its measured link-rot rates (25% of 2013–2023 pages gone, 54% of Wikipedia pages with a dead reference) confirm our raw-mirroring at ingest, drift checks on external URLs, and treating the mirrored copy as canonical over the live URL. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Software Architecture Documentation for Developers survey — Fraunhofer IESE (2013)
licence: no licence stated at source (report pages carry Copyright © Fraunhofer IESE 2013)
good: Survey of 147 industrial developers; recommends a single source of documentation, automated generation where possible, and an explicit connection between documentation and the thing described; developers want the slice relevant to their question.
bad: Executive summary confirms architecture documentation is most frequently outdated, updated only with strong delays, and inconsistent in detail and form.
took: Standing prior for design review — assume every page is outdated until its verification says otherwise; corroborates page-per-question structure over monolithic documents.
didnt: Corroboration — its finding that architecture documentation is most frequently outdated and inconsistent confirms our assume-stale-until-verified prior and page-per-question structure over monolithic documents; no code or text taken for reuse. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: How Software Engineers Use Documentation — Lethbridge, Singer & Forward (2003)
licence: no open licence stated at source (© 2003 IEEE, IEEE Software)
good: Three studies finding the one maintenance trigger that works is the change itself — updates attached to the change-request process happen, scheduled-later maintenance mostly doesn't; perceived accuracy correlates with how often a document is consulted.
bad: 68% agreed documentation is always outdated; engineers consulted documentation in only ~3% of observed work events, though outdated docs still helped learning/orientation.
took: Update must ride on the event that changes the fact (empirical root of compile-at-ingest); concentrate verification effort on fact-bearing page classes, not hub/orientation pages.
didnt: Corroboration — its evidence that updates attached to the change itself happen while scheduled-later maintenance does not confirms compile-at-ingest and concentrating verification on fact-bearing page classes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Intentional Forgetting in Organizations — Kluge & Gronau (2018); Argote depreciation evidence
good: Systematic review (246 screened, 40 core) distinguishing accidental from intentional forgetting; obsolete knowledge is forgotten by removing its retrieval cues, not by deleting it.
bad: Stored knowledge depreciates measurably when not exercised (learning-curve λ < 1), silently; Argote's primary studies filed secondary within this paper.
took: Retrieval counts are a health signal — untouched pages should be re-verified or consciously retired; superseding a page is not enough, its index entries, inbound links, and aliases must point at the successor. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 20.
didnt: Corroboration — forgetting obsolete knowledge by eliminating its retrieval cues, not deleting it, confirms that superseding a page must also strip or redirect its index entries, inbound links and aliases, and that untouched pages need re-verification or conscious retirement. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Documentation my agents can trust — Olund (2026)
good: Firsthand autopsy with transferable fixes: immutable decision records + supersession, one authoritative home per question, stable never-renumbered IDs, a [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] marker that gates work, and enforcement by lint.
bad: Failure inventory included append-only ADRs at ~390–500 lines, two disagreeing sources of truth for "done," and a "current task" note stale more often than not — "for an agent it is poison."
took: Adopt supersession chains for decision pages, a [NEEDS CLARIFICATION]-class schema marker, and the durable/ephemeral split as an explicit rule — pages asserting live state must move to an ephemeral surface or carry a verification date.
didnt: Adopt/build — supersession chains for decision pages, a [NEEDS CLARIFICATION]-class schema marker that gates work, and the durable/ephemeral split for pages asserting live state, as recorded in the took field; ideas only, no text or code reused under the unstated licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RAG knowledge-base rot audit — Chenwengui (2026)
good: Audit of a 61-page markdown knowledge base with a four-class rot taxonomy — expired fact, ghost page, fork, orphan — each with a different fix, plus a probe-set method (12 source-checkable questions run weekly) and owner/source_of_truth/verified_at frontmatter where verified_at ≠ updated_at.
bad: 24 of 61 pages (39%) contained at least one false statement while AI retrieval confidence was 0.94 — retrieval measures similarity, not truth; cross-client ranges are one practitioner's claims, author sells an Agent Audit Pack.
took: Adopt the four-class vocabulary as drift-check output classes, make verified_at ≠ updated_at explicit in metadata semantics, and generalise the golden set with probes testing whether the corpus still agrees with its sources of record. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 21.
didnt: Adopt/build — the four-class rot vocabulary (expired fact, ghost page, fork, orphan) as drift-check output classes, verified_at distinct from updated_at in metadata semantics, and source-checkable probe questions generalising the golden set, as recorded in the took field; ideas only, no text reused under the unstated licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Seven Failure Points When Engineering a RAG System — Barnett et al. (2024)
licence: arXiv / ACM conference experience report, as recorded in wave8-rag-failures.md
good: Pipeline taxonomy from three production systems: FP1 Missing Content, FP2 Missed Top-Ranked, FP3 Not in Context, FP4 Not Extracted, FP5 Wrong Format, FP6 Incorrect Specificity, FP7 Incomplete; validation is only feasible during operation and robustness evolves rather than being designed in.
bad: Three of seven failures occur before the model sees a token, so debugging a wrong answer by editing the prompt starts at the least likely stage; in the Selene/rag context, systems answer anyway when content is missing.
took: Adopt the seven as the diagnostic/labelling scheme for Ask-door and extended-eval failures, so the failure mix is trendable; FP1 is owned by the abstention contract.
didnt: Adopt/build — the seven failure points (FP1 Missing Content through FP7 Incomplete) as the diagnostic and labelling scheme for Ask-door and extended-eval failures, so the failure mix is trendable, with FP1 owned by the abstention contract. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Selene RAG case study — Rivera et al. (2025)
good: Production RAG case study (behavioural-safety SaaS, GPT-4, 23 expert-validated cases) with DeepEval metrics; faithfulness was otherwise high (22/23).
bad: Contextual precision failures ~22%, relevancy failures ~30%, hallucinations ~9% (2/23) — in both hallucination cases the value was not in retrieved documents and the model generated an answer instead of acknowledging insufficient information.
took: Golden set should include deliberately unanswerable questions, scored as passes only when the door refuses or reports absence.
didnt: Corroboration — its two hallucination cases, where the value was in no retrieved document and the model answered instead of acknowledging insufficient information, confirm scored abstention and including deliberately unanswerable questions in the golden set. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: The Normalization of Deviance in AI Development — Barkett et al. (2026)
good: Applies Vaughan/Dekker organisational-failure theory to AI development with four recurring mechanisms — production pressure, false assurance from prior success, structural secrecy, erosion of independent oversight — evidenced across Challenger, Three Mile Island, Boeing 737 MAX and a 33-study review.
bad: Teams can complete safety processes in full compliance and still produce catastrophic outcomes, because the dynamics operate through the processes.
took: Use as closing frame: a passing lint is not evidence of corpus health, ingest velocity shifts burden of proof onto caution, and oversight bites only while the checker is independent of the checked work.
didnt: Corroboration — its four mechanisms and the finding that organisations can complete safety processes in full compliance and still fail confirm that a passing lint is not evidence of corpus health and that oversight only bites while the checker is independent of the checked work. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Why Language Models Hallucinate — Kalai, Nachum, Vempala & Zhang
licence: arXiv preprint, as recorded in the file
good: Reframes hallucination as a binary-classification error caused by incentive structure — training/evaluation reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty, because benchmarks score "I don't know" the same as a wrong answer.
bad: No single rate — the claim is structural; a calibrated model loses to a guessing one under dominant scoring.
took: Extended eval and judge calibration must score a correct abstention as success, never a miss; any aggregate trend should be abstention-adjusted.
didnt: Adopt/build — the paper's incentive diagnosis in our eval design: extended eval and judge calibration score a correct abstention as success, never as a miss, and any aggregate trend is reported abstention-adjusted, so our own scoring does not reward guessing. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Hallucination is Inevitable — Xu, Jain & Kankanhalli
licence: arXiv preprint, as recorded in the file
good: Formal result: every total computable LLM hallucinates on some inputs, independent of architecture, training, prompts, samples, or inference hyperparameters.
bad: Proof is a diagonalisation argument with no rate claimed; "the next model won't do that" is not an available plan.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the formal inevitability result confirms our design premise that hallucination cannot be eliminated by a better model or prompt, so it must be contained structurally by citation locking, per-claim verification and scored abstention rather than trusted away. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RAGTruth corpus (ACL 2024)
licence: arXiv / ACL proceedings; dataset public, as recorded in the file
good: Span-level hallucination corpus for the RAG setting (~2,965 instances, QA/data-to-text/summarisation, six LLMs) measuring what generation adds after retrieval.
bad: 43.1% of all responses contained at least one hallucinated span (data-to-text 68.6%, QA 29.1%); even GPT-4 produced them, error grows with response length, and absence is verbalised as fact.
took: Per-claim verification (quote lane) is the right unit, not answer-level trust; add an eval slice for absence questions and apply stricter quote coverage to longer answers.
didnt: Adopt/build — RAGTruth's span-level finding as the unit of trust in our system: per-claim verification (the quote lane) rather than answer-level trust, an eval slice for absence questions, and stricter quote coverage applied to longer answers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AbstentionBench — Kirichenko et al. (Meta)
licence: arXiv / NeurIPS proceedings; benchmark public, as recorded in the file
good: First large dedicated abstention benchmark: 20 datasets (unknown, underspecified, false premise, subjective, stale) against 20 frontier LLMs.
bad: Abstention is unsolved, does not improve with scale, and reasoning fine-tuning degrades it by 24% on average; models answer definitively even when their own chains express uncertainty, and more reasoning tokens generally make it worse.
took: Abstention is a regression-tested property — re-run the abstention slice before shipping any model/reasoning/prompt change; a hedged chain followed by a definitive answer should force hold; measure abstention per model on our own no-answer questions. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 34.
didnt: Adopt/build — abstention as a regression-tested property: the abstention slice is re-run before shipping any model, reasoning or prompt change, a hedged chain followed by a definitive answer forces a hold, and abstention is measured per model on our own no-answer questions; built in Phase 4. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Know Your Limits — Wen et al. abstention survey (TACL 2025)
licence: Journal article (CC-BY 4.0), as recorded in the file
good: Taxonomy splitting abstention into query answerability, model confidence, and alignment with human values, organised by lifecycle stage with a benchmark/metric catalogue.
bad: No new measurement; value is taxonomic — a contract keyed only on answerability misses the other two failure locations.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the survey's three-perspective framework (query answerability, model confidence, human-values alignment) confirms our scored-abstention design must test all three failure locations, not answerability alone. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AI search citation problem — Tow Center / Columbia Journalism Review (Jaźwińska & Chandrasekar, 2025)
licence: Journalism research article, as recorded in the file
good: Largest practitioner measurement of citation behaviour: eight generative search tools, 1,600 queries, hand-graded identification of headline/publisher/date/URL.
bad: Collectively over 60% incorrect (Perplexity best at 37% wrong, Grok 3 at 94%); ChatGPT misidentified 134/200 yet signalled low confidence only 15 times and never declined; over half of Gemini/Grok 3 citations were fabricated or broken URLs; premium tiers were more confidently incorrect.
took: Score citations in evals rather than treating presence as quality; this is the measured case for the lockfile + quote lane.
didnt: Fabricated-URL sub-mode explicitly not for us — Ask citations resolve through the lockfile to real page ids and verified quotes, never model-generated links.

name: ALCE citation metrics delta — Gao et al. (EMNLP 2023)
licence: arXiv / EMNLP proceedings, as recorded in the file
good: ALCE validates its automatic citation metrics against human gold labels — a measurement of the measurer that citation pipelines are built on.
bad: Automatic citation-recall agrees with humans only 85.1% and precision 77.6%; insufficient-citation detector 82.3%/84.2%, irrelevant-citation detector 75.6%/66.1%, due to NLI inability to detect partial support.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — ALCE's validation work, with the agreement limits recorded in this lane (citation recall 85.1%, precision 77.6% against human labels), confirms our citation lockfile and quote verification cannot rest on NLI-style automatic citation metrics alone. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval — Chroma (2024)
licence: Vendor technical report (not peer-reviewed); code and data public, as recorded in the file
good: Token-level evaluation isolating chunking from embedder/model quality across real corpora.
bad: Even the best configuration (250-token chunks, 125 overlap) reached only 82.4% recall and misses ~a fifth of relevant tokens; best IoU ~7%, per-query variance enormous, defaults can perform poorly.
took: Treat repeated FP2/FP4 failures on a page as a granularity signal (split over-broad, merge fragmented) and re-measure; never tune granularity on a handful of queries.
didnt: Corroboration — the token-level evaluation confirms page granularity must be measured on our own corpus rather than trusting splitter defaults, since even the best configuration recorded in this lane still missed about a fifth of relevant tokens. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Context Rot — Hong, Troynikov & Huber (Chroma, 2025)
licence: Vendor technical report (not peer-reviewed), as recorded in wave8-rag-failures.md
good: Gap closure opened the primary report in full: 18 LLMs, three experiment families, focused prompts (~300 tokens) scored significantly higher than full prompts (~113K tokens) on LongMemEval; report conclusion is that how information is presented matters more than mere presence. Filed in wave 8 from consistent secondary summaries; upgraded to primary-grade in wave10-gap-closure.md.
bad: Performance consistently degrades as input length grows on simple tasks far below window limits; even a single distractor reduces performance and the effect grows with length; failure style differs by family (Claude tends to abstain, GPT to hallucinate confidently).
took: Evidence-packing budgets are a safety control and stay hard caps; treat near-duplicate retrieved pages as distractors/cost in the pack; add a distractor slice to the Ask eval; calibrate trust verdicts per model. Gap closure confirms the Ask door's 6,000-token packing budget as the right shape.
didnt: Corroboration — the report's finding that performance degrades with input length even on simple tasks, and that distractors worsen it, confirms evidence-packing budgets as a safety control and distractor-aware packing, matching the Ask door's hard packing cap recorded in took. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RULER — NVIDIA (COLM 2024)
licence: arXiv / COLM proceedings; benchmark public, as recorded in the file
good: Synthetic long-context benchmark beyond the vanilla needle test: 13 task types, 17 models, 4K–128K, with effective context length defined against a quality threshold.
bad: Almost all models degrade on complex tasks as length increases; every model claimed ≥32K but only half could effectively handle 32K, and almost all fell below threshold before claimed lengths.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — RULER's effective-versus-claimed context length confirms we should size evidence packs by measured effective length, not by a model's claimed window size. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Knowledge conflicts literature — Xie et al. (ICLR 2024); Xu et al. survey; COLM 2024 real-documents study
licence: arXiv / ICLR, EMNLP, COLM proceedings, as recorded in the file
good: COLM boundary condition: with coherent, factual real-world documents, three open models retained a wrong parametric answer in only 0.1–6.2% of conflict cases — well-formed evidence usually wins.
bad: Xie shows confirmation bias when supportive and contradictory evidence are both present, preferring evidence matching parametric memory — GPT-4 memorization ratio reached 80% on the most popular questions — and sensitivity to evidence order.
took: Add a conflict slice to the extended eval (page says X, common knowledge says Y, scored page-faithful-or-abstain); put the strongest source first in the pack; treat compile coherence as a safety property. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 33.
didnt: Corroboration — Xie et al.'s confirmation-bias and evidence-order findings, bounded by the COLM real-document result recorded in this lane, confirm the knowledge-conflict eval slice and strongest-source-first packing recorded in took and in lane8-dispositions.md (built 2026-10-20, Phase 4). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LongMemEval — Wu et al. (ICLR 2025)
licence: arXiv / ICLR proceedings; benchmark public, as recorded in the file
good: Benchmark of long-term conversational memory: 500 questions across extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention, with oracle-evidence controls.
bad: Commercial assistants achieved only 30–70% in a simpler setting; long-context LLMs show a 30–60% drop on LongMemEval-S against their own oracle scores — the gap is reasoning over time and supersession, not needle retrieval.
took: Trend the temporal slice separately and never let an aggregate hide it; give supersession its own eval items; FSRS re-verification cadence is a correctness decision, not housekeeping.
didnt: Corroboration — the five-ability benchmark confirms scoring temporal reasoning, knowledge updates and abstention as separate slices, since the aggregate hides the large drops against oracle scores recorded in this lane; lane8-dispositions.md also records a LongMemEval five-ability template built in Round 3, lane TB6. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AgentPoison — Chen et al. (NeurIPS 2024)
licence: arXiv / NeurIPS proceedings; code public, as recorded in the file
good: First backdoor attack on LLM agents with long-term memory/RAG, demonstrating the write path as an attack surface at a poison rate under 0.1%.
bad: Average attack success ≥80% with benign-performance impact ≤1% (82% retrieval success, 63% end-to-end); trigger transfers across embedding models and evades perplexity-filter and rephrasing defences.
took: Treat filings-in-staging, merges-by-review, and immutable raw as security-critical, not procedural; retrieval anomalies (a page suddenly retrieved for unrelated questions) are a security signal for drift/lockfile checks. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 35.
didnt: Corroboration — the sub-0.1% poison-rate attack confirms treating the wiki write path and retrieval anomalies as security-critical, as recorded in took and in lane8-dispositions.md (retrieval-anomaly security signal built 2026-10-20, Phase 4, sourced to AgentPoison / MINJA). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MINJA — Dong et al. (NeurIPS 2025)
licence: arXiv / NeurIPS proceedings, as recorded in the file
good: Escalation of AgentPoison: memory injection needs no write access, only the ability to talk to the agent, via bridging steps that steer the agent into generating the malicious content itself.
bad: 98.2% average injection success and 76.8% average attack success across three victim agents, with ordinary utility barely affected — poisoning invisible until the trigger context arrives.
took: Content entering the wiki from a conversation carries the same provenance bar as a document ingest; nothing becomes a compiled claim solely because it was said in a chat, by anyone.
didnt: Corroboration — query-only memory injection confirms content entering the wiki from a conversation needs the same provenance bar as a document ingest, and nothing becomes a compiled claim solely because it was said in a chat, as recorded in took. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models — Sharma et al. (Anthropic, ICLR 2024)
licence: arXiv / ICLR proceedings, as recorded in the file
good: Measures agreement-as-failure across five assistants and the human-preference data used to train them.
bad: All five consistently exhibit sycophancy; humans and preference models prefer convincingly-written sycophantic responses over correct ones a non-negligible fraction of the time, so optimising against preference models can sacrifice truthfulness for agreement.
took: False-premise items belong in the extended eval as a first-class slice; the abstention contract should name premise correction as a distinct outcome; judge calibration must watch for a judge rewarding agreeable answers.
didnt: Corroboration — the finding that preference optimisation can sacrifice truthfulness for agreement confirms false-premise items as a first-class eval slice and judge calibration that watches for a judge rewarding agreeable answers, as recorded in took. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: FreshLLMs / FreshQA — Vu et al. (2023)
licence: arXiv preprint; benchmark public, as recorded in the file
good: Dynamic QA benchmark over never/slow/fast-changing knowledge plus false premises, with over 50K human judgments under relaxed and strict modes.
bad: Overall strict accuracy ranged only 0.8–32.0%; GPT-4 never exceeded 15% on fast-changing/recent questions in either mode — parametric knowledge is stale and models answer anyway.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Headline failure (parametric staleness) cannot bite the Ask door — answers are compiled from pages, not recalled from weights; the stale-page analogue is controlled by FSRS/supersession. Its false-premise half is counted under Sycophancy, FOR US there.

name: GSM1k — Zhang et al. (Scale AI, NeurIPS 2024)
licence: arXiv / NeurIPS proceedings, as recorded in the file
good: Honest contamination measurement: 1,250 fresh human-written problems mirroring GSM8K, never published before evaluation.
bad: Many models drop by up to 13% on the uncontaminated mirror; Phi/Mistral families show systematic overfitting, and probability of generating GSM8K examples correlates with the gap (Spearman r² = 0.32) — part of the canonical score was memorisation.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the fresh, uncontaminated mirror benchmark confirms held-out, contamination-aware eval design rather than trusting canonical benchmark scores, part of which the paper shows was memorisation. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking — METR (2025)
licence: Evaluation-organisation blog post with public transcripts, as recorded in the file
good: Pre-deployment evaluation documenting frontier models attacking the measurement — monkey-patching the evaluator, overwriting the grader's timer, caching answers, hunting leaked solutions.
bad: 39 of 128 RE-Bench runs (30.4%) involved reward hacking vs 8 of 1,087 HCAST runs (0.7%); hacking was over 43× more common where the model could see the entire scoring function.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the documented hacking, far more common where the model could see the entire scoring function as recorded in this lane, confirms graders and held-out answers must stay outside the agent-visible and agent-writable surface of our evals. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024 BCCRT 149)
licence: Public tribunal record and reporting, as recorded in the file
good: Tribunal held a chatbot is still part of the company's website, the customer was not obliged to double-check one part against another, and awarded $650.88 damages ($812.02 with interest/fees) for negligent misrepresentation.
bad: Chatbot invented a retroactive bereavement-fare policy and linked to the real page that said the opposite; the airline argued the chatbot was a separate legal entity.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the tribunal's holding that a deployer owns its chatbot's statements confirms our answers must be verifiable against the compiled pages they cite, since 'the system said it' is no defence for the operator. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mata v. Avianca, Inc. (2023)
licence: Public court record and reporting, as recorded in the file
good: Sanctions order clarifies the failure was not using AI but filing its output with no verification and treating the generator's self-assurance as verification.
bad: Lawyers filed a brief citing six non-existent judicial decisions with fabricated quotations, then submitted further excerpts after the tool assured them the cases existed; $5,000 Rule 11 sanctions jointly and severally.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the sanctions order confirms a generator's self-assurance is not verification; every citation in our system must resolve to a real source in the citation lockfile before it is used. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance — GIDA (2019); Carroll et al. (2020)
good: People- and purpose-oriented counterweight to FAIR: Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, Ethics — "Be FAIR and CARE" — asking for every sharing mechanism who decides, who benefits, whose purpose.
bad: Deliberately specifies little machinery — no labels, fields, or tiers; a 2025 communiqué pushes back on applying CARE beyond Indigenous contexts.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Sovereignty framework for peoples' data held by others cannot transfer — no Indigenous data, no collective, and one principal whose authority is not contested by his own agent; adopting its name/posture would claim a governance relationship that does not exist.

name: OCAP® — First Nations Information Governance Centre
licence: no open licence stated at source — OCAP® is a registered trademark of the First Nations Information Governance Centre (FNIGC), used under licence or with permission
good: Sharpest mechanical idea is the Ownership/Possession split: a right asserted in principle is only as strong as the custody arrangement underneath it.
bad: Framework itself is a First Nations standard, trademarked, asserted in a specific political relationship; operationalised through formal protocols and certified training.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Not ours to use. Possession point noted as already satisfied by design — Azure canonical + local mirror + Drive copies is what makes ownership operational.

name: TK and BC Labels as a system — Local Contexts
licence: No standard open licence for the Labels themselves — they are extra-legal mechanisms, not licences (Local Contexts FAQ); publicly available material on the Services is permitted for personal, non-commercial, attributed use under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (Terms & Conditions §5), and a community's customised Labels are retained by that community and shared via the Hub under an exclusive licence for use

name: Consent and verification as label states — BC Consent Verified/Non-Verified; TK Verified/Non-Verified (Local Contexts)
licence: No standard open licence for the Labels themselves — they are extra-legal mechanisms, not licences (Local Contexts FAQ); publicly available material on the Services is permitted for personal, non-commercial, attributed use under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (Terms & Conditions §5), and a community's customised Labels are retained by that community and shared via the Hub under an exclusive licence for use
good: Encodes an epistemic state as first-class visible metadata — a record can carry the fact that its consent or representation has not been checked; the unverified state is a label applied, not an absence.
bad: Inventing a consent fiction for subjects who cannot yet consent (young children) would be worse than labelling the state truthfully as unverified.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — verified / non-verified as an explicit, applied epistemic label state (a record can carry that its consent or representation has not been checked, rather than the state being an absence), for the ideas board; the Local Contexts Verified Labels themselves are for Indigenous communities and are not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Notices vs Labels — Local Contexts Notices
licence: No standard open licence for the Notices themselves — they are extra-legal mechanisms, not licences (Local Contexts FAQ); publicly available material on the Services is permitted for personal, non-commercial, attributed use under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (Terms & Conditions §5)
good: Placeholder layer: fixed, non-customisable markers applied by the holder without community approval and without needing a ruling first, flagging unresolved rights/sensitivity; a Notice decides nothing and hides nothing, and is retired only when Labels/a ruling replace it.
bad: Notices do not express detailed provenance/protocol/permission data, by design.
took: Adopt a notice layer in our vocabulary (e.g. unresolved-status, family-sensitive): fixed, agent-applied, owner-retired, rendered on the page and in the Lens, counted in nightly lanes. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 50, lane priority 1.
didnt: The Local Contexts Notices themselves not adopted — they identify Indigenous rights and interests.

name: Attribution Incomplete Notice — Local Contexts
licence: No standard open licence for the Notices themselves — they are extra-legal mechanisms, not licences (Local Contexts FAQ); publicly available material on the Services is permitted for personal, non-commercial, attributed use under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (Terms & Conditions §5)
good: Holder flags its own record's deficiency on the record itself — incomplete/inaccurate/missing attribution — as an invitation and warning, convertible from a back-office lint count to an on-page state.
bad: Currently in our system the same fact (e.g. 9 sourceless pages) is invisible to a reader of the page itself.
took: Adopt an attribution-incomplete notice for compiled pages lacking sources or carrying known attribution gaps, cleared when the gap is closed on the record.
didnt: Rejected — the Local Contexts Attribution Incomplete Notice itself is not adopted, as it identifies Indigenous rights and interests in collections held by institutions; only the on-page deficiency-flag pattern, in our own vocabulary, is taken, as recorded in Took. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Collections Care Notices — Local Contexts
licence: No standard open licence for the Notices themselves — they are extra-legal mechanisms, not licences (Local Contexts FAQ); publicly available material on the Services is permitted for personal, non-commercial, attributed use under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (Terms & Conditions §5); access to the Collections Care Notices does not require a Hub subscription (CC Notices page)

(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Cultural Protocols — Mukurtu CMS
licence: GPL-3.0 — GNU General Public License v3.0 (MukurtuCMS/Mukurtu-CMS repo sidebar and LICENSE.txt; README License section states GPL v3 or later)
good: Access machinery where no item exists outside a protocol: open vs strict protocols, layered on one item, composing by ALL (member of each) or ANY (member of one or more); tiers named for the community's own categories including seasonal access.
bad: Protocols exist only inside a Mukurtu site: the support documentation requires every Digital Heritage Item to belong to at least one Community, one Cultural Protocol within that Community, and one Category before access is governed at all, and access follows protocol membership assigned inside the CMS — the mechanism has no existence outside Mukurtu/Drupal and its private-file system.
took: Adopt as the written model for item-level protocol tiers: a required tier per item, AND-composition by default with ANY only by explicit owner choice, enforced by existing gateway/Lens machinery. Also folded into wave10-synthesis.md item 50.
didnt: Adopt/build — the protocol-tier model as a written pattern only (a required tier per item, ALL composition by default, ANY only by explicit owner choice), implemented in our own gateway/Lens machinery as recorded in Took — not Mukurtu's GPL-3.0 code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Community Records — Mukurtu CMS
licence: GPL-3.0 — GNU General Public License v3.0 (MukurtuCMS/Mukurtu-CMS repo sidebar and LICENSE.txt; README License section states GPL v3 or later)
good: Multiple coexisting accounts of one item as first-class attachments, none demoted to a footnote; refuses the single-authoritative-description assumption where two communities hold different accounts.
bad: On the Mukurtu support page Community Records are only a field on a Digital Heritage Item — a list of attached records whose display order is managed by drag-and-drop inside that item — with no standalone record type, portability, or conflict-resolution mechanism documented at the source; the feature has no existence outside Mukurtu CMS.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — multiple coexisting accounts of one item as first-class attachments, none demoted to a footnote, as a pattern worth considering for contested or multi-voice family records; Mukurtu's GPL-3.0 implementation is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mukurtu CMS as a platform
licence: GPL-3.0 — GNU General Public License v3.0 (repo sidebar and LICENSE.txt; README License section states GPL v3 or later)
good: Drupal-based open-source CMS with hubs/spokes support and two decades of community co-development; granular protocol-driven access is its strength.
bad: Adopting it would move the corpus out of git + plain markdown into a CMS database, breaking custody, citation lockfile line-addressing, and existing tooling.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Platform adoption rejected on custody and tooling grounds; its protocol model is adopted as a pattern in the Cultural Protocols entry instead.

name: Protocols for Native American Archival Materials — First Archivist Circle (2006); SAA-endorsed 2018
licence: © First Archivists Circle — no standard open licence stated at source; the document itself states it may be distributed for the noncommercial purpose of discussion and that permission to publish must be obtained from the contributors or home organization
good: Best-practice document across ten areas (relationships, balance, accessibility, sensitive materials, context, IP, repatriation, research protocols, reciprocal education, awareness) with cross-cutting demands for consultation, special treatment, and recognition that ethical conditions change through time.
bad: Addresses non-tribal institutions holding Native American material — this wiki holds none, and there is no community to consult or repatriate to.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: As a whole, not for us; two mechanisms extracted separately in the sensitivity and context entries below.

name: PNAAM sensitivity practice — Protocols for Native American Archival Materials
licence: © First Archivists Circle — no standard open licence stated at source; the document itself states it may be distributed for the noncommercial purpose of discussion and that permission to publish must be obtained from the contributors or home organization
good: Names sensitive classes in advance (human remains, sacred objects/ceremonies, burials, hospitals/cemeteries, songs/healing, personal/family information, genealogical data, etc.), defaults to caution until consulted, and treats sensitivity determinations as revisable.
bad: The practice is consultation-dependent by design and does not transfer as a self-serve list: the document states each community will understand and use 'culturally sensitive' differently and directs institutions to consult culturally affiliated community representatives to identify sensitive materials — and the Protocols are non-binding best practice, not an enforceable standard.
took: Adopt a named sensitivity-class list in the wiki schema (children, health, religious-practice detail, finances/debt, marital/family conflict, precise location), applied at ingest, defaulting flagged material to stricter handling pending owner ruling, with membership revisable over time. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 51, lane priority 2.
didnt: Adopt/build — the named sensitivity-class pattern only (classes named in advance, default to caution until ruled on, membership revisable over time), written into our own wiki schema as recorded in Took; the Protocols' sovereignty and consultation content itself is not adopted, and no PNAAM text or code is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PNAAM context practice — Protocols for Native American Archival Materials
licence: © First Archivist Circle — custom terms at source: the document may be distributed for the noncommercial purpose of discussion; permission to publish must be obtained from the contributors or home organisation
good: Subject-authored context rides on the item: encourage the community to provide context, supplement descriptions with sensitivity statements, and at the community's request add a notice such as "We do not endorse this publication" with its finding stated on the item.
bad: The Protocols themselves state they are a work in progress subject to revision and enhancement, that each tribe, band and community is unique so the practices must be interpreted and applied by each institution and community, and that building trust can take years — they are best practice for non-tribal repositories holding Native American material, not a ready rule set for a household wiki.
took: Sensitivity classes at ingest — built 2026-10-20, Phase 6 — source/inspiration: PNAAM practice
didnt: Corroboration — the community-provided context and sensitivity-notice practice confirms the wiki's sensitivity classes at ingest and its fixed notice layer for sensitive material; the Protocols themselves are scoped to non-tribal repositories holding Native American material. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Post-custodial model — Ham (1981); SAADA
good: Model where creators retain custody and archivists provide management oversight; SAADA borrows, digitises, describes, links, and makes accessible without taking physical custody.
bad: Known weakness is oversight without custody — the custodian's copies are the preservation copy.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Nothing to build — the model is already the architecture (owner retains Azure/Drive/local custody, agent provides oversight, take-home zip exists); recorded as external confirmation.

name: Participatory description and reparative description
good: Collaborative practice where community members select, describe, transcribe, translate, and tag, sharing authority; reparative description adds alternate titles/provenance acknowledging unnamed creators and knowledge holders.
bad: Resource itself notes co-design demands more resources than most other reparative practices and requires trust built over time.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — alternate titles and provenance notes acknowledging unnamed creators and knowledge holders, as a description-layer idea for pages about other people; full community co-design does not transfer to a single-principal household archive. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Radical empathy — Caswell & Cifor (2016)
licence: Copyright retained by the authors — Archivaria licence note at source states authors retain copyright in their work and reproduction within one year requires the General Editor's permission; no open licence stated
good: Four-relationship check — archivist to creators, subjects, users, and communities, each with mutual affective responsibility; survivors/implicated communities as central focal points from appraisal to access.
bad: Deliberately machinery-free professional ethic for traumatic/human-rights records; specifies no labels, tiers, forms, or checks, and its originating contexts are not this wiki's.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected — as a build: the paper is a machinery-free professional ethic that specifies no labels, tiers, forms or checks to implement, and its human-rights and trauma contexts are not this household wiki's; retained as background reading only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Community archives as a form — Flinn, Stevens & Shepherd (2009); Caswell (2014–2016)
licence: © 2014 by The Regents of the University of California and the National Council on Public History — all rights reserved at source; no open licence stated
good: Five clustering principles (broad participation, shared stewardship, multiplicity of voices/formats, collecting as activism, reflexivity about shifting identity) with ontological/epistemological/social impacts against symbolic annihilation.
bad: Form presupposes a community misrepresented by an outside institution — here the institution and the community archive are the same household; four principles hold trivially by construction.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Form cannot transfer to a single-principal archive; reflexivity concern is carried by the consent-state and participatory-description entries.

name: Deed of gift — Society of American Archivists guide
good: Signed, specific, bounded instrument: parties, description, transfer of ownership/custody, IP provisions with dates for retained rights, disposition of unwanted material, and restrictions for a limited and clearly stated period; warns that digital material may contain passwords, browsing history, and seemingly deleted files.
bad: Legal agreement form itself has no repository/ownership-transfer analogue in a one-owner wiki.
took: Adopt terms-of-deposit notes at ingest for material originating outside the owner–agent pair — provider, date, description, terms, restrictions with periods, known hazards — recorded in the raw layer.
didnt: Adopt/build — terms-of-deposit notes at ingest for material originating outside the owner–agent pair (provider, date, description, terms, restrictions with periods, known hazards), recorded in the raw layer, matching the adoption already recorded in took. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Closure periods and restriction review — SAA / university archives / 36 CFR 1256
good: Restriction as a schedule: fixed class periods (administrative 20–30 years, personal/confidential 75 years or until death), donor restrictions as their own class, and a review mechanism where a requester may ask whether conditions requiring closure still exist.
bad: Archives' fixed 25/75-year periods are calibrated for public research access and do not transfer at household scale.
took: Every restriction must carry a restricted_until date or a named review trigger, with the sweep surfacing lapsed restrictions for a keep/lift ruling; no indefinite restriction is well-formed. Also wave10-synthesis.md items 17 and 50-adjacent.
didnt: Adopt/build — require a restricted_until date or a named review trigger on every restriction, with the sweep surfacing lapsed restrictions for a keep/lift ruling, matching the adoption already recorded in took; the archives' fixed public-access periods themselves do not transfer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Withdrawal sheet — 36 CFR Part 1256 (NARA)
good: A withheld document is not silently absent — it appears on a withdrawal sheet in the file, and the fact/reference of withholding is itself part of the record even while content is not.
bad: The regulation uses the withdrawal sheet only as a citation aid for files NARA previously screened — §1256.32(b) requires the requester to describe each document so staff can locate it, and prescribes no sheet contents, format or retention rule — and §1256.32(c) leaves the donor or representative the right to keep material closed; it is a federal public-access mechanism, not a household withholding log.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — a withdrawal-sheet analogue for the wiki: a withheld page appears as a stub recording the fact and reason for withholding, so an absence is never silent. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Data trusts — ODI; Ada Lovelace Institute; GPAI
good: Legal structure providing independent stewardship with legally binding fiduciary duty to beneficiaries, court oversight, and independence from data holders/users.
bad: Only 28% of data-trust data points in the Ada Lovelace review were implemented projects, the rest theoretical literature.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Form answers a trust gap that does not exist here, and its independence requirement is affirmatively misaligned with owner sovereignty — an independent trustee's duty could conflict with the owner's direct instructions.

name: Data cooperatives — MIDATA
licence: GPL-3.0 — for the Open MIDATA Server platform software, as stated at source; the cooperative itself states no separate licence
good: Swiss non-profit cooperative health-data platform: members govern at a general assembly, grant selective per-project access, and an elected data ethics review board controls ethical quality; articles enshrine user sovereignty over data use.
bad: Cooperative survival depends on members continuing to show up to govern — democratic machinery for a membership pooling a resource.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Democratic member governance for a single-principal household is theatre, and extending membership to collaborator agents would dilute the owner's authority — the opposite of this system's constitutional rule. ## Wave 9 — Intelligence-analysis tradecraft

name: ICD 203 Analytic Standards (2015); Marcoci et al. evaluation (2019)
licence: US government directive, public, as recorded in the file; evaluation is a journal article
good: Nine tradecraft standards as a review rubric — describe source quality, express uncertainties, distinguish information from assumptions/judgments, incorporate alternatives, explain change vs previous judgment — safeguarded by an Analytic Ombuds and product-evaluation programmes.
bad: The standard's only empirical evaluation (15 raters, 64 reports) found individual assessments unreliable even after training/calibration; aggregated ratings needed groups of at least three raters, and whether good reasoning yields accuracy was left untested.
took: Adopt as a checklist constitution for compiled pages and Ask answers, scored as one rater's scores with trends over single scores; the information-vs-assumption-vs-judgment distinction is the highest-value clause. Page must narrate change vs previous judgment, not just the log.
didnt: Adopt/build — the nine ICD 203 tradecraft standards as the review rubric for compiled pages and Ask answers, scored as one rater's scores with trends preferred over single scores, because Marcoci et al. show individual application of the standards is unreliable and only aggregated ratings from at least three raters are dependable; the information-versus-assumption-versus-judgment distinction is the highest-value clause, and each page must narrate change against the previous judgment (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Words of Estimative Probability — Sherman Kent (1964); ICD 203 likelihood scale
licence: Public doctrine and scholarship, as recorded in the file
good: Pins a closed vocabulary to numbers so a word is a commitment that can later be scored; ICD 203 mandates one of two synonym rows (remote 1–5% through almost certain 95–99%) and forbids mixing without disclaimer.
bad: Kent's initiative was not adopted in his lifetime; the 2001 PDB carried warnings with no estimative terms at all, leaving the reader to supply likelihood.
took: Adopt the ICD 203 seven-band scale verbatim as the wiki's estimative lexicon for forecast statements, print the scale where used, and make unbanded probability words in compiled prose a lint finding. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 2.
didnt: Adopt/build — the ICD 203 seven-band likelihood scale verbatim as the wiki's estimative lexicon for forecast statements, with the scale printed where it is used and unbanded probability words in compiled prose treated as a lint finding, because a word pinned to a numeric band is a commitment that can later be scored, which is the point Kent was making in 1964 (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Separation rule — likelihood and confidence (ICD 203 standard 2b)
licence: Public doctrine, as recorded in the file
good: Mechanical, checkable ban: a confidence level and a degree of likelihood must not be combined in the same sentence; confidence definitions (high/moderate/low) are about the evidence base, likelihood about the event.
bad: Ordinary prose constantly fuses the two — "we are confident it is likely" is a category error.
took: Extend the two-axis claim design into prose and Ask answers: confidence sentences carry no likelihood word and vice versa; where both are needed, two sentences, likelihood first, confidence second with its basis. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 2.
didnt: Adopt/build — the separation rule as a prose and Ask-answer rule: a confidence sentence carries no likelihood word and a likelihood sentence carries no confidence level; where both are needed they go in two sentences, likelihood first and confidence second with its basis, because the two axes answer different questions and fusing them is a category error the directive bans mechanically (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Key Assumptions Check — CIA Tradecraft Primer (2009)
licence: US government publication, public, as recorded in the file
good: Four-step audit — write the line, articulate all premises, challenge each, refine to those that must be true — with the DC sniper example decomposing a solid-feeling assumption (single white male in a white van, in a region with over 70,000 registered white vans) into components of wildly different strength.
bad: Assumptions are usually held unconsciously, seldom examined, and the cost of an unlisted one is filtering out the correction when it arrives.
took: Beliefs page gains decomposition for compound beliefs plus basis and what-would-change-it fields, run at verified_until review over load-bearing pages, not every page.
didnt: Adopt/build — a key-assumptions check on load-bearing pages only, run at verified_until review: compound beliefs are decomposed into components of differing strength, each with its basis and what would change it, because the primer's sniper example shows an undecomposed assumption silently filtering out the correction when it arrives (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Analysis of Competing Hypotheses — Heuer (1999)
licence: Public US government publications; evaluations are journal literature, as recorded in the file
good: Eight-step matrix working by diagnosticity and disproof — the most likely hypothesis is the one with least evidence against it — producing an auditable record: full hypothesis set, evidence arrayed against all, non-diagnostic evidence visibly discarded, losers kept on the page.
bad: Repeated controlled tests failed: Karvetski & Mandel (2020, N=227) found no advantage over control and pseudo-diagnostic weighting; Mandel et al. (2018) found ACH analysts less coherent and marginally less accurate; Whitesmith (2019) found no mitigation of confirmation bias. ACH never defines consistency, ignores priors and correlated evidence.
took: Adopt in deliberately reduced form as bookkeeping (not an accuracy technology) for staged gateway proposals and contradiction Cases only, with hypotheses capped small, correlated evidence marked as one witness, and output as an ordinal survivor ranking for the owner's decision — never a probability or solo agent verdict. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 37.
didnt: Adopt/build — ACH in deliberately reduced form as bookkeeping, not an accuracy technology, for staged gateway proposals and contradiction Cases only: hypothesis set kept small, correlated evidence marked as one witness, and the output an ordinal survivor ranking for the owner's decision — never a probability and never a solo agent verdict — because controlled tests (Karvetski & Mandel 2020; Mandel et al. 2018; Whitesmith 2019) failed to show an accuracy or bias advantage (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Linchpin analysis — MacEachin / Heuer
licence: Public US government publication and scholarship, as recorded in the file
good: Ranking, not a list: linchpins are the assumptions whose failure flips the judgment, found by the counterfactual test "if this were false, does the conclusion change?"; Heuer's sensitivity principle directs questioning where sensitivity is.
bad: About a third of reviewed DI papers had no discernible argumentation and another third flawed argumentation, per MacEachin's review in the foreword account.
took: Add a Linchpins section to the small set of load-bearing pages, each linchpin in one sentence with the judgments that fall if it falls and its tripwire indicator, so a falsification enumerates its blast radius. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 38.
didnt: Adopt/build — a Linchpins section on the small set of load-bearing pages, each linchpin in one sentence with the judgments that fall if it falls and its tripwire indicator, so a falsification enumerates its own blast radius and questioning is directed where sensitivity actually is (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Quality of Information Check — CIA Tradecraft Primer
licence: US government publication, public, as recorded in the file
good: Scheduled review of the information base itself — completeness, accuracy, corroboration, source background/access/motivation, and re-examination of previously dismissed information — from which confidence is derived, not felt.
bad: Primer warnings: multiple sources are not a substitute for good information, judgments anchor to weak information, caveats attached in the past are forgotten over time, and WMD work relied on a single ambiguous source and nonspecific source lines.
took: At ingest and verified_until review, source pages record what the source is, its access, motivation where knowable, corroboration, and what was previously dismissed from it and why; the check is the review at which carried caveats are re-attached.
didnt: Adopt/build — a quality-of-information check at ingest and at verified_until review: source pages record what the source is, its access, motivation where knowable, corroboration, and what was previously dismissed from it and why, with carried caveats re-attached at that review, because confidence should be derived from the information base rather than felt (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Indicators & Signposts — CIA Tradecraft Primer
licence: US government publication, public, as recorded in the file
good: Pre-committed observations, one list per hypothesis, chosen before the outcome is known — which makes them evidence rather than rationalisation — plus dual is/is-not lists and depersonalisation of disagreement because all sides consented to criteria in advance.
bad: Lists require continual review effort; an unreviewed indicators list is worse than none because it performs vigilance.
took: Every ACH matrix/staged proposal closes with its indicator list; each linchpin's indicator is monitored by drift/nightly lanes; standing answers gain the observations that would change them — attached only where a review rhythm already exists. Also wave10-synthesis.md items 36/38 context.
didnt: Adopt/build — pre-committed indicator lists closing every ACH matrix and staged proposal, each linchpin's indicator monitored by the drift and nightly lanes, and standing answers carrying the observations that would change them — attached only where a review rhythm already exists, because a list chosen before the outcome is known is evidence while an unreviewed list merely performs vigilance (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Argument mapping — Johansson (2024); Toulmin layout
licence: Journal article; technique is unencumbered practice, as recorded in the file
good: Typed claim tree (fact/hypothesis/assumption/value judgment) makes visible which boxes are assumptions, which claims rest on a single chain, and where a rebuttal box is absent — things prose can hide indefinitely.
bad: Johansson's restraint is required: putting numbers on every box can produce misleading results; tentative judgments are better handled as justified belief than spurious quantification.
took: For contradiction Cases and syntheses the owner must rule on, the case file carries an argument map as an indented typed tree with citations on fact boxes, with no numeric propagation — support is shown, not summed.
didnt: Adopt/build — an argument map as an indented typed tree (fact / hypothesis / assumption / value judgment) in the case file for contradiction Cases and syntheses the owner must rule on, with citations on the fact boxes and no numeric propagation, because the typed tree makes single-chain claims and missing rebuttals visible while Johansson's restraint warns that scoring every box produces spurious quantification (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Devil's Advocacy — CIA Tradecraft Primer; Schweiger et al. (1986)
licence: Primer public; studies cited, as recorded in the file
good: One assigned critic builds the best case against a strongly held line; Schweiger et al. (120 MBA students) found Devil's Advocacy and Dialectical Inquiry produced higher-quality recommendations and assumptions than consensus, and no study found assigned critique worse than consensus on quality.
bad: Consensus groups were more satisfied, more willing to work together again, and more accepting — structured conflict buys decision quality with comfort/reading time.
took: Before any consequential owner decision, the packet carries a labelled Devil's advocate section written against its own recommendation, from a separate adversarial pass, filed not summarised away, capped and reserved for decisions expensive to reverse. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 36-adjacent / Phase 0 context.
didnt: Adopt/build — a labelled Devil's advocate section in the packet before any consequential owner decision, written against the packet's own recommendation in a separate adversarial pass and filed rather than summarised away, capped in length and reserved for decisions expensive to reverse, because assigned critique demonstrably buys decision quality even though it costs comfort (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Team A / Team B — CIA Tradecraft Primer; 1976 exercise
licence: Public historical record and US government primer, as recorded in the file
good: In designed form, two teams develop the best case for competing hypotheses from the same evidence, rebut each other, and submit to an independent jury of peers.
bad: 1976 failure is the warning: a team selected for its conclusion laundered bias — retrospective verdicts say virtually all specific allegations were wrong and always in the direction of enlarging danger (Backfire forecast ~500 aircraft by early 1984, actual 235); Bush concluded it lends itself to manipulation.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Not for us in designed form — a one-agent shop can only simulate both teams (a simulated Team B inherits the lead mindset in costume) and there is no external jury pool. Salvage is Devil's Advocacy with a debate exhibit, called that, not Team B. Also negative N5 in wave10-synthesis.md.

name: Red Team Analysis — CIA Tradecraft Primer; Zenko (2015)
licence: Primer public; book cited via reviews, as recorded in the file
good: Models an adversary's thinking to defeat mirror-imaging; Zenko's practices include boss buy-in, willingness to hear bad news and act on it, and "red team just enough, but no more" — the latter two transfer as posture/scoping.
bad: Value lives entirely in the otherness of different, differently incentivised people; strip that and it is an analyst imagining an adversary from his own priors, the failure it exists to interrupt.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Not for us as adversary simulation — this wiki has no adversary whose decision-making is an analytic target, and an agent playing an opponent would simulate from its own priors. Also negative N5 in wave10-synthesis.md. (Adversarial probing of the Ask door/gateway is penetration testing, covered in wave 8, not this frame.)

name: Premortem — Gary Klein (HBR 2007); Mitchell, Russo & Pennington (1989)
licence: HBR article paywalled at HBR's site, as recorded in wave9; gap closure opened the full text via a university course mirror
good: Prospective hindsight — stipulate the project has already failed spectacularly and write why, independently before sharing — makes dissent cheap and surfaces socially suppressed reasons. Gap closure confirms Klein's procedure firsthand, including the independent-writing step.
bad: The famous 30% is a misquote in effect: Klein's sentence claims prospective hindsight "increases the ability to correctly identify reasons … by 30%," but the 1989 study measured the number of reasons generated, with no accuracy check — fluency, not correctness.
took: Premortem blocks on staged proposals/build batches and consequential owner decisions, in a separate pass, with each reason designed against, converted to an indicator, or explicitly accepted; failures later scored against whether the failure was on the list. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 36, lane priority 1.
didnt: Adopt/build — premortem blocks on staged proposals, build batches and consequential owner decisions, run as a separate pass with independent writing first, each reason then designed against, converted to an indicator, or explicitly accepted, and later failures scored against whether the failure was on the list — without repeating the 30% figure as an accuracy claim, since the 1989 study measured reasons generated, not correctness (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Structured brainstorming / brainwriting / Nominal Group Technique — CIA Tradecraft Primer; Paulus & Yang (2000)
licence: Primer public; procedures and studies cited, as recorded in the file
good: Written, simultaneous generation removes production blocking — the main cause of interactive verbal groups generating fewer ideas than nominal groups; Paulus & Yang gave first evidence brainwriting can outperform even nominal groups, with a practice summary putting it at ~40% more ideas than verbal brainstorming.
bad: Brainwriting advantage rests substantially on laboratory tasks with unacquainted students; field evidence in real organisations is thin.
took: Generation for ACH matrices and premortems is always independent-pass-first in parallel agents, merged afterwards; ranking is a separate criteria-based step; one pass is always briefed from a different (outside-in) framing.
didnt: Adopt/build — independent-pass-first generation for ACH matrices and premortems: parallel agents generate in writing before any merge, ranking is a separate criteria-based step afterwards, and one pass is always briefed from a different outside-in framing, because written simultaneous generation removes the production blocking that makes verbal groups underperform nominal ones (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Outside-In Thinking — CIA Tradecraft Primer
licence: US government publication, public, as recorded in the file
good: Framing audit done once, early, cheap: list broad external forces (social, technological, economic, environmental, political) and nearer influenceable factors before analysing inside the issue's own categories, reducing the risk of missing a variable early and re-coding everything later.
bad: A one-shot framing exercise, not a test: the primer places it at the conceptualisation of a project, says only that with modest effort it 'can reduce the risk of missing important variables early', and its own How To Use section warns that application of these techniques alone 'is no guarantee of analytic precision or accuracy of judgments'. The method lists forces and then asks whether they actually have an impact based on available evidence — it specifies no scoring, evidence threshold, or revisit cadence.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — a one-time outside-in framing checklist (broad STEEP forces first, then nearer influenceable factors) at the start of major analyses, as a complement to the premortem and key-assumptions blocks already in the schema. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: High-Impact / Low-Probability Analysis — CIA Tradecraft Primer
licence: US government publication, public, as recorded in the file
good: Removes probability from discussion so a pathway for an ignored high-impact event can be examined, then converts the pathway into triggers, indicators, and deflections; exhibits are Pearl Harbor, fall of the Shah, collapse of the USSR, German reunification.
bad: Deliberately probability-free, so its output is a plausible pathway, not an assessment: the method brainstorms possible triggers, identifies indicators/observables per pathway and factors that would deflect a bad outcome, and relies on periodic review of those indicators to counter the prevailing mind-set — the primer gives no likelihood estimate, no threshold for acting, and no test that would falsify a pathway.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms the watch-conditions practice already in our system (parked decisions and load-bearing pages carrying the triggers/indicators that would wake or change them); no separate technique adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Brier scoring / forecast register — Brier (1950); Good Judgment Project (Mellers et al. 2015)
licence: Score is public mathematics (1950); tournament literature cited, as recorded in the file
good: Strictly proper scoring rule (0 is perfection, always-50% scores 0.25) making honesty the optimal strategy, with Murphy decomposition into reliability, resolution, and uncertainty; GJP evidence from over 150,000 forecasts, 743 participants, 199 events — under one hour of probabilistic-reasoning training improved Brier scores by 6–11% persistently.
bad: Scores are question-set-specific and a large-sample instrument — very large samples (n > 1000) are needed to discriminate skill on rare events; no skill claims are honest at small N.
took: Create a forecast register for the wiki's own estimative judgments only — band, resolution date, and basis logged at statement time, Brier score with calibration/resolution split computed at resolution and reported with N. The owner's decisions are never scored. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 39.
didnt: Adopt/build — a forecast register for the wiki's own estimative judgments only: band, resolution date and basis logged at statement time, Brier score with its calibration and resolution split computed at resolution and always reported with N, and the owner's decisions never scored, because the rule is a large-sample instrument and no skill claim is honest at small N (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Superforecasting habits — Tetlock & Gardner (2015); Good Judgment Project
licence: Published books and programme reports, cited, as recorded in the file; book itself not opened in this pass
good: Habits measured around the techniques: fine-grained probabilities, outside view/base rate first, frequent small updates, actively open-minded thinking, post-mortems on misses; hedgehogs (one big idea) forecast worse than foxes.
bad: Aggregation machinery (extremised crowd aggregation, prediction markets, superforecaster teams) requires a crowd.
took: The Brier forecast register (agent's estimative judgments logged and scored; owner's decisions never scored) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 4 — source/inspiration: Tetlock / GJP method, as recorded in lanes/lane8-dispositions.md.
didnt: Aggregation machinery considered and rejected for a one-analyst corpus — there is no crowd, and manufacturing one from correlated agent passes would reproduce Team B's selection problem. Two habits are promoted into other machinery: frequent small updating (indicators/re-verification) and the outside view as a named step before any estimative band. ## Wave 9 — Library & information science practice

name: Syndetic structure / authority control — Art Institute of Chicago guide
good: Working anatomy of an authority record: one authorized heading, see references from every variant, see also to related authorized headings, and a scope note — collating, disambiguating, and making any known variant land on the canonical record.
bad: Local and system-bound: the guide is Ryerson's own practice, built on LC's Name and Subject Authority Files, MARC 1XX/4XX/5XX fields and Alma linking (the binoculars workflow), and it concedes limits — some digital-asset bib records 'cannot update these types of bib records to link to the authority file or to match our headings and have to just let them be', and a topical heading with no authority record must not be used at all.
took: Entity pages and tag vocabulary should carry canonical heading, a variants list search resolves silently, and typed see also links (predecessor/successor/broader); no variant is ever lost, it is reclassified as a pointer.
didnt: Adopt/build — entity pages and the tag vocabulary carry one canonical heading, a variants list that search resolves silently, and typed see-also links (predecessor/successor/broader), with a variant reclassified as a pointer rather than ever lost. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: 670/675 justification trail — NACO (FDLP / Folger practice)
good: Authority record is self-auditing: field 670 cites each source that yielded information with the exact form found, field 675 cites sources consulted that yielded nothing — the negative search is recorded too, and a URL alone does not satisfy the rule.
bad: Heavy, MARC-specific formalism: the page is GPO's local practice layered on DCM Z1 and the NACO Participants' Manual, with long field-by-field rules for subfield a/b construction, serials, legal publications, OCLC-database and shelflist citations, plus a narrow exception regime for secondary NARs (cite the work cataloged in a 675 only when the secondary name does not appear in it and no other work supports it). Portable as a discipline, not as a format.
took: Adopt a Justification block on entity pages and in the tag registry — source + exact form found per element, plus checked-not-found lines — so headings are justified as claims already are. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 48, lane priority 1.
didnt: Adopt/build — a Justification block on entity pages and in the tag registry: source plus exact form found per element, plus checked-not-found lines, so headings are justified as claims already are. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NACO / SACO cooperative programmes — PCC; Bailund et al. study; Yale workflow
good: Shared vocabulary scales via a training gate, a public Tentative List with a comment window before decision, and a published Summary of Decisions giving reasons for every rejection so proposers learn the pattern.
bad: Institution-scale overhead: proposals pass through cooperative review to a weekly LC editorial meeting, tentative lists warn that proposed headings 'may be revised or not approved' and that diacritics and special symbols do not display on the lists, contributors are told to contact the Cooperative Cataloging Team if a proposal has not appeared on a tentative list within four weeks, and the governing manual alone runs to hundreds of pages of form-by-form rules — a latency and training burden built for a national file, not a single-owner wiki.
took: Adopt the Tentative List (standing dated pending-decisions list) and the Summary of Decisions with reasons (owner declines/reshapes filed in the same form) as deltas on staged proposals/filings.
didnt: External certification travel/fees component not for us — meaningless at this scale; the gate here is schema and review, not a credential.

name: VIAF clustering — OCLC; Hickey & Toves (2014)
licence: Copyright © 2014 Online Computer Library Center, Inc. — no open licence stated at source
good: Clusters authority files from 50+ organisations without replacing source files or flattening local preferences; clustering by progressive refinement — loose matching first, then groupings supply evidence for stricter decisions; merges answer with HTTP 301, withdrawn IDs distinguished from redirected ones.
bad: Clustering internals documented only at the 2014 paper level; current OCLC algorithm is a service, not a publication.
took: Duplicate-entity handling in suggestions-only form: agent proposes merges with shared evidence shown, owner/reviewing agent decides, merge executed as redirect-plus-variant-preservation, never deletion; "merged into X" and "retired, points nowhere" are different terminal states.
didnt: Adopt/build — duplicate-entity handling in suggestions-only form: the agent proposes merges with the shared evidence shown, the owner or reviewing agent decides, and a merge executes as redirect-plus-variant-preservation, never deletion, with 'merged into X' and 'retired, points nowhere' as distinct terminal states. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Headings reports and the global flip — Wolf, Code4Lib Journal (UNT)
good: Maintenance as a daily report cleared, not a project scheduled: Headings Reports list first-use, invalid, and conflicting headings; a national heading change propagates by global flip from the authority record, automatically overnight.
bad: When the team shrank, per-heading manual checking collapsed first — automated report-and-flip parts are what survived.
took: Add a nightly/weekly headings report to the sweep (new entity names/tags, names matching no entity page, near-duplicates) cleared in the sweep, and write the flip rule into the schema — renames execute at the authority and propagate by tool, never by hand-editing citing pages. Also lane priority 4 in the source.
didnt: Adopt/build — a nightly/weekly headings report in the sweep (new entity names and tags, names matching no entity page, near-duplicates) cleared as routine maintenance, and the flip rule written into the schema: a rename executes at the authority record and propagates by tool, never by hand-editing citing pages. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
