name: Catalogue audit by random sampling — Oxford / Bodleian technique
good: Quality as a rate with a method: random sample scored in both directions (catalogue→collection and collection→catalogue), field by field as acceptable/incorrect/missing; access-point errors weighted most serious because they break retrieval.
bad: Costly and partial: the abstract records practical difficulties generating a random sample (the Bath pilot sample 'was not strictly random'), finds the technique 'effective for picking up errors in descriptive cataloguing but less sound for name and subject headings', and the simplified technique drops the test for uncatalogued and duplicate items; the revised chapter's own sample sizes (400-1500 records for a usable margin of error) make it a staff-time commitment, not a quick check.
took: Periodic sampled audit — N random compiled pages scored against raw sources field by field in both directions — giving one honest corpus-quality number per quarter and a trend line beside the Ask-door eval. Also lane priority 5 in the source.
didnt: Adopt/build — a periodic sampled audit: N random compiled pages scored against their raw sources field by field in both directions, giving one honest corpus-quality number per quarter and a trend line beside the Ask-door eval. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Literary warrant and user warrant — Hulme; ANSI/NISO Z39.19; ISKO
licence: © 2005 NISO — no open licence stated at source
good: Vocabulary growth is demand-led from two directions and supply-led from none: a heading is created only when a work needs it (literary warrant) or when askers keep reaching for it (user warrant).
bad: Narrower in the source than in our two-warrant version, and monolingual by design: Z39.19's title and scope cover monolingual controlled vocabularies only, and section 5.3.5 lists three warrants — literary, user and organizational — so a literary-plus-user-only rule omits the organizational-warrant test the standard itself requires; warrant is also framed there as a term-selection criterion (terms should 'match as closely as possible the prevailing usage in the domain's literature'), not a standalone creation threshold.
took: Write into the schema: a tag/entity page is created when a source being ingested needs it or when the owner's questions keep reaching for it — never to complete a pattern.
didnt: Adopt/build — written into the schema: a tag or entity page is created when a source being ingested needs it (literary warrant) or when the owner's questions keep reaching for it (user warrant) — never to complete a pattern. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Dewey Editorial Policy Committee exhibits — OCLC Dewey
licence: Proprietary — all copyright rights in the Dewey Decimal Classification system are owned by OCLC, Inc., as stated at source; no open licence
good: Classification revision as written, numbered, commentable Exhibits (background, change, effects) reviewed by a ten-member committee, posted publicly for feedback, with a fast-track lane for urgent cases (the COVID-19 number).
bad: Editors explicitly note "we don't catalog books" — editorial office needs practitioner expertise because production cataloguers see needed changes first.
took: AGENTS.md amendments become short written exhibits (triggering case from real ingest, proposed schema text, pages affected, cost of not changing) filed before the change, with a standing fast-track when ingest is actively blocked.
didnt: Adopt/build — AGENTS.md amendments become short written exhibits (triggering case from real ingest, proposed schema text, pages affected, cost of not changing) filed before the change, with a standing fast-track when ingest is actively blocked. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Local subject headings policy — UCLA Library Ethical Description
good: Prices deviation honestly: local headings are difficult to maintain, require local extension, and will not receive upstream global flips; ordered preference is acceptable official heading, another established vocabulary, then propose the change upstream through SACO.
bad: Every local deviation is a fork maintained forever that silently diverges.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms our design choice to rely on established vocabularies and headings rather than maintain local forks that silently diverge, proposing changes upstream instead. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Guidelines for Behavioral Performance of Reference Providers — RUSA (2023)
good: Six movements (Inclusion, Approachability, Engagement, Searching, Evaluation, Closure) with the premise that users seldom start and end with the same inquiry: restate and confirm before searching, show choices during search, check mid-search, and at closure explain beyond-scope while helping identify the right place — a referral, not a refusal.
bad: The Preface itself warns that some guidelines 'might not prove applicable in all contexts' and should be adapted as appropriate; many prescribed behaviours are in-person human cues (visibility, eye contact, body language) with no direct equivalent for a text Ask door, and the document provides no measurement or test for compliance.
took: Adopt as the Ask door's interaction contract: vague questions get a restated confirmable form before retrieval, every answer shows its search/sources and why, and closure is a check plus an honest beyond-scope referral. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 61 (governing form).
didnt: Adopt/build — the Ask door's interaction contract (restate-and-confirm before searching, show search choices and sources during search, closure as a check plus an honest beyond-scope referral), as recorded in the existing took field. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Neutral (sense-making) questioning — Ross & Dewdney
good: Sense-making questions are open questions engineered free of the librarian's assumptions, in four stem families — situation, the person's own view, gaps, uses — paired with paraphrase-and-check; closed questions smuggle in the librarian's guess at the dimensions.
bad: First question is often a contact probe, not the real need; premature diagnosis is the named failure.
took: The Ask door's clarifying turn should be one sense-making stem (situation/gap/use) generated from the question, not a facet menu of candidate refinements; paraphrase the first interpretation back rather than silently searching it. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 61 and C3 (this form governs over wave 7's facet-generated questions).
didnt: Adopt/build — one assumption-free sense-making clarifying stem (situation/gap/use) plus paraphrase-back in the Ask door, rather than a facet menu of candidate refinements, as recorded in the existing took field. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Five discovery facets — Park University Library reference guide
good: Compresses the interview into five cheap, search-changing facets — Type, Quantity, Purpose, Level, Timing — and names the doorknob question: the real follow-up asked on the way out, caught by a designed closing move.
bad: The guide is a brief student-employee checklist: it states the five facets in a few lines with no evaluation, evidence or worked failure cases, and it exempts directional questions from any reference interview, so it gives no guidance for ambiguous short queries.
took: Adopt as the Ask door's intake schema; Timing explicitly routes instant answer vs queued deep-research pickup, Level maps to the owner's standing context, Purpose to deliverable choice; end substantive answers with a one-line reopening.
didnt: Adopt/build — the Ask door's intake schema (Type, Quantity, Purpose, Level, Timing), with Timing routing instant versus queued answers, as recorded in the existing took field. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: IFLA Digital Reference Guidelines
good: Digital reference must meet the same standard as traditional service, with a written reference policy (planning, staffing, training, interface, legal, evaluation, collaboration), neutral questioning, and explicit turnaround expectations for asynchronous service.
bad: Full text not opened — filed on a conference paper's summary, confined to the administrative point.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms our Ask-door service design (a written reference policy, neutral questioning, and explicit turnaround expectations for asynchronous service), duplicating ground already covered by the RUSA guidelines rather than adding a new mechanism. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CREW: A Weeding Manual for Modern Libraries — Larson (Texas State Library, 2012)
licence: CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 (2012 rev., as recorded in the file)
good: Weeding as Continuous Review, Evaluation, and Weeding: per-class X/Y formulas (years since copyright / years since last circulation) plus MUSTIE defects, where either gate alone is insufficient and formulas nominate while the librarian decides item in hand.
bad: The manual's home is reportedly withdrawn/unmaintained by the Texas State Library — the benchmark weeding text is itself an unmaintained artefact (withdrawal not verified firsthand in the lane).
took: Use as template for a wiki review queue with disposal replaced by our terminal states: per page-class formulas nominate pages for re-verification/owner review, feeding FSRS machinery with a second nomination source; nothing is deleted. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 43, lane priority 3.
didnt: Adopt/build — the weeding-as-triage review queue: per-class formulas nominate pages only with a defect attached, disposal is replaced by our terminal states (re-verification and owner review, feeding the FSRS machinery as a second nomination source), and deletion is never an outcome; built 2026-10-20, Phase 5. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MUSTIE — CREW manual defect vocabulary
licence: CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 (via the CREW manual, as recorded in the file)
good: Closed defect vocabulary turning "this feels stale" into a checkable claim: Misleading, Ugly, Superseded, Trivial, Irrelevant, Elsewhere — each letter a different defect with a different remedy.
bad: An item normally needs the CREW formula plus at least one letter — a defect alone is not a nomination.
took: Adopt as the triage vocabulary of the review queue, translated letter by letter to routes (M→corrections ledger, U→repair pass, S→redirect machinery, T→owner keep/fold, I→user-warrant failure, E→pointer page). Also wave10-synthesis.md item 43.
didnt: Adopt/build — MUSTIE as the triage vocabulary of the review queue, translated letter by letter to routes (M→corrections ledger, U→repair pass, S→redirect machinery, T→owner keep/fold, I→user-warrant failure, E→pointer page), with a defect attached to a formula nomination rather than nominating alone; built as part of the weeding-as-triage queue 2026-10-20, Phase 5. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Selection & Reconsideration Policy Toolkit: Weeding — ALA
good: Policy guardrails: objective criteria named in advance, named exception areas exempt from routine weeding, human override with a reason (including the last loanable copy check), multi-step approval for contested removals, and weeding never used as a deselection tool for controversial materials.
bad: The page itself states that step-by-step guidelines on weeding and removal procedures are not typically found in a policy but in a procedural manual, so the toolkit supplies policy language only — no operational procedure, thresholds or test for a specific collection.
took: Review queue's charter should name its exception classes in advance, require the held-elsewhere/inbound-citation check before a page is proposed as superseded/elsewhere, and keep owner approval as the multi-step gate.
didnt: Board — name exception classes in advance in the review queue's charter, require a held-elsewhere/inbound-citation check before proposing a page as superseded, and keep owner approval as the multi-step gate. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Deselection formulas in production — Seminole State College; CCNY Libraries
good: Portfolio-shaped thresholds: e.g. not more than a quarter of the collection over 25 years old, a title not circulated at least 3 times in 15 years is deselected — with standing exceptions and projected use as an explicit factor.
bad: The formulas are print- and institution-specific — Seminole's 25-year / three-circulations-in-15-years rule and CCNY's 'held by 3 or more CUNY libraries' criterion depend on circulation records and consortial holdings a personal wiki does not have — and neither page offers any evaluation that the thresholds improve outcomes.
took: Sweep can report a corpus age-and-retrieval profile as one health number alongside per-page nominations; a "needed for X" projected-use annotation exempts a nominated page with a named, dated, expiring reason.
didnt: Board — report a corpus age-and-retrieval profile as one health number in the sweep alongside per-page nominations, with a named, dated, expiring projected-use annotation exempting a nominated page. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Shelf-reading / stack maintenance — University of Richmond Music Library
good: Disciplined humble practice: a mis-shelved item "is LOST, to all intents and purposes"; everyone shelf-reads 15 minutes per shift; the log records name, date/time, and the last call number read so the next shift resumes exactly there and full coverage is arithmetic.
bad: Rests on institutional practice documents stating the discipline confidently but citing no controlled measurement.
took: Every lint lane should record its coverage position (pages examined, through what point, as of when) so "green" means complete through a date; lanes that cannot finish rotate by bookmark instead of restarting. Also lane priority 4 in the source.
didnt: Board — every lint lane records its coverage position (pages examined, through what point, as of when) so a green result means complete through a date, and lanes that cannot finish rotate by bookmark instead of restarting. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Inventories / stocktakes — Libraries Tasmania
good: Full-collection reconciliation on a 1–2 year cycle (or running monthly) that treats "the catalogue says we hold it" and "it is actually there and correctly described" as separate claims; yields missing items, corrected database, and nominations for weeding/repair/relocation.
bad: Rests on institutional practice documents, no controlled measurement cited.
took: Periodic inventory pass for wiki vs raw vs index agreement — every raw source compiled/queued/explicitly uncompiled-with-reason, every citation resolvable, every index entry live, every page reachable from the index. Filed as the scheduled form of the sampled audit.
didnt: Board — a periodic inventory pass reconciling wiki against raw sources and index (every citation resolvable, every index entry live, every page reachable from the index), filed as the scheduled form of the sampled audit. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Interlibrary Loan Code for the United States — RUSA STARS (2023)
good: Request protocol designed so no request ends in silence: complete accurate description, special requirements up front, patron identity kept out, supplier must respond before expiry, may answer conditionally with terms, must state due dates/restrictions, and must give a reason for an unfilled request that routes the next step; unfilled requests rotate onward.
bad: The code's own explanatory text states it is adopted voluntarily by U.S. libraries and is not enforced by an oversight body, its scope is library-to-library exchange of material within the United States when no other agreement applies, and it does not override individual, consortial, state or regional agreements — so its duties bind only by adoption, not by the document itself.
took: Use as template for agent-to-agent asks: complete citation plus what was already tried; the answering side owes fill, conditional-fill-with-terms, or unfilled-with-a-reason; a queued question that will not be answered must be answered as unfilled, with its reason, before it ages out.
didnt: Adopt/build — use the code as the template for agent-to-agent asks: a complete description plus what was already tried, with the answering side owing a fill, a conditional fill with terms, or an unfilled answer with a reason before the request ages out, as recorded in the existing took field. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CONTU Rule of Five
good: Classic rate-limit-with-receipts shape: per-source budget (five recent articles per title per year), per-request attestation mark (CCG/CCL), and records retained three years.
bad: Rule governs US copyright in interlibrary copying under §108(g)(2) — a regime this wiki is not in.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Not for us as a rule — importing the numbers would be cargo-cult compliance; only the shape is recorded as precedent if a future workflow needs a throttle, with our own numbers.

name: Guidelines for Interlibrary Loan Operations Management — RUSA STARS; licence-tracker practice
good: Service levels are negotiated commitments you staff to, not aspirations; permission knowledge in contracts is compiled into a desk-level licence tracker consulted at request time, maintained with the people who negotiate the licences.
bad: The opened guidelines are scoped only to the management of interlibrary loan and document delivery operations — qualifications, hiring, training and supervisory skills — and set out no desk-level licence-tracker procedure, no request-time workflow and no numeric service levels; the text is the 2011 STARS-approved, 2012 RUSA Board-approved revision.
took: Compile a permissions page for the wiki's own sources and tools (quotation limits, agent-seat access, export permissions) consulted at work time instead of re-deriving policy; state pickup cadences as commitments with an owner beside the service policy.
didnt: Adopt/build — compile a desk-level permissions page for the wiki's own sources and tools, consulted at work time instead of re-deriving policy, and state pickup cadences as staffed commitments with an owner, following the guidelines' model of compiling contract and consortial knowledge for use at request time (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Appeal factors / readers' advisory — Joyce Saricks
good: Recommendation matches appeal, not subject: pacing, characterization, story line, frame/setting, tone/mood, language/style elicited by pointed questions; subject headings describe a book as "survival; divorce" and miss everything that made the reader love it. Companion rules: don't summarise plot, you needn't have read or liked the book.
bad: Framework filed from secondary renderings — Saricks' books are print/paywalled and were not opened as primary text.
took: Assign a small experiential appeal vocabulary to compiled pages at compile time (dense/sparse, narrative/tabular, settled/contested, quick-brief/deep-dive) so "more like this" can mean feels like this; describe suggested pages in chat by appeal/fit, not by dumping summaries.
didnt: Adopt/build — assign a small experiential appeal vocabulary to compiled pages at compile time and describe suggested pages in chat by appeal and fit rather than by summary, following Saricks's appeal factors (pacing, characterization, story line, frame/setting, tone/mood, style/language) as set out in her handout (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Face-out display studies — Hollands (Booklist); Colorado Library Research Service
licence: © 2002 Colorado Library Research Service — permission granted to reproduce for nonprofit purposes; no licence stated at source for the Booklist (Hollands) article
good: Measured display effect with identical holdings/catalogue: face-out books circulated 48.4% vs 14.2% spine-out (at least 3.5–4× more likely, faster to first checkout); display copies checked out +93% fiction and +25% nonfiction in the Colorado duplicate study.
bad: Hollands is a practitioner-run test in two libraries, not a refereed study; post-weeding circulation rises (up to +40%) are practitioner claims.
took: Treat the Lens Briefing as the wiki's face-out shelf and judge it as one — a small rotating deliberately chosen set of full-face pages, refreshed as items are taken; review queue partly serves as shelf room via demote-don't-delete.
didnt: Adopt/build — treat the Lens Briefing as the wiki's face-out shelf: a small, rotating, deliberately chosen set of full-face pages, refreshed as items are taken and judged by uptake, as display raised circulation in both studies (48.4% vs 14.2% face-out vs spine-out in Hollands; +93% fiction and +25% nonfiction for display copies in the Colorado study) (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Five Laws of Library Science — S. R. Ranganathan (1931)
good: Five one-line acceptance tests resolving every ambiguity toward use: books are for use; every reader his/her book; every book its reader; save the time of the reader; the library is a growing organism.
bad: Formulated in 1931 for a print-only collection: the presenting source notes books were pretty much the only media then, the original wording uses masculine pronouns and is often modernised, and the laws strike readers as obvious, almost cliché. They are five principle statements with no operational mechanism, enforcement or record-keeping procedure attached.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the five laws confirm resolving design ambiguities toward use and saving the reader's time, principles already embodied in the wiki and the Lens; no law is imported as a rule (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Bound-book discipline — lab notebook procedure (UTA; BakerHostetler; Dirnagl & Przesdzing)
good: Bound, sequentially numbered, un-removable pages in permanent ink, chronological, blanks crossed out, never obliterate — strike through so the original stays legible; raw data kept behind any transcription; institution retains notebooks long-term because a patent can be litigated over ~20 years.
bad: A blank space is an invitation to later insertion and makes every surrounding date suspect; thermal printouts fade.
took: Mostly as named confirmations of the git design, plus the no-silent-blanks convention: a gap in chronology carries an explicit "nothing recorded between X and Y" line; raw behind transcription always; perishable captures copied into the durable record at ingest.
didnt: Corroboration — the bound, numbered, permanent-ink, strike-through-never-obliterate discipline confirms the wiki's git-based record design; the one addition is the no-silent-blanks convention, with perishable captures copied into the durable record at ingest (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Guidelines for Keeping a Laboratory Record — Rice BIOC 311 / Kanare discipline
good: Record directly into the notebook during the work, never on scratch paper for later copying; chronology is the spine with a current table of contents over it; thread interleaved work with "continued on/from page ##"; name who actually did each procedure; recopy a messy page only as a new page that back-references the original, which stays.
bad: Transcription from scraps is where dates drift, details vanish, and backdating creeps in.
took: Capture/ingest is written in the record, not drafted elsewhere; unavoidable later write-ups say so on their face; interleaved wiki work carries explicit continued-on/from threading; the recopy rule validates the corrections ledger's never-delete design.
didnt: Corroboration — the record-directly, never-from-scraps, continued-on/from threading and recopy-as-new-page rules validate the wiki's capture-in-the-record and never-delete corrections design, with interleaved work carrying explicit threading and unavoidable later write-ups saying so on their face (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Witnessing and the corroboration rule — Finnegan; Medichem v. Rolabo
good: An inventor's own testimony must be corroborated by a non-inventor who understands the work, signing promptly "read and understood" — "it is the witness's date that determines the date of invention."
bad: In Medichem, notebooks were unwitnessed with minimal corroborative value, a non-inventor's notebook was unsigned/unwitnessed, and inventors admitted backdating entries; the Federal Circuit held the evidence insufficient and priority went to the other party. Case filed secondary (Law.com paywalled).
took: A consequential entry's evidentiary date/weight comes from its independent check, not its writing: owner attestation must be the owner's act, never the writing agent's self-attestation; review acts are dated entries in the record; backdating is the one unforgivable sin — late entries are legitimate only if dated as late. Also wave10-synthesis.md Phase 0 item 5.
didnt: Adopt/build — give a consequential entry its evidentiary date and weight from its independent check rather than its writing: owner attestation must be the owner's own act, never the writing agent's self-attestation, review acts are dated entries in the record, and late entries are legitimate only when dated as late, per the corroboration rule applied in Medichem (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ELN validation / 21 CFR Part 11 — CASRAI; Dirnagl & Przesdzing
good: Part 11 re-implements the bound book in software: validation detecting altered records, complete retrievable copies, authorised access only, secure time-stamped audit trail retained at least as long as the record, and §11.50 signature meaning (review/approval/responsibility/authorship) linked to its record so it cannot be transplanted; ELN practice adds witnessing-and-freezing (immutable after author + witness sign).
bad: Capturing an audit trail is not enough — inspectors expect evidence the trail is reviewed on a defined schedule, and long-term readability must be planned against the vendor disappearing.
took: Make signature meaning explicit on every signed act; owner-attested pages become harder to change and must use the visible-correction path; audit-trail review is a scheduled act (the nightly sweep), not a stored artefact.
didnt: Adopt/build — make signature meaning explicit on every signed act, route owner-attested pages through the visible-correction path instead of direct editing, and make audit-trail review a scheduled act rather than a stored artefact, following Part 11's re-implementation of the bound book in software as set out in the eCFR text (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ship's official log — Merchant Shipping Act 1894 §239; MarineInsight
good: Entries as soon as possible after the occurrence; a late entry is dual-dated to show both occurrence and entry dates; every entry signed by master and mate/another crew member and admissible in evidence; routine readings are recorded whether or not anything is wrong so abnormality is visible; chief engineer countersigns daily.
bad: Destroying, mutilating, rendering illegible, or falsely entering/signing the log is an offence.
took: Dual dating as a schema rule (occurred + recorded); routine readings — a clean sweep run is a recorded normal value; countersignature cadence is a distinct review act, never the same act/agent as the watchkeeper's signature where the record is consequential. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 6.
didnt: Adopt/build — dual-date late entries (date of occurrence and date of entry) as a schema rule, record routine readings as recorded normal values, and keep countersignature a distinct review act from the entry itself, following section 239(4)–(5) of the Merchant Shipping Act 1894 (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: A Mechanic's Signature — Savvy Aviation (FAR 43.9 / 43.11)
good: Two signatures, two meanings defined by rule: FAR 43.9 entry means only "the work I performed was performed satisfactorily" for that work alone; FAR 43.11 inspection signature certifies the whole aircraft airworthy — or signs it unairworthy with a signed, dated discrepancy list handed to the owner and kept until items are fixed. A negative finding is itself a signed record, never a silence or a withheld entry.
bad: Confusing the two meanings causes real disputes between owners and shops.
took: Every signed act in the wiki declares which kind of signature it is — performance records for build/integration entries, fitness meaning reserved for audit/attestation — and a failed audit issues a signed itemised discrepancy list kept visible until each item is cleared. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 5.
didnt: Adopt/build — declare which kind of signature every signed wiki act is (performance record for build/integration entries, fitness meaning reserved for audit/attestation) and issue a signed, itemised discrepancy list for a failed audit, kept visible until each item clears, because the article shows the two FAR signature meanings are distinct by rule (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Handoff programme / I-PASS — Starmer et al. (NEJM 2014); ship's watch relief
licence: Copyright © 2014 Massachusetts Medical Society, all rights reserved (paper); I-PASS copyrighted by Boston Children's Hospital, with its materials stated in the paper to be freely available
good: Handover as a signed structured act completed by synthesis by receiver: I-PASS (Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness/contingency, Synthesis by receiver) cut medical errors 23% and preventable adverse events 30% across nine hospitals and 10,740 admissions with no increase in duration; maritime relief is signed as read-and-understood and deferred while a manoeuvre is in progress.
bad: Communication failure at handoff is a leading cause of medical error and navigational accidents; maritime half filed secondary (search-rendered standing-orders material).
took: Adopt the I-PASS shape for session/subagent handovers — state, summary, action list, contingencies, and receiver synthesis before acting — and do not hand over mid-manoeuvre; a forced boundary during a multi-step operation defers or explicitly logs the in-progress state as a hazard. Also wave10-synthesis.md item 7.
didnt: Adopt/build — the I-PASS shape for session and subagent handovers (state, summary, action list, situation awareness/contingency, and synthesis by receiver before acting) and no handover mid-manoeuvre, with in-progress state at a forced boundary logged as a hazard, because the study shows that bundle cut errors without lengthening handoffs (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Writing Ethnographic Fieldnotes — Emerson, Fretz & Shaw (2011)
licence: no licence stated at source — copyright page states © 1995, 2011 by The University of Chicago, all rights reserved
good: Fieldnotes are made in stages: headnotes (perishable memory, a prompt never a record), jottings (in/near the moment), and the desk write-up where the fieldnote is actually created — promptly, because jottings' power to re-evoke decays within hours to days; asides/commentaries are written in but marked as a different voice, and memoing is a distinct artefact from the notes.
bad: Book's own text paywalled — structure/doctrine verified via publisher's contents and a scholarly review.
took: Jottings have an expiry — raw captures should be compiled the same session, and a late compile is a reconstruction marked as one; keep agent interpretive commentary visibly distinct from the sourced record at writing time; analytic memos are a different artefact class from source-compiled pages, filed separately and cross-referenced.
didnt: Adopt/build — jottings carry an expiry (raw captures compiled the same session, a late compile marked as a reconstruction), agent commentary kept visibly distinct from the sourced record at writing time, and analytic memos filed as a separate artefact class from source-compiled pages, following the book's staged headnotes/jottings/desk write-up and its separate coding-and-memoing chapter (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: A Vocabulary for Fieldnotes — Sanjek (1990); Wedgwood notebooks
good: Precise layer vocabulary — scratch notes, fieldnotes proper (immutable records from a past observation), fieldnote records, and headnotes which "always evolve and change over time" and therefore can never be the archive; Wedgwood left left-hand pages blank and wrote later additions in pencil beside the ink original.
bad: Conflating the layers is how records get misread later; a headnote silently updates itself to match what you now believe. Wedgwood detail filed secondary.
took: Name the layers in AGENTS.md and never let the living layer impersonate the fixed one; later additions belong adjacent to and visibly distinct from the original (dated amendment blocks, callouts, corrections ledger), never overwritten text.
didnt: Adopt/build — name the note layers in our governing rules and never let the living layer (headnotes) impersonate the fixed one: later additions sit adjacent to and visibly distinct from the original as dated amendment blocks and corrections-ledger entries, never overwritten text, following Sanjek's layer vocabulary (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Problem-Oriented Medical Record / SOAP — Lawrence Weed
good: Record organised around a numbered problem list, each note separating Subjective (reported, attributed), Objective (measured/observed), Assessment (clinician's interpretation), and Plan (next, per problem) — so an assessment can be wrong without contaminating the observations it was drawn from.
bad: The old source-oriented chart, filed by author/department, could not answer what is being done about a problem and whether it is working.
took: Label the four voices explicitly on consequential pages (status, decisions, money, health-adjacent) and keep a problem list as the spine pages hang from, rather than mixing reported/measured/assessment/plan in running prose.
didnt: Adopt/build — label the four SOAP voices explicitly on consequential pages (reported/subjective, measured/objective, assessment, plan) and keep a problem list as the spine pages hang from, so an assessment can be wrong without contaminating the observations it was drawn from, following Weed's problem-oriented record (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: EMR audit trails — Frier Levitt (HIPAA audit controls)
good: Audit trail as a legal object: never delete or overwrite, correct only by a properly dated/time-stamped addendum stating the reason, never backdate, and once notice of audit/claim arrives change nothing except by explained addendum; a properly identified late entry is generally acceptable, a disguised one is treated as falsification/spoliation.
bad: The printed chart can look clean while metadata shows every late and altered entry, and courts/boards/payors routinely obtain the trail.
took: State the clinical formulation as a wiki-wide law — correction by dated addendum leaving the original readable, with the litigation-hold rider that a record under dispute/review freezes except for labelled addenda — extending the corrections-ledger expectation to every layer.
didnt: Adopt/build — state the article's formulation as a wiki-wide law: correction only by properly dated/time-stamped addendum stating the reason, the original left readable, never backdated, and a record under audit/dispute frozen except for explained addenda, extending the corrections-ledger rule to every layer (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: A New Method of Making Common-Place-Books — John Locke (1706)
licence: Public domain (original work published 1686; English edition 1706, after the author's death in 1704)
good: Abolished pre-allocation: write each entry on the next blank page under a head chosen at capture ("some important and essential word"), and maintain a front index grid (20 consonants × 5 vowels, filed by first letter + first following vowel) with chained page numbers; choosing the head was the intellectual act and instilled the passage in mind.
bad: Newton's 37-head guess at page counts was "rather unsuccessful"; the index is highly personalised and could not be easily interpreted by others.
took: The head is chosen at capture by the capturer as a claim about what the item is for, and no pre-allocation — structure lives in the index, not reserved folders; heads should be drawn from a shared small vocabulary, not private shorthand, in a multi-agent wiki.
didnt: Adopt/build — the head is chosen at capture by the capturer as a claim about what the item is for, with no pre-allocation of space (structure lives in the index, not reserved folders), and heads drawn from a shared small vocabulary rather than private shorthand in a multi-agent wiki, following Locke's index-grid method (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: De arte excerpendi / note closet — Vincent Placcius (1689); Thomas Harrison scrinium literatum
licence: Public domain (1689 work; author Vincent Placcius, 1642–1699)
good: Movable slips on labelled hooks under over 3,000 heads — excerpts re-sortable without copying — with a cross-referenced index, designed for collaborative use; answers the bound book's rigidity where a wrongly filed excerpt is filed forever.
bad: The same mobility is the hazard: Krapp records that loose sheets could imperil the entire project if their positions varied, and that the ability to sort and shift entries was long perceived not as a feature but as a dangerous weakness of excerpting, copying and note-taking. The closet also hangs slips under a pre-established system of heads, so its order is only as good as the heads fixed in advance.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — movable slips on labelled hooks under thousands of heads with a cross-referenced index confirm our index-first design, in which excerpts can be re-linked and re-sorted without copying and structure lives in the index rather than in a bound order; the historical artefact itself offers nothing buildable for a digital wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Too Much to Know — Ann Blair (2010)
good: Scholars coped with post-print overload by note-taking, and great compilations were manufactured from slips cut and pasted under headings; the finding device is built alongside the notes from the start, because a compilation without one is unusable at the scale that made it worth compiling.
bad: The labour was social and hidden — amanuenses/helpers did much of the excerpting, so the record's authority quietly depends on unnamed hands the title page never credits.
took: Build the finding device with the notes (index-first, same-session index/log updates are the existing obedience); name the compiling hand on the work, because attribution is part of the record's credibility, not bookkeeping.
didnt: Adopt/build — build the finding device alongside the notes from the start (index-first, with same-session index and log updates) and name the compiling hand on the work, because Blair shows a compilation without a finding device is unusable at the scale that made it worth compiling and that its authority quietly depends on the helpers who did the excerpting (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Beethoven's sketchbooks
licence: Public domain (copyright expired, per the Beethoven-Haus Bonn sketchbook artwork record)
good: ~8,000 surviving sketch pages in two tiers (pocket book in pencil for field fragments, desk book in ink for serious work) preserving rejected variants alongside chosen ones — at least fourteen drafts of one retransition — so later scholars can reconstruct why the final version is as it is.
bad: Beethoven's letters claim he composed whole in his head, a claim the sketches flatly contradict — the process record outranks the maker's retrospective account.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Board — preserve rejected variants alongside the chosen version (as the sketchbooks preserve successive drafts, at least fourteen of one passage) so a later reader can reconstruct why the final version is as it is, and treat the process record as outranking the maker's retrospective account, for the ideas board (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci / zibaldone — Codex Trivulzianus
licence: No open licence — the digital asset at the source states 'Rights: Comune di Milano. All rights reserved'
good: Capture virtues: always carried, everything admitted, drawing and text in one medium.
bad: Record properties are the opposite of every other tradition — mirror writing in effect a private cipher, never indexed for another reader, never witnessed or handed over, and after death loose sheets were scattered and rebound by others in an order not his.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Not for us as a record model — a record optimised purely for its maker's present use fails the professions' test of usability by another person (or the same person years later); its capture habits are already catalogued in wave 7.

name: Judicial benchbook — Federal Judicial Center Benchbook for U.S. District Court Judges
good: Pre-compiled procedural manual at arm's reach — chronological checklists, scripted colloquies, evidence summaries, sentencing matrices — built so a ruling can be made correctly in the moment, including rare situations not handled in years, because a missed required step can invalidate a plea on appeal.
bad: It lags (editions years apart) and is advisory, never authority — judges are cautioned to verify current law independently and must not cite it as such.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — its pre-compiled checklists, scripted colloquies and matrices at the moment of use confirm our compiled-page-over-raw-source design, without adopting its judicial content (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition (1804–06)
licence: Public domain in the United States for the original 1804-1806 journals — a reproduction at the source states no entity holds copyright on the body of the work; the modern Moulton edition's new editing, selection and compilation are separately claimed by University of Nebraska Press
good: Jefferson ordered several copies multiplied against loss; the captains improved it to independent journals — seven keepers by Apr 1805 — buying corroboration and recovery: Clark's lost day of 14 Jul 1804 was recovered from the sergeants' journals.
bad: Only four of seven enlisted journals survive in any form — redundancy raised the odds, it did not guarantee them; copies protect against loss, not against error.
took: Independent redundancy beats copied redundancy for the most consequential facts (witness/audit acts provide the second independent record); daily writing is the standing rule, because skipped days leave gaps no later effort can fill.
didnt: Corroboration — the captains' improvement from copied journals to independent journals, buying corroboration and recovery of a lost day, confirms independent redundancy over copied redundancy for consequential facts (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: U.S. public-land survey field notes (1804–56); USGS Field Records Collection
licence: Public Domain — the USGS Field Records Collection page states 'Sources/Usage: Public Domain.'
good: Field notes are the legal original and the plat map is derivative — boundaries are re-established from notes and monuments, not the prettier compiled map — and the books name the whole party (surveyor, chainmen, flagmen) because a measurement must be retraceable by strangers a century later; notes from 1804–56 are still operative for Illinois boundaries.
bad: Filed partly secondary (ArchiveGrid/statute search-rendered; Illinois volumes not examined).
took: State the precedence rule explicitly — where a compiled page and its raw source disagree, the raw source is the record and the page is the plat — and name the whole party/crew on compiled work, not the lead alone.
didnt: Corroboration — field notes as the legal original from which the plat map is compiled confirms stating a raw-source-over-compiled-page precedence rule and naming the whole crew on compiled work (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Glossa Ordinaria
licence: Public domain for the manuscript images and content at OPenn — 'free of known copyright restrictions and in the public domain' under the Creative Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0; OPenn metadata is separately CC-BY-4.0
good: Layout as discipline for five centuries: source text central, larger, continuous and double-spaced; interlinear and marginal glosses smaller, attributed per excerpt to named authorities, all comment on a passage on the same page as the passage — a reader can always tell Scripture from someone on Scripture, and a wrong gloss can be superseded without altering a word of text.
bad: Glossed books were expensive and, given the complex layout, scribes often struggled with writing a central text alongside variable-sized glosses. Later transmission compounds the problem: the printed Rusch edition includes numerous interpolations from later versions for some books, and the Migne Patrologia Latina edition is described at the source as of no scholarly value.
took: For heavily quoting compiled pages, quote in the centre, gloss in the margin as visibly distinct blocks/callouts attached to the passage they gloss, each carrying its source — keeping voices apart structurally, not in one interleaved prose stream.
didnt: Corroboration — five centuries of central source text with attributed marginal and interlinear gloss on the same page confirm keeping quoted source and gloss structurally apart, each gloss carrying its source (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Giving AI Agents a Memory That Outlives the Session — Graham Fischer-Corners, SeraphimGate Systems (2026)
licence: Practitioner blog post; practices unencumbered, text is the firm's, as recorded in the file
good: Independent practice on the same Karpathy pattern arriving at graduated index-first reads, lint/commit gates over prose rules, and claim-kind promotion gates (a document claim requires the document was opened, a non-existence claim names the search run, a number carries its source, assumptions in a dedicated frontmatter field the linter can list).
bad: Their audit found roughly one in seven substantive findings wrong, most corrections from the human, agent self-checks catching almost none; a closed-out diagnostic fix was archived untracked and the identical failure recurred eight days later. Practitioner self-audit, sample of one practice.
took: Three deltas — an assumptions: frontmatter field the lint can enumerate, claim-kind gates at ingest (especially non-existence claims naming the search), and ledger close rules (closed only with evidence, deferred only with operator approval, nothing archived into untracked).
didnt: Adopt/build — the three deltas only: an assumptions: frontmatter field the lint can enumerate, claim-kind promotion gates at ingest (especially non-existence claims naming the search that was run), and ledger close rules (closed only with evidence, deferred only with operator approval, nothing archived into untracked); the firm's own service is not taken, only these practices. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Context Language Models — Shao, Shen, Yin et al. (2026)
licence: Paper CC BY 4.0 per arXiv listing; code licence not checked in this pass, as recorded in the file
good: Model natively manages its own context as a file it rewrites/prunes/restructures; zero-shot it beats SOTA context strategies (11.4% higher accuracy with 21.5% fewer FLOPs on BrowseComp-Plus, 65% greater improvement on a 24-hour swarm task), and evolved natural-language context instructions improved held-out accuracy by up to 35.9 points.
bad: A model that edits its own context can also plant its own instructions in it — governance of the editing is the remaining work.
took: Filed as evidence for two standing choices (lean rewritten-not-appended front page; multi-agent contexts coexisting as files), not as a thing to install; the caution is that editable context sits under human-owned schema, a commit gate, and datamarking.
didnt: Corroboration — the paper confirms two standing choices (a lean front page rewritten rather than appended; multi-agent contexts coexisting as files) and the governing caution in the recorded take: editable context sits under a human-owned schema, a commit gate, and datamarking, because a model that edits its own context can also plant its own instructions in it; unrestricted model self-editing of context is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MemoType / Memory Type Varies — Wen, Xu, Jia et al. (2026)
licence: arXiv paper; dataset/framework as described, code availability not verified, as recorded in the file
good: Classifies memory as episodic, personal-semantic, and general-semantic with a learned router choosing retrieval strategy per type; theoretically proves any single retrieval strategy has a fundamental upper bound on expected precision in multi-class corpora, and empirically improves Recall@1 by up to 16.18%.
bad: Memory scenarios are topic-rich, scenario-complex, and boundary-blurred, so classification itself is the hard part.
took: Ask/search strategy should key to page type asked about (decisions/claims vs sources/raw) as an explicit routing step, rather than letting one ranking function average across types.
didnt: Adopt/build — type-keyed routing as an explicit step in Ask/search: the retrieval strategy keys to the page type asked about (decisions/claims vs sources/raw) rather than letting one ranking function average across types; MemoType's learned router model itself is not installed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MemComposer — Xie, Xu, Fan et al. (2026)
licence: arXiv paper; no code claim verified, as recorded in the file
good: Memory assembly (which items, how many, in what order) is a separate learnable step trained on task success, not retrieval metrics; outperforms the strongest baseline per executor while reducing memory-token usage by 16.9% and 4.9%, and transfers to unseen domains/executors/banks.
bad: Semantic similarity alone does not guarantee memory usefulness, per the paper's opening claim.
took: Filed as confirmation of evidence packing with strongest-first ordering, plus the sharpening that pack size should be a decided quantity, not merely a budget residue; no build proposed from this lane.
didnt: Corroboration — the paper confirms evidence packing with strongest-first ordering and sharpens it: pack size should be a decided quantity, not merely a budget residue; MemComposer's RL-trained composer itself is not adopted and no build is taken from it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: REMORY — Xia, Chen, Ge et al. (2026)
licence: arXiv paper CC BY 4.0 per the listing, as recorded in the file
good: Quantifies what a plain summary loses: on SummHay it improves source attribution at nearly unchanged insight coverage and approaches the full-context joint score using only 5.2% of input positions, with substantially fewer repeated tool outputs/errors on agent benchmarks.
bad: A textual summary alone may not support every subsequent decision — insight coverage survives summarisation, source attribution does not.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — the paper quantifies what our citation-locking design assumes: summarisation preserves insight coverage but loses source attribution, so compiled pages must carry their citations rather than rely on a summary alone; Remory's neural soft-token memory itself is not adopted, as it is model-internal and not inspectable in our local-first stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Hy-Memory-30B-A3B — Fei et al., Tencent HY team (2026)
licence: arXiv paper; model release terms not verified in this pass, as recorded in the file
good: Argues the memory writer is a specialisable job trained across frameworks (Mem0, MemOS, vendor's own) with over-storage controls and per-chunk answerability probes, optimising downstream answerability rather than a general-purpose model behind framework prompts.
bad: Vendor research on fixed 20% benchmark subsamples and the vendor's own harnesses; headline margin is small (55.49% macro average vs 54.62% for Claude Opus 5).
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected — a specialised trained memory-writer model does not fit our stack: the evidence is vendor research on fixed 20% benchmark subsamples and the vendor's own harnesses with a small headline margin (55.49% macro average vs 54.62%), and our write path stays a general model behind approval-gated, inspectable ingest rather than a purpose-trained 30B writer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: When Context Changes: Stale Binding — Guo, Fang, Gu et al. (2026)
licence: arXiv paper CC BY 4.0 per the listing, as recorded in the file
good: Diagnostic separates having the current value from using it: probes can still recover the updated value when the model answers with an old one, and an inference-time attention intervention corrects most old-value errors while preserving nearly all correct answers.
bad: Stale binding — even frontier models answer with an old value when old and new sit in context together (snapshot questions answered correctly, update histories answered stale), via attention drift where several old mentions together outweigh one current value; a correct reasoning trace did not protect the final answer.
took: Answers should be served from the compiled snapshot (current-state page), not by replaying history; a superseded value should be removed from an answer's evidence, not merely out-ranked; answers are judged at final text, never at their trace.
didnt: Adopt/build — serve answers from the compiled snapshot (the current-state page), not by replaying history; remove a superseded value from an answer's evidence rather than merely out-ranking it; and judge answers at final text, never at their trace; the paper's attention intervention itself is not adopted, as it requires model-internal access our stack does not use. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Governing facts / SCR-T — Abeke, Mohammad & Mahmoud (2026)
licence: Journal article, open access per coverage; text not reproduced, as recorded in the file
good: Distinguishes episodic facts (topical) from governing facts (constraints, preferences, identity, commitments, roles) which bind every query; SCR-T, consulting validity intervals and supersession edges to return exactly the currently binding set, is reported as the only strategy holding fidelity, consistency, and minimality at 1.0 across every revision depth.
bad: Impossibility results: any type-blind similarity top-k retriever can be defeated by topically related noise, and no conflict-blind retriever can guarantee governance consistency (error grows linearly in revision depth); naive retrieval returned up to fifteen stale superseded facts per query, and even pinned rule blocks and metadata-filtered retrieval accumulated eight stale facts per query. Filed secondary — journal primary text not opened.
took: Superseded claims are excluded from Ask evidence packs by register lookup, never merely out-ranked; any standing-instruction surface that is appended to rather than recompiled will silently carry superseded rules, so the pinned layer must itself be rewritten on correction (stated as a refinement of practice).
didnt: Adopt/build — superseded claims are excluded from Ask evidence packs by register lookup, never merely out-ranked, and any standing-instruction surface is itself recompiled on correction rather than appended to, so the pinned layer cannot silently carry superseded rules; built 2026-10-20, Phase 2. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Fresh at Decision, Stale at Action — Merimi, Bakkali & Sakat (2026)
licence: arXiv paper; no code claim verified, as recorded in the file
good: Decision ledger storing each decision with its times, evidence, and background knowledge, indexed by watch conditions written at decision time so post-decision information is routed back to open decisions — "a ledger retrieves what yesterday's decisions still need."
bad: Freshness ceiling theorem: under a constant rate of change, the probability evidence still holds at action time is bounded by the execution gap whatever the freshness at decision time; accuracy depends on routing and temporal judgment, not decision-time diligence alone.
took: At decision/staging time, items carry watch conditions (entities/sources/events whose change would reopen them), and the nightly sweep/filings pickup routes matches to the open item instead of merely logging them.
didnt: Adopt/build — watch conditions written at decision/staging time on open items (entities, sources, and events whose change would reopen them), with the nightly sweep and filings pickup routing matches back to the open item instead of merely logging them; built 2026-10-20, Phase 4. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Accurate but Not Humble — Sun et al. (2026)
licence: arXiv paper; benchmark as described, as recorded in the file
good: Operationalises epistemic humility as three trajectory behaviours — Identify the conflict, Solve it through bounded tool use, Escalate residual uncertainty — each scoreable separately.
bad: Higher task accuracy does not correspond to greater humility: agents frequently detect conflicts early but fail to maintain/resolve them in later steps, and do not communicate unresolved uncertainty in incorrect final answers; interventions improving humility often cost task accuracy, and humility emerges from model + harness + environment, not the model alone.
took: Score the eval conflict slice as ISE separately (Identify/Solve/Escalate), and treat a detected-but-unresolved conflict undisclosed in the final answer as a contract failure; escalation must live in the harness (trust verdict hold/review), not the model.
didnt: Adopt/build — score the eval conflict slice as ISE separately (Identify/Solve/Escalate), treat a detected-but-unresolved conflict undisclosed in the final answer as a contract failure, and keep escalation in the harness (trust verdict hold/review), not the model; built 2026-10-20, Phase 4. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ArcticQA / ArcticAbstain — Wilcox et al. (2026)
licence: arXiv paper; dataset/benchmark released via GitHub per the abstract, as recorded in the file
good: Paired design separating abstention frequency from sensitivity: every question exists in answer-present and answer-absent conditions (correct answer replaced by a verified contradicted distractor), with support/contradiction automatically checked against source evidence across 9,312 responses.
bad: Answer-present abstention rates ranged 0.0% to 63.0% across models while removing the answer increased abstention by only 5.05 percentage points on average — a single abstention rate is uninterpretable.
took: Abstention regression should be paired — each no-answer item generated from an answerable item by removing/replacing its supporting evidence with a verified contradicted distractor — and reported as baseline rate plus the answer-absent delta together.
didnt: Adopt/build — paired abstention regression: each no-answer item is generated from an answerable item by removing or replacing its supporting evidence with a verified contradicted distractor, and results are reported as the baseline rate plus the answer-absent delta together; the Arctic dataset itself is not adopted, only the paired design. name: AI Hallucination Statistics: October 2026 — First Page Sage (2026)

name: LLM Wiki (nashsu/llm_wiki)
licence: GPL-3.0 (LICENSE file; GitHub metadata NOASSERTION is a detector miss)
good: A Claude Code plugin maintaining an interlinked wiki with TF-IDF full-text search with snippet extraction, block references and transclusion (`[[page#heading]]`, `![[page#section]]`), a backlink panel with unlinked-mention detection, and a Dataview-like frontmatter query language. Its distinctive mechanism is a 9-tier freshness system running from `live` (15 minutes) to `permanent` (never expires), coupled to maintenance that flags pages past their tier TTL, merges near-duplicates, upgrades confidence by source count and regenerates the index, plus an FSRS-based spaced-repetition review interface and self-contained HTML/Markdown/JSON exports.

Maturity evidence on the page is thin: 50 stars but only 1 commit recorded, despite an extensive feature list. Additionally: GPL-3.0 copyleft — idea-only, re-implement, do not copy code.

name: Alibaba-NLP/DeepResearch (Tongyi DeepResearch)

didnt: Board — Tongyi DeepResearch's IterResearch loop as the reference pattern for long-horizon research runs: model-scale adoption is a board decision, and the hosted/API route sits uneasily with local-first custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

didnt: Board — RAG-Anything's multimodal indexing (specialised processors for images, tables and equations feeding a multimodal knowledge graph with modality-aware retrieval): a pipeline adoption decision, not a small build. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zjunlp/DeepKE

The original virtual-software-company system is now legacy — ChatDev 1.0 was moved to the chatdev1.0 branch for maintenance when 2.0 (DevAll) was released in January 2026.

name: THUDM/AgentBench

The KnowledgeGraph task depends on an online Freebase/SPARQL service the README says 'now is not stable', requiring a local deployment and data download, and the original setup pins older dependencies (Python 3.9, numpy~=1.23.x) and multiple Docker images.
took: Boarded Tier B, per the find disposition and compiled page: "AgentBench" — adopting a standard agent-eval harness is a tooling decision for the board.
didnt: Board — a standard agent-eval harness, in particular its containerised Knowledge Graph, Database and OS tasks, as evaluation tooling for our own agents; the heavy Docker, RAM and local-Freebase setup keeps it a board-level tooling decision rather than a wiki build. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GROBID — France (Inria)
good: Machine-learning library extracting and parsing scholarly PDFs into structured XML/TEI (header metadata, reference/citation extraction and resolution at ~0.87 F1 on its PubMed Central set, full-text structuring with PDF coordinates), in production at ResearchGate, Semantic Scholar and CERN; technique: segment a PDF into typed structures as a compilation step, not chunking.
