The opened repo page shows 0 releases/tags and 43 commits, and its design deliberately defers retrieval infrastructure ('No vector database until you need one').
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and scope: it is another guide, starter vault and skill set for the same Claude Code + Obsidian pattern our wiki already implements, not a component to adopt; its contradiction-recording and no-vector-database-until-needed rules corroborate choices already in our design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: domleca/llm-wiki — "LM Wiki"
good: Obsidian community plugin, local-first (Ollama by default); extracts entities/concepts/9 connection types, hybrid search with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, "knows when it doesn't know — says so instead of making things up"; "the cleanest in-editor, no-second-app UX in the set".
bad: "Honest onboarding cost: first extraction of a 600-note vault ≈4 hrs on an M2 Air." Small scale: 177★.
took: Cited for gap 6 (living editor surface inside Obsidian) and gap 4 hybrid search.
didnt: Board — LM Wiki's in-editor Obsidian surface (cited for gap 6) and its hybrid-search-with-stated-abstention behaviour (cited for gap 4) for the ideas board as reference designs; the plugin itself is not adopted, since our wiki is canonical on Azure and edited through our own Lens and doors. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: tobi/qmd — Query Markup Documents
good: The search engine Karpathy's gist itself recommends; on-device BM25 + vector + LLM reranking (GGUF, query expansion/HyDE, RRF fusion), CLI + MCP + SDK; qmd-style parameters in the 2026-10-13 report: ~900-token chunks at markdown boundaries, 15% overlap.
bad: In the 2026-10-13 report pitfalls: "`embed` is a separate step in qmd-like tools — an un-embedded page is invisible to vector search"; whether qmd's current release matches the summarised parameters "was not verified against the qmd repository itself".
took: 2026-10-13 concrete upgrade is "qmd-style, all local: SQLite FTS5 (BM25) + sqlite-vec embeddings → RRF fusion → local cross-encoder/LLM rerank"; landscape recommendation 5: "Add a hybrid-search scale path (integrate or bundle qmd, or BM25+vector+rerank)".
didnt: Adopt/build — the qmd-style all-local hybrid-search scale path recorded in the took field (SQLite FTS5 BM25 plus sqlite-vec embeddings, RRF fusion, local reranking) for when index-only navigation passes the gist's ~100-source ceiling, with qmd itself (MIT) as the reference implementation the gist names. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HKUDS/LightRAG
good: "Simpler/faster GraphRAG (EMNLP 2025): dual-level graph+vector retrieval, incremental updates, multimodal parsing, built-in WebUI with graph visualisation, Docker/K8s deploys" — "The maintained, productised GraphRAG alternative."
bad: Heavy operational surface for a personal wiki: the README says all four default in-memory storages are intended 'only for small-scale testing, evaluation, and debugging, and are not suitable for production,' with PostgreSQL (or MongoDB/OpenSearch, Milvus/Qdrant, Neo4j/Memgraph) recommended instead. It also documents LLM timeouts during entity-relation extraction on models running below ~50 tokens/second, endless-output loops in some locally deployed models, and that switching embedding models requires rebuilding vectors or, if the working directory is deleted, full re-ingestion.
took: Survey wave-2 notes: "LightRAG's dual-level retrieval (split the query into entity keywords + theme keywords, fuse) is a recipe our BM25+PPR hybrid could adopt inside the already-approved search line."
didnt: Board — LightRAG's dual-level retrieval recipe (split the query into entity keywords plus theme keywords and fuse), as noted for our BM25+PPR hybrid inside the already-approved search line; the LightRAG server/storage stack itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mem0
good: "Memory layer for AI agents": multi-level memory, single-pass ADD-only extraction in the 2026 rewrite, entity linking, multi-signal (semantic+BM25+entity) retrieval, temporal reasoning; ships as library, Docker server, cloud, CLI, skills, browser extension; benchmarks above the fold (LoCoMo 92.5, LongMemEval 94.4, BEAM, with caveat that managed numbers include proprietary optimisations). 2026-10-13 report credits its cost/latency trade-off (2025: ~1,764 vs ~26,031 tokens/query vs full context).
bad: 2026-10-13 report: graph variant added only ~2 points (66.9% → 68.4%); selective memory "lost on accuracy and won on cost" vs full context in 2025; "contradictory facts embed to nearly identical vectors, so without an explicit update/invalidation step both the stale fact and its correction surface together; extraction errors compound silently"; 2026 headline scores are vendor self-report, Weak evidence. Delta correction withdraws the claimed 2026-10-20 "State of AI Agent Memory 2026" delta — "Mem0's latest releases are v2.2.1 / ts-v3.3.1 (2026-09-25), no change since 2026-10-19".
took: "Make the ingest schema operation explicit and auditable: every ingest commit must classify each touched claim as ADD / SUPERSEDE / CONTRADICT / NOOP"; "Retrieval should apply recency/access decay at ranking time only — never decay-delete canonical pages.". Additionally: Built (marathon records): Claim-level append-only index with temporal multi-signal fusion
didnt: "Avoid: Mem0's 2025-style LLM-decided DELETE of facts (irreversible, unauditable)"; explicitly not recommended: "adopting … a hosted memory service (Mem0/Zep/Cognee platforms) as the wiki's substrate" (report.md, llm-wiki-world-class-rd-20261013-0836).

name: Cognee
good: Four-verb API "remember / recall / forget / improve"; ECL pipeline to knowledge graph + vectors; runs with no LLM key (local GLiNER + local embeddings); many graph/vector backends; SDKs, HTTP API, MCP, plugins, bundled `cognee-cli demo`, importers from Mem0/Letta/Zep/Graphiti. Its candid BEAM reporting is "more trustworthy as process than as score" (2026-10-13 report).
bad: 2026-10-13 report: "cognify is not incremental (re-runs everything; cost scales as chunks × LLM calls), graph-completion latency self-reported at 25–30s p50 on a small corpus, and disk-growth/log issues"; "a three-database stack for a single-user wiki" is to be avoided.
took: "Borrow the separation of stores as derived artifacts: relational/SQLite index = provenance + hashes; vector index = retrieval; markdown = truth" and "compilation must be incremental and content-hash-gated".
didnt: "Avoid: Full re-cognify/re-compile on every ingest; a three-database stack"; not recommended as substrate (see Mem0 DIDNT).

name: Graphiti (Zep)
good: "Temporal context graphs — the closest analogue to 'severance'." Bi-temporal facts (validity window + transaction time); "old facts are invalidated — not deleted"; episodes as provenance ground truth; hybrid semantic+BM25+graph retrieval, sub-second; paper results DMR 94.8% vs MemGPT 93.4%, LongMemEval 71.2% vs 60.2% full-context with latency and token reductions (2026-10-13 report). Correction: v0.31.2 published 2026-10-20, a security-driven release.
bad: "requires a graph DB (Neo4j/FalkorDB/Neptune); Zep Community Edition was deprecated (Apr 2025)"; "it regressed on single-session-assistant recall (94.6% → 80.4%) — extraction into a graph loses detail"; full Zep product is commercial, OSS is the engine only. Survey Not-for-us: "Zep's hosted direction (its open repo is now examples-only; the self-hosted edition is deprecated)".
took: "Add bi-temporal fields to wiki frontmatter and claim blocks: valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at, superseded_by, status: current|superseded|contested. Schema rule: agents never delete a superseded claim; they close its validity interval and link forward."
didnt: "Avoid: Adopting Neo4j + Graphiti for a personal wiki to chase the DMR number; the transferable asset is the temporal data model, not the stack."

name: Letta (ex-MemGPT) / MemGPT
good: Stateful-agent platform: tiered self-edited memory (core blocks + recall/archival), sleep-time compute, MemFS git-tracked memory filesystem; Letta Filesystem scored 74.0% on LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini using only grep, semantic file search and open/close tools — above Mem0's reported graph variant.
bad: "recursive summarization is lossy; self-edited core blocks can be silently corrupted by the agent itself (last-write-wins conflicts in multi-agent use); the agent runtime owns your loop — adopting Letta wholesale replaces, rather than upgrades, a markdown wiki"; human-readability is "not its model — a deliberate contrast with a markdown wiki"; evidence for LLM-rewriting-memory "dreaming" on shared benchmarks is weak-to-absent.
took: "Steal two things, not the platform: (1) a tiny always-loaded core tier … always injected, with everything else retrieved on demand; (2) run consolidation as a separate, reviewable offline pass producing git commits / PRs, never as silent in-place rewrites." Survey: Letta Context Repositories (memory as a git repo, subagents merging via worktrees) recorded as field convergence on Usman's shape.
didnt: "Avoid: Letting a sleep-time agent edit canonical pages unreviewed"; not adopted wholesale for the reason in BAD.

name: Khoj
good: Self-hostable "AI second brain": chat with web + docs, custom agents, scheduled automations / newsletters / smart notifications, semantic search, access from browser, Obsidian, Emacs, desktop, phone, WhatsApp; any local/online LLM; live cloud app at app.khoj.dev; Docker self-host.
bad: The hosted Khoj Cloud service was shut down on April 15, 2026 (deprecation notice at app.khoj.dev); the notice itself says hand-building data integrations was a long tail of effort and that the cloud-first subscription bets — complex document syncs, custom integrations, six clients — made it very difficult to scale in utility, leaving self-hosting as the remaining route.
took: Cited as evidence for gaps 7 (provider breadth), 9 (scheduled automations) and 11 (phone/WhatsApp access).
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only under our licence discipline, the hosted cloud it was cited for no longer exists, and its self-hosted second-brain/agent features duplicate our existing wiki stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tolaria (refactoringhq)
good: Desktop markdown-KB app (Tauri): files-first, git-first, offline-first; built-in MCP server; block editing, types-as-lenses, keyboard-first; Homebrew install; getting-started vault on first launch; author dogfoods it on 10,000+ notes.
bad: "Known hole, called out by reviewers: no mobile app."
took: Cited for gaps 2 (Homebrew + signed installers), 3 (starter vault), 6 (keyboard-first editing with git built in) and the "Your files, forever" README principle.
didnt: Board — Tolaria's product ideas for the ideas board, as cited in the took field (Homebrew and signed installers, gap 2; starter vault, gap 3; keyboard-first editing with git built in, gap 6; and the files-first, your-files-forever principle); its AGPL-3.0-or-later code is ideas-only under licence discipline and none is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Basic Memory
good: "The closest shipped analogue to the target system": markdown files are the source of truth, SQLite index (FTS + sqlite-vec + local embeddings) is a derived, rebuildable cache; observations/relations parsed by syntax rules with no LLM in the parse path; MCP CRUD, hybrid search and build_context graph traversal via memory:// URLs; Cloud adds sync, mobile/web, Teams co-editing, snapshots.
bad: "capture is manual/explicit only — nothing is saved unless someone asks (a feature for trust, a gap for coverage); single-user/single-machine in spirit; AGPL-3.0 license matters if embedding commercially; one review noted a reported SQL-injection issue".
took: "Adopt its two invariants verbatim: (1) files are truth, every index is disposable and rebuildable from files + hashes; (2) deterministic syntax-level structure … so graph extraction doesn't need an LLM call".
didnt: Board — Basic Memory's two invariants for the ideas board as design principles, as recorded in the took field (files are truth and every index is disposable and rebuildable from files; deterministic syntax-level structure so graph extraction needs no LLM call); its AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only under licence discipline and none is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gknowledge
good: "Newer native alternative gknowledge (MIT, GTK4, MCP, ships a demo project with six classic AI papers pre-ingested) explicitly tables itself against nashsu/Tolaria/Khoj/Reor".
bad: Very early and small: the repo shows 72 commits and 24 stars and the launch post calls it v0.2. Its own README workflow table marks Lint, the knowledge graph, web clipper, folder watch and deep research as 'Planned' (Git-diff review also planned), and it is a native GTK4/GNOME app installed primarily for Ubuntu 24.04+/Debian 13+, so it is Linux-desktop bound.
took: Cited for gap 3 (demo project with pre-ingested papers) and §3 comparison-table pattern.
didnt: Board — the review-queue pattern and its planned lint (orphans, contradictions, stale pages) for the ideas board; the native GNOME client itself duplicates our Lens/web stack rather than replacing it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LoCoMo / LongMemEval / BEAM (benchmark trio)
licence: LongMemEval: MIT; BEAM: MIT; LoCoMo: CC BY-NC 4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International, per LICENSE.txt in snap-research/locomo)
good: "LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and BEAM are the standard trio" for agent memory. Survey: LongMemEval gives "the five-ability taxonomy"; BEAM is the "first benchmark with contradiction resolution and event ordering as first-class categories".
bad: Published scores for the same system "diverge wildly by harness"; Mem0's 2026 report lists judge model, answer model, top-k, prompt format, dataset revision and grading as confounds; "Independent summaries also allege LoCoMo ground-truth defects (~99 bad answers in one audit claim)"; survey Mnemoverse note: "an independent audit found ~6.4% of LoCoMo's keys wrong".
took: Survey For-us: LongMemEval's knowledge-updates and abstention categories and BEAM's contradiction-resolution and event-ordering categories for "a bigger, sharper eval set" (shortlist item 4).
didnt: "Do not import any vendor's architecture on the strength of its score" and do not quote LoCoMo/LongMemEval numbers across papers as commensurable (report.md, llm-wiki-world-class-rd-20261013-0836).

name: GraphRAG-Bench
good: arXiv:2506.05690, ICLR 2026; controlled comparison: complex reasoning graph win (53.4 vs 42.9), contextual summarization graph win (64.4 vs 51.3).
bad: "simple fact retrieval is a tie (text 60.9 vs graph 60.1)" — graph does not help the majority fact-lookup class.
took: Used to justify routing to the graph only for complex/synthesis questions, and 1-hop wikilink expansion instead of a built KG.
didnt: Corroboration — its controlled fact-retrieval tie versus graph wins on complex reasoning and contextual summarization confirm our existing routing stance (graph only for complex/synthesis questions, 1-hop wikilink expansion instead of a built KG); no benchmark code adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HippoRAG / HippoRAG 2
good: "Personalized PageRank over a lightweight entity graph reports up to +20% on multi-hop QA at 10–30× lower cost than iterative retrieval"; indexing ~9M tokens vs ~115M for full GraphRAG in one comparison.
bad: Index portability is brittle: the README says persisted indexes without an index_manifest.json, or whose endpoint/model/identity no longer matches the active configuration, are rejected rather than mixed, so users must re-index into a fresh save_dir. Setup also assumes a Python 3.10 environment plus an external LLM/embedding provider (OpenAI, Bedrock, or a GPU-served vLLM model), and the README TODO still lists more embedding models, embedding endpoints and vector-database integration as outstanding.
took: Cited as the cheap-graph alternative in the graph-question section; no adoption recorded beyond that comparison.
didnt: Corroboration — Personalized PageRank over a lightweight entity graph confirms the cheap-graph alternative already weighed in our graph-question section; we kept 1-hop wikilink expansion instead of building a KG, so no HippoRAG code was adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sleep-time compute paper (Berkeley/Letta, arXiv:2504.13171)
good: Survey wave 3: "precompute standing-question answers while idle, ~5× test-time saving on predictable queries — the research basis for an anticipatory nightly sweep".
bad: 2026-10-13 report naming trap: the paper "is about pre-computing answers to predictable future queries, not about memory consolidation, and one careful research note found the evidence for LLM-rewriting-memory 'dreaming' on shared benchmarks weak-to-absent".
took: Survey wave-3 shortlist: "anticipatory sweep" item joined Ideas as Waiting.
didnt: "Avoid: conflating speculative pre-computation with consolidation" and letting a sleep-time agent edit canonical pages unreviewed.

name: Tracelane audit format / Attestor
licence: Tracelane: Apache-2.0 (per docs.tracelane.dev); Attestor: no licence stated at source
good: Production pattern examples (index-only): "per-entry SHA-256 chain + Ed25519 signature per entry or per Merkle batch + RFC 6962-style Merkle checkpoints anchored to Sigstore Rekor (e.g. Tracelane audit format, Attestor flight recorder)".
bad: Tracelane's own docs state limits: A2A/A2UI drift, browser stuck-loops and argument drift are roadmap detectors that do not fire on LLM traffic today, gateway-level enforcement is opt-in (observe-first by default), and an ML ensemble is still on the roadmap.
took: The right-sized upgrade modelled on them: nightly signed Merkle/HEAD checkpoint committed to a separate repo/remote, with CI verification.
didnt: "Avoid: 'Blockchain the wiki,' per-entry public anchoring of private content, hash chains marketed as proof of truth, and letting the same agent that writes entries also hold the signing key".

name: Sigstore / Rekor / gitsign
good: "Sigstore's model — sign, then record in an append-only public transparency log — is the established production analogue from software supply-chain security"; git-native signed commits plus gitsign for keyless signing.
bad: Survey wave 6: public transparency logs and keyless signing are recorded NOT FOR US because "the signer's identity becomes permanently public, and gitsign's verify path never checks identity at all".
took: Signed commits with per-agent SSH keys registered in an allowed_signers file, with Agent/Session/Sources/Operation trailers.
didnt: Public transparency logs (Rekor) and gitsign — see BAD (wave-6 shortlist reasoning in wiki-feature-survey-2026-10-19.md).

name: Obsidian (graph view / Web Clipper / Smart Connections / Copilot)
licence: Proprietary (Dynalist Inc. Terms of Service: Obsidian is licensed, not sold, under a non-transferable, non-exclusive per-user licence with all rights retained by the company; not open source)
good: Karpathy's gist tips: Obsidian Web Clipper, graph view ("the best quick way to see the wiki's shape — hubs, clusters, orphans"), Marp, Dataview, git-as-history; "Obsidian is the IDE; the LLM is the programmer".
bad: "there is no strong HCI evidence found that free-form graph exploration improves comprehension or recall"; graph views "degrade into hairballs at thousands of nodes". Survey Not-for-us: Dataview/Datacore as mechanisms because "query results never land in the markdown, so they are invisible to git, the Lens and any AI reader"; Copilot for Obsidian V4 is AGPL + hosted backend and "replaces the agent workflow".
took: Landscape recommendation 7: "Declare Obsidian compatibility (wikilinks + YAML frontmatter + vault mode)"; graph used only in local / lint / filtered modes. Survey harvests Smart Connections' per-page related-pages rail and Obsidian Web Clipper templates as ideas/patterns.
didnt: "Avoid: Global-graph-as-homepage"; Dataview/Datacore as mechanisms and Copilot for Obsidian V4 as a product (wiki-feature-survey-2026-10-19.md, Not for us).

name: Tencent Hy Memory 2.0 (Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-Memory)
licence: "repo licence field reads NOASSERTION despite an Apache-2.0 badge — ideas only until that is resolved, per licence discipline"
good: New entrant, repo created 2026-10-15: "dual-system cognitive memory (Chat / Working / Coding scenes), the MemHub local app, and the Hy-Memory-30B-A3B memory-writer model".
bad: Licence caution above.
took: Source/inspiration for two Round 3 builds, as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md: Expiring intentions (`scripts/wiki_expiring_intentions.py`) — built in Round 3, lane TB1 — source/inspiration: Hy Memory 2.0 (Apache-2.0); and Per-claim version-evolution diff-chains — built in Round 3, lane TB2 — source/inspiration: Hy Memory.
didnt: Ideas only until the licence is resolved (correction).

name: Hy-Memory-30B-A3B (paper)
good: arXiv 2610.22196, submitted 2026-10-15: "attributed reinforcement learning for long-term memory WRITING — admission/attribution for what enters persistent memory; the write-path-governance angle is directly relevant to our gateway staging discipline".
bad: Headline evidence is narrow by the paper's own framing: all four-harness results are on fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, and the claimed lead is 55.49% macro average versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5 — vendor-run, subsampled figures, with the model card likewise stating every main-matrix benchmark was evaluated on a fixed 20% subsample.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: "Recorded; no build taken this run" (2026-10-20-landscape-delta-correction.md).

name: OpenMyMemo (MyMemoAI)
good: Launched 2026-10-14: "AI memory as a local folder of plain Markdown shared across MCP apps; changes to the user's own writing and private topics wait for approval, one-click undo — a direct-pattern entrant with an approval gate shaped like ours".
bad: Very young and small: repo created 2026-10-11, at v0.2, with 10 stars and 0 forks when opened. The desktop app is Mac-only (macOS 12 or later); the README's Works-with table marks ChatGPT/Claude mobile apps 'Not tested', web apps reach it only through the optional paid MyMemo Cloud relay, and the Assistant / search-by-meaning features need an optional model download, a paid MyMemo plan, or the user's own API key.
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: Corroboration — a local plain-Markdown memory folder shared across MCP apps, with changes to the user's own writing and private topics waiting for approval and one-click undo, confirms our local-first, approval-gated design; it is a personal-memory folder, not a citation-locked wiki, so there is no missing mechanism to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: R2R / Onyx
licence: MIT patterns (R2R line as written in the survey)
good: "three distinct Ask modes exposed as separate operations: Search (passages only) / Answer (one-shot, cited) / Deep Research (multi-step, decomposed)".
bad: Survey Not-for-us note for Onyx as a product: "Onyx (enterprise connectors; borders on auto-discovery)".
took: Ask-door three modes in shortlist item 3.
didnt: Onyx as a product — enterprise connectors bordering on auto-discovery.

name: gbrain (garrytan/gbrain)
good: "answers that state their own coverage gaps: what the brain does not know yet and how stale the newest evidence is" — survey marks "(system not for us)".
bad: Not-for-us grouping: "garrytan/gbrain as a system (24/7 daemon ingesting meetings, mail, calls; DB-backed, 155k pages at his scale)".
took: Coverage-gap answers harvested.
didnt: The system — automatic ingest of life activity, the rejected pattern, and DB-backed.

name: ai-vault-wiki
good: "`/eval` golden questions scored per-question by a fresh agent, with trend tracking plotted against wiki size"; layered leak guards and a quantified automation-readiness gate (≥5 runs in 14 days, ≤1 corrected judgment error).
bad: Days-old personal vault, not a reusable package: created 2026-10-18, 22 commits, 0 stars and 0 forks when opened, README in Korean only, and no LICENSE file in the repo root. Its private layer lives in a separate private repo that is not part of this repo, and its workflows are personal (Velog and Notion flows for its owner).
took: Ideas only, both mechanisms in the harvest.
didnt: Board — the /eval golden-question scoring with trend tracking against wiki size, the layered leak guards, and the quantified automation-readiness gate (≥5 runs in 14 days, ≤1 corrected judgment error) as ideas; no licence at source, so ideas only and no code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DeepRefine-Skill
good: "refines the wiki from its own query log: dry-run first; every proposed edit evidence-labelled HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW; apply refuses LOW by default; staged validated swap of graph + wiki together". Re-verified firsthand.
bad: Tied to one host system: it refines a Graphify (graphifyy) knowledge graph, so setup requires graphify plus deeprefine-cli and its terminal mode additionally needs FAISS and an API/vLLM inference setup, with separate install steps per agent CLI. It is also young — created 2026-06-01, at v0.2.0, 93 stars when opened.
took: Shortlist item 5: "Query-log refinement loop … (DeepRefine-Skill, MIT)".
didnt: Adopt/build — the query-log refinement loop pattern (dry-run first, every proposed edit evidence-labelled HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW, apply refuses LOW by default, staged validated swap of graph and wiki together), as shortlisted; the Graphify-specific implementation does not transfer to our non-Graphify wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Gnosis / gnosis-markdown
good: "WARC-archived web ingests with a byte-level SHA-256 provenance block, Ed25519-signed ingest records, and ai.txt consent recording".
bad: It is a web scraper/converter, not a wiki system: the provenance, WARC and signing mechanics sit around page conversion, WARC replay depends on pywb, and the optional QMD integration pulls in torch and transformers. Anything beyond the ingest-evidence mechanics (crawling, conversion) is outside what our wiki needs.
took: Shortlist item 9: "signed, WARC-archived records for web ingests (CiteIndex, Gnosis — both MIT)".
didnt: Adopt/build — signed, WARC-archived web-ingest records with a byte-level SHA-256 provenance block, Ed25519-signed ingest records and ai.txt consent recording (MIT), as shortlisted in item 9; the crawler/converter itself as a system is not taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: verified-memory-vault
good: "`memory_guard.py`: a pre-commit guard that refuses mass deletion (file-count and removed-lines caps) and history rewrites of the memory file; `memory_check.py` grades exit codes by risk class, with 2 = provenance breach".
bad: Deliberately minimal and manual: the author's own description says it is not an autonomous system and not a plugin collection — a structure with two small scripts, aimed at dozens of durable facts in a single memory file, run as a habit (fill the daily note, promote facts, run the check) at v0.9. That scale and manual loop do not cover a large multi-thousand-page wiki on their own.
took: Shortlist item 8: "Memory guard — a pre-commit guard that refuses mass deletion or history rewrite … plus a provenance-breach check with its own exit code (verified-memory-vault)".
didnt: Adopt/build — the memory guard pattern: a pre-commit guard refusing mass deletion (file-count and removed-lines caps) and history rewrites, plus a provenance-breach check with its own graded exit code, as shortlisted in item 8. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cmds-llm-wiki
good: "a PostToolUse hook that verifies raw sources are verbatim after write; a single canonical settings source symlinked across agent harnesses".
bad: No formal licence at source (no LICENSE file in the root; the README only invites forking the template). The template is also fragile to move: agent settings are symlinks from a single canonical source, and the README warns ZIP/Windows delivery breaks the links — restoring them needs its setup script, Windows Developer Mode or admin rights for symlinks, and Git Bash/WSL for the bash hooks.
took: Ideas only; survey note: "(Its purpose gate overlaps the owner's pending Mark Chen decision — recorded as an external implementation, not a recommendation.)"
didnt: Rejected — code: no formal licence at source, so ideas only; and its purpose gate overlaps the owner's pending Mark Chen decision, recorded as an external implementation, not a recommendation. The verbatim-after-write PostToolUse hook idea stays in the harvest. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: scholar-llm-wiki
good: "pre-commit leak scan treating absolute paths and usernames as leaks; audits that speak exit codes, wired into CI"; with nkt, "the tag vocabulary as data: a closed, registered vocabulary with an audit that fails on unregistered tags".
bad: Narrowly scoped and harness-dependent: the README states it is not a general notes app (no todos, diary or boards) but a research-literature compiler, its docs are in Chinese, and the full experience requires the DSH (DeepSeek Harness) host plus Obsidian — without DSH the three skills do not auto-trigger. The tag and team vocabularies ship empty, and the repo is very young (created 2026-10-06, 15 commits, 6 stars, no releases when opened).
took: Listed in Verification and in Schema/governance harvests.
didnt: Board — audits that speak exit codes wired into CI, and the tag vocabulary as data (a closed, registered vocabulary whose audit fails on unregistered tags), as harvested under Verification and Schema/governance. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

took: MIT ideas in the harvest.

name: wikiskill / AsDecided / ex-rac-core / Agent-Memory-Hub / world-model-mcp
licence: wikiskill (ashutoshsinghpr7/wikiskill): MIT; AsDecided / ex-rac-core (asdecided/core, formerly itsthelore/rac-core): Apache-2.0; Agent-Memory-Hub (liuyang0508/Agent-Memory-Hub): Apache-2.0; world-model-mcp (SaravananJaichandar/world-model-mcp): MIT.
good: wikiskill: "a proposed change lands only if it strictly beats the best held-out benchmark score, else it rolls back — and rejected proposals stay on record"; AsDecided/ex-rac-core: "a CI gate that rejects references to superseded decisions"; Agent-Memory-Hub: "contradictions as Cases closed only by digest-bound owner resolutions — any later edit reopens the case"; world-model-mcp: "Ed25519-signed Merkle-chained ledger epochs with an offline verifier".
bad: wikiskill: its own README's live-results table records proposals that hurt and were rejected, an invalid run thrown out after dead sessions were phantom-graded, and an honest negative that accumulation needs a stronger model on the weak model tried; its bundled bench is a small 22-task auto-graded set. AsDecided / ex-rac-core: its README's governance section states the core is solo-maintained and supported on a best-effort basis, and its scope is a deterministic typed-Markdown decisions corpus with no embeddings or hosted index. Agent-Memory-Hub: its README shows the installer installs hooks and that a prompt hook injects memory into agents — automatic injection at odds with owner-directed ingest — and the repo is small (23 stars at opening). world-model-mcp: its README states the memory half ships as a local SQLite knowledge graph and promotes a managed hosted companion (etch.systems) for the same signed audit chain, and its hybrid post-quantum signing is heavier than a private personal wiki needs.
took: Wave-2 shortlist includes "superseded-decision gate; eval-gated promotion; contradiction Cases" (Waiting).
didnt: Board — the four governance patterns, not the systems themselves, for the ideas board / Wave-2 shortlist: wikiskill's eval-gated promotion (a change lands only if it strictly beats the best held-out score, with rejected proposals kept on record), AsDecided/ex-rac-core's CI gate rejecting references to superseded decisions, Agent-Memory-Hub's contradiction Cases closed only by digest-bound owner resolutions, and world-model-mcp's Ed25519-signed Merkle-chained ledger epochs with an offline verifier. The systems themselves do not fit as adopted products — wikiskill is Hermes-bound skill evolution, AsDecided is an engineering-decisions corpus engine, Agent-Memory-Hub's hook-based auto-injection conflicts with owner-directed ingest, and world-model-mcp's memory half is another SQLite graph; all four are MIT or Apache-2.0, so the patterns are licence-clean to re-implement. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

good: CaMeLS: "capability/provenance-tagged data flow plus a quarantined extractor LLM that can never call tools — the only injection defence found with a design-level guarantee"; Biscuit: "offline attenuation plus discharge caveats — owner approval expressed cryptographically, the closest published match to our gateway scopes"; in-toto: "an owner-signed pipeline definition with a signed receipt per step"; pass^k: "a task counts only if all k trials pass".
bad: CaMeLS's released code is explicitly a research artifact: its README warns the interpreter implementation likely contains bugs, might not be fully secure, is not a Google product, and is not planned to be supported or maintained; the defence also adds token overhead over undefended runs. Biscuit and in-toto solve capability-token and software-supply-chain attestation problems respectively, so neither drops into a personal wiki without substantial adaptation, and τ-bench's pass^k multiplies evaluation cost by requiring every one of k trials to pass.
took: Wave-3 shortlist: "Ask-door injection defence by design; judge calibration + pass^k" joined Ideas as Waiting.
didnt: Corroboration — capability/provenance-tagged data flow with a quarantined extractor that can never call tools confirms the Ask-door injection-defence design, and pass^k confirms counting a task only when all k trials pass; the CaMeLS extractor itself stays quarantined and is not adopted as running code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Shepard's / KeyCite (citators); GRADE; PharmGKB
licence: Proprietary for the citators and GRADE: Shepard's (LexisNexis) and KeyCite (Westlaw/Thomson Reuters) are subscription citator services and GRADE is a published, copyrighted method/handbook; PharmGKB data is distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0. No open licence covers the citator data itself — signals and ideas only.
good: Citators answer "does the cited claim still stand? Treatment signals (followed / questioned / caution / negative) … point-scoped flags on the claim rather than the page, and Overruling Risk: a claim resting on a superseded claim inherits 'questioned' transitively". GRADE: "every certainty grade records which domain moved it". PharmGKB: "computed evidence scores with published breakdowns, and overrides allowed only with the written justification displayed".
bad: "legal matter-file/KM literature is paywalled and was NOT verified to standard — none catalogued; citators verified via vendor + law-library guides, not live reports".
took: Wave-4 shortlist (approved under build delegation): "citation treatment signals" queues after wave-3 builds.
didnt: Board — citation treatment signals scoped to the claim rather than the page (followed / questioned / caution / negative, with a claim resting on a superseded claim inheriting 'questioned' transitively), GRADE-style recording of which domain moved a certainty grade, and PharmGKB-style computed scores with published breakdowns and overrides only with written justification. No proprietary citator code or data is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Genealogical Proof Standard / Mills 3×3 / ʿilm al-rijāl
licence: Copyrighted / no open licence stated at source: the Genealogical Proof Standard and Mills's citation classes are published, copyrighted standards and books (the BCG page opened states its material is protected by copyright, personal-study copies only, republication not permitted); the classical rijāl texts are historical works but no open licence is stated for the modern editions or survey treatment — ideas only.
good: GPS: "five-element bar for accepting a conclusion"; Mills: "3×3 citation classes (original/derivative/authored × primary/secondary/undetermined × direct/indirect/negative evidence); the independent-corroboration test (two citations sharing one informant count as one witness)". Rijāl: "grades narrators on two disjoint axes (ʿadālah/ḍabṭ) in a fixed vocabulary, checks chain continuity, hunts hidden defects (ʿillah), and runs matn criticism".
bad: All three are manual, domain-bound disciplines with no software or automation at source: the GPS bar (reasonably exhaustive research, complete citations, analysis/correlation, conflict resolution, a soundly reasoned written conclusion) is labour-intensive by design and is framed for genealogical questions; Mills's 3x3 classes assume genealogical sources and informants; ʿilm al-rijāl assumes Arabic transmitter biographies and specialist judgement, so both transfer to claim grading only by analogy.
took: Wave-4 shortlist (approved): "genealogy proof bar + citation classes + corroboration test + research log; rijāl-style two-axis source grading with matn checks".
didnt: Board — the genealogy proof bar and the 3x3 citation classes with the independent-corroboration test (two citations sharing one informant count as one witness), plus rijāl-style two-axis source grading (ʿadālah/ḍabṭ) with chain-continuity checks, hidden-defect (ʿillah) hunting and matn criticism, as a grading vocabulary for claims and sources. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

Ideas boarded; no code from these small projects is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LOCKSS / BagIt (RFC 8493) / NDSA Levels
licence: Standards and doctrine, not licensed code: BagIt is IETF RFC 8493, published under the IETF Trust's standard RFC copyright and licence terms; LOCKSS is a preservation doctrine/programme with no single code licence stated in the sources checked; the NDSA Levels are a published NDSA document (v2.0 via OSF) with no open licence stated at source. All three are usable as specifications and ideas.
good: LOCKSS doctrine: "poll the copies' hashes, repair an outvoted copy from a proven one, escalate split votes to the owner" — for copies that "are never compared". BagIt "makes the take-home zip self-verifying in someone else's hands". NDSA Levels: "a scorecard as an annual self-audit page".
bad: "the LOCKSS protocol paper wouldn't fetch (verified via the DPC); NDSA v2.1 unconfirmed against OSF (v2.0 is the verified baseline)".
took: Wave-6 shortlist (approved): "cross-copy fixity poll; BagIt take-home packaging; the NDSA scorecard" among twelve items.
didnt: Board — cross-copy fixity polling with an outvoted copy repaired from a proven one and split votes escalated to the owner (LOCKSS doctrine), BagIt packaging so a take-home export is self-verifying in someone else's hands, and the NDSA Levels as an annual self-audit scorecard. Specifications and doctrine only; no code is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OpenTimestamps / RFC 3161 TSA / minisign / age (signing pack)
licence: age: BSD-3-Clause (GitHub licence metadata and BSD-style LICENSE header at source); minisign: permissive ISC/BSD-style licence in the jedisct1/minisign repo; OpenTimestamps client code: LGPL-3.0 (python-opentimestamps) — external tool use only, never adopted as code; RFC 3161 is an IETF RFC under standard RFC terms.
good: Wave 6 build order: "OpenTimestamps anchoring of the head hash into Bitcoin (only a digest leaves); an RFC 3161 timestamp as a second anchor on the opposite trust root; minisign over artefact manifests; age-sealed key backups so the signing keys are survivable"; plus git SSH signing with in-repo allowed_signers and a C2SP checkpoint with one private witness.
bad: The pack is operationally fragmented: each anchor is a separate tool and trust root to run and monitor — OpenTimestamps proofs only become Bitcoin-anchored after calendar aggregation and block confirmation, so a proof is not instant, and an RFC 3161 token is only as trustworthy as the TSA that issued it. minisign and age protect artefacts and key backups but do nothing for the content pipeline itself, and losing an age or minisign secret key makes sealed backups unverifiable/unrecoverable.
took: Wave-6 shortlist (approved): "the signing pack — SSH commit signing, witnessed Black Box checkpoints, manifest signing; dual timestamp anchoring".
didnt: Board — dual timestamp anchoring of the head hash (OpenTimestamps into Bitcoin, plus an RFC 3161 token from a second, opposite trust root), minisign over artefact manifests, and age-sealed signing-key backups; the pack is run as external tools and specifications, not adopted as library code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ARK (?info) / DataCite tombstones / W3C Web Annotation / SKOS / Dublin Core application profiles
licence: No single licence — a standards bundle: the ARK specification is an IETF Internet-Draft subject to BCP 78 and the IETF Trust's legal provisions (copyright IETF Trust); W3C Web Annotation and SKOS are W3C documents under the W3C Document License; DCMI (Dublin Core) documents and RDF/XML schemas are CC BY 4.0; the DataCite Metadata Schema documentation states no licence at source.
good: ARK: "`?info` inflection returns a record plus a commitment statement"; DataCite: "tombstone ritual is the compiled-layer half our erasure certificates lack"; Web Annotation: "citations a dual anchor (line position + exact text quote)"; SKOS "formalises the registered tag vocabulary"; Dublin Core profiles "give the schema obligation grades (M/MA/R/O)".
bad: "no resolver was exercised live — identifier verdicts are design judgements from read specifications".
took: Wave-6 shortlist (approved): "compiled-layer tombstones + relation vocabulary; dual-anchored citation selectors; SKOS tag registry; schema as application profile".
didnt: Adopt/build — the patterns in the approved Wave-6 shortlist, implemented in our own code from the specifications: a ?info-style commitment lookup, compiled-layer tombstones with a relation vocabulary, dual-anchored citation selectors, a SKOS-style tag registry, and Dublin-Core-style obligation grades for the schema; no third-party code is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Readability Consortium studies / Atkinson Hyperlegible / Firefox Reader View / axe-core / BDA pattern
licence: Mixed bundle: Atkinson Hyperlegible — SIL Open Font License 1.1; axe-core — Mozilla Public License 2.0 (MPL-2.0); Firefox Reader View — part of Firefox, no separate licence stated on the Mozilla support pages opened; Readability Consortium papers and the BDA dyslexia pattern — no licence stated at source.
good: "the right font and spacing per reader is worth ~38 WPM on average with comprehension unchanged — and readers cannot pick their own best (80% believed their preferred font was their best; it was true for 18%)"; buildable form is a Lens reading profile "set by a timed calibration, not a settings page"; "WCAG numeric targets, the BDA dyslexia pattern (spacing beats font choice), axe-core as a smoke-suite lane, line-focus masking".
bad: Limits are visible at the sources: axe-core's own README says it finds on average only 57% of WCAG issues automatically, returning the rest as 'incomplete' where manual review is needed; Mozilla support says Reader View is limited to article/blog-like pages it can simplify and gives up on other structures; and the Readability Consortium study itself stresses that no one font fits all and that a reader's preferred font was seldom their best, so a fixed or self-chosen font cannot be assumed to work.
took: Wave-7 shortlist (approved): "a Lens reading profile by calibration + accessibility gates".
didnt: Adopt/build — a Lens reading profile set by timed calibration rather than by reader preference, with axe-core (MPL-2.0) as an automated accessibility smoke lane and WCAG numeric targets plus the BDA spacing pattern as gates, as in the approved Wave-7 shortlist. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RSVP speed displays / Bionic Reading
licence: RSVP is a long-standing presentation technique with no single licence; its best-known commercial implementation, Spritz, is proprietary and licensed to partners, and Bionic Reading is a proprietary commercial product of Bionic Reading GmbH (paid Premium plans and a licensed API) — no open licence stated at source for either product.
good: RSVP displays present one word, or a few, at a single fixed point in rapid sequence, removing the eye movements across lines that normal reading requires, and Spritz-style implementations align each word on its optimal recognition point; Bionic Reading bolds the opening letters of each word as artificial fixation points, intended to guide the eye while the brain completes the rest of the word.
bad: "Two popular reading fads are NOT FOR US with receipts: RSVP speed displays (the speed–comprehension trade-off is biological) and Bionic Reading (eye-tracking: bolding made reading slower, no subgroup benefited)."
took: Nothing taken.
didnt: NOT FOR US — reasons in BAD. Wave 10 lists "speed-reading displays" among the strongest evidenced negatives (never build).

name: Org-mode capture templates / Evernote email-in grammar / ABBYY OCR verification queue
licence: Org-mode — GPL-3.0-or-later; Evernote email-in — proprietary commercial service, no open licence stated at source; ABBYY FineReader — proprietary commercial licence (paid, activation/sales-based).
good: Org capture grammar is "the lane's most valuable idea: `%a` provenance filled by the harness, prompts only for unknowables"; Evernote grammar: "`[Title] ![date] @[notebook] #[tag]`, trailing `+` = append"; ABBYY queue: "low-confidence words with magnified image + suggestions; 'checked, kept'".
bad: Each leg carries a custody or lock-in cost visible at its source: Org capture lives inside GNU Emacs, so the grammar is inseparable from Emacs in normal use; Evernote email-in puts captured mail into a proprietary cloud account and forwarding requires a paid plan; and ABBYY FineReader is commercial, sales-gated software, so its verification queue cannot be self-hosted, inspected or audited.
took: Wave-7 shortlist (approved): "the capture-template specification with harness-filled provenance; email-in capture at the gateway inbox; an OCR verification queue".
didnt: Org-mode code not taken — GPL, specification only.

name: EPPI-Mapper / LifeFlow / Argdown / Few (bullet graphs) / Tufte sparklines
licence: Argdown — MIT; LifeFlow — CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 Unported, as stated on the UMD HCIL LifeFlow slides; EPPI-Mapper — available at no charge to EPPI-Reviewer users, no open licence stated at source; Few's bullet graphs and Tufte's sparklines are published design forms, no licence stated at source.

bad: Limits at the sources: EPPI-Mapper only consumes an exported JSON file from EPPI-Reviewer in an exact format — its own page warns the map will not work if the coding structure changes and a template cannot be reused for another project unless the data structures are identical; LifeFlow is a 2011 UMD HCIL research prototype, later superseded by the separately licensed EventFlow, not maintained product software; and Argdown's image export depends on headless Chrome/Chromium, which its API documentation flags as liable to cause problems in some Linux installations.
took: Wave-7 shortlist (approved): "state-shaped views — the evidence-and-gap matrix, claim-history aggregation, Argdown maps; the Briefing honesty stack".
didnt: Adopt/build — the state-shaped views from the approved Wave-7 shortlist (evidence-and-gap matrix, claim-lifecycle aggregation, Argdown argument maps) plus the briefing honesty stack, built in our own code; Argdown's MIT code is the only part eligible for direct reuse, and LifeFlow (CC BY-NC-ND) is taken as an idea only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Histography / Gource / word clouds
licence: Gource — GNU General Public License version 3.0 (GPLv3), per its project licence/man-page copyright notice; Histography — a one-off design project, no licence stated at source; word clouds are a generic visualisation form implemented by many libraries under their own licences, no single licence at source.
good: Histography renders Wikipedia's historical events as an interactive dot timeline spanning about 14 billion years, each dot clickable through to the event with category filtering and adjustable time ranges; Gource renders a source-control repository's history as an animated tree — directories as branches, files as leaves, developers appearing as they contribute — with built-in log generation for Git, Mercurial, Bazaar and SVN; word clouds render a text with each word's size proportional to its frequency, giving an at-a-glance summary of its terms.
bad: "Rejected precisely because their beauty is the lie: Histography dot-density (density reads as importance), Gource (activity as progress), word clouds (length-confounded)."

name: NASA LLIS / Dan Luu failure taxonomy (failure literature)
licence: No licence stated at source for either: the GAO/NASA material is a US federal government publication carrying no licence statement on the pages opened, and Dan Luu's post-mortems GitHub repository states no licence at source.
good: NASA LLIS is NASA's official agency-wide repository for lessons learned: lessons are screened for relevance and for sensitive or proprietary content before entry, and the system held over 900 lessons spanning programme management through technical causes of failure, searchable by NASA users. Dan Luu's post-mortems collection aggregates hundreds of real incident reports from many companies into failure categories in one searchable place, so cross-company failure patterns can be studied together.
bad: LLIS: "GAO found mandated users didn't use it (search drowned in irrelevant lessons; negative lessons withheld for reputational fear); the 2012 OIG audit — ~$750k/yr, ~1 lesson/yr from most centers — concluded it 'is not an effective tool'". Luu taxonomy: "'Uncategorized' (230+) dwarfs every curated category — categorisation costs effort at ingest".
took: Wave-8 shortlist (approved) includes "post-mortem action-item discipline" and related failure-derived items.
didnt: Corroboration — a documented failure of a lessons database that mandated users would not use confirms our design direction: lessons must surface at the point of work under post-mortem action-item discipline rather than sit in a passive repository, and ingest-time categorisation must stay cheap, because Luu's 'Uncategorized' bucket (230+) dwarfs every curated category. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RAGTruth / Tow Center citation study / Xie et al. memorisation / AbstentionBench / AgentPoison / MINJA
licence: Papers and reports with no single licence: no licence is stated on the arXiv paper pages opened for RAGTruth, AbstentionBench, AgentPoison or MINJA, and the Tow Center citation study is a Columbia Journalism Review publication with no open licence stated at source.
good: Together they supply the field's measurement instruments: RAGTruth contributes nearly 18,000 naturally generated, word-level-annotated RAG responses for benchmarking hallucination frequency and detection methods; AbstentionBench evaluates abstention across 20 datasets and 20 frontier LLMs; the Tow Center study field-tests eight generative search engines on their ability to retrieve and cite news accurately; and AgentPoison and MINJA are reproducible red-team attacks on RAG memory and knowledge bases, AgentPoison reporting over 80% average attack success at under 0.1% poisoning and MINJA 98.2% injection success through query-only interaction.
bad: "RAGTruth: 43.1% of responses carry ≥1 hallucinated span"; "Tow Center: >60% incorrect; 154/200 Grok-3 citations pointed at error pages"; Xie et al.: "GPT-4's memorisation ratio at 80% on popular questions"; AbstentionBench: abstention "degrades with reasoning fine-tuning (−24% average)"; "AgentPoison ≥80% success at <0.1% poison through the ordinary write path; MINJA 98.2% with query access only".
took: Wave-8 shortlist (approved): "a knowledge-conflict eval slice + strongest-source-first packing; abstention as a regression-tested property; a retrieval-anomaly security signal".
didnt: Adopt/build — the evaluation uses in the approved Wave-8 shortlist, built into our own eval harness: a knowledge-conflict eval slice with strongest-source-first packing, abstention as a regression-tested property, and a retrieval-anomaly security signal modelled on the AgentPoison and MINJA results; the papers themselves are taken as evidence, and no paper code is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ICD 203 / ACH / Team B (1976) / Klein premortem / Brier scoring
licence: no licence stated at source — the ICD 203 directive text opened at dni.gov contains no licence statement; the companion items in this lane (Heuer's ACH, the 1976 Team B exercise, Klein's premortem article and Brier's scoring paper) are published works that likewise show no open licence at their sources

good: A persistent, file-based project brain for coding agents (578 stars, 57 commits, 5 releases, version 0.4.1) defined as an open, agent-agnostic file contract: a BRAIN.md protocol file plus a brain/ directory of plain Markdown in the repo, read and written only through one zero-dependency Node CLI, so any agent that can read BRAIN.md can use it across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Pi. Each page pairs a rewritable compiled_truth (current best understanding) with an append-only timeline (chain of evidence), and update-truth rewrites the truth and appends its timeline entry in one atomic write, so understanding cannot change without a trace — the page calls this correct-by-construction, with frontmatter always generated by the CLI and no validator needed. It enforces exactly one brain per project (location resolved by the CLI, redirectable via brainRoot, never a shadow brain), wires only a marked block into CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, offers SessionStart hooks limited to an 8 KiB metadata snapshot, and applies a clear inclusion test: will this still matter in six months and is it hard to reconstruct from code itself.
bad: Project-scoped coding memory only — decisions, requirements and constraints for a code repo, not a general knowledge wiki with sources and syntheses. All writes must go through the brain CLI and hand-editing brain files is prohibited by its protocol, which conflicts with a human-edits-Markdown wiki workflow, and its Codex hooks require Codex CLI 0.153.4+, Node 18+ and a POSIX shell (native Windows shells unsupported), with hook commands embedding an absolute project path that must be uninstalled before moving a project.
